questions.title: Autumn 2023 · Part 1 · Question 1
questions.promptMarkdown:
Question 1:
The market is an important institution in a capitalist economic system. Which of the
following statements characterizes the market as an institution?
options: The buyer often gets the worse deal – it's the firms who profit from market transactions in a capitalist system.
Transactions in a market are based on voluntariness. Therefore, both buyer and seller benefit from market transactions.
In a market system, it's the firms that decide what we buy – consumer interests come second.
In a capitalist economic system, everything (unfortunately, some say) can be bought and sold for money.
hints: Think about why both parties voluntarily agree to a market transaction.
Compare each party’s gain with their own next-best alternative; the two gains need not be equal.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Question 1:
The market is an important institution in a capitalist economic system. Which of the
following statements characterizes the market as an institution?
• The buyer often gets the worse deal – it's the firms who profit from market
transactions in a capitalist system.
• Transactions in a market are based on voluntariness. Therefore, both buyer and
seller benefit from market transactions.
• In a market system, it's the firms that decide what we buy – consumer interests
come second.
• In a capitalist economic system, everything (unfortunately, some say) can be bought
and sold for money.

questions.title: Autumn 2023 · Part 1 · Question 2
questions.promptMarkdown:
Question 2:
GDP per capita is often used to measure economic growth and differences in living
standards between countries. However, many criticize this measure for omitting important
factors affecting living standards. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: GDP only captures the value of what is traded in private markets. Since the value of public healthcare and free public schools is not included, we should be cautious using GDP as a measure of living standards.

Production activity can have strong negative environmental effects. The costs of environmental degradation are often not counted in how we measure GDP, so we risk overstating growth in living standards if we only look at changes in GDP per capita.
GDP only captures producer surplus (firm profits), and says little about the value of production for consumers.
It is impossible to know what GDP was in the late 1800s and early 1900s. Such statistics don’t exist, and therefore we can’t know if living standards were higher then or now.
hints: Start by distinguishing recorded production from overall wellbeing.
Consider environmental damage, unpaid work, income distribution and how public services are valued. Explain the limitation rather than just naming it.

Question 7:
Which of the following statements is false?
options: Market equilibrium in competitive markets is characterized by everyone who wants to buy the product at the market price finding a seller.

questions.title: Autumn 2023 · Part 2 · Question 1
questions.promptMarkdown:
Question 1:
Assume a person has preferences for two things: consumption and number of leisure hours
per day. These preferences can be represented by indifference curves. Briefly explain what
such indifference curves show.
rubricChecks: Verify key point: Grading guide: An indifference curve shows all combinations of consumption and leisure hours that a person considers equally good.
Verify key point: By “equally good,” we mean that they provide the person with the same level of utility.
Verify key point: Thus, every point on an indifference curve represents a different combination of consumption and leisure that gives the person the same level of utility.
hints: Think of several bundles of consumption and free time that someone judges equally good.
One indifference curve represents one utility level. Its slope describes the local willingness to trade the two goods; other curves represent other utility levels.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Grading guide:
An indifference curve shows all combinations of consumption and leisure hours that a
person considers equally good. By “equally good,” we mean that they provide the person
with the same level of utility. Thus, every point on an indifference curve represents a
different combination of consumption and leisure that gives the person the same level of
utility.
Points will be deducted if it is clear from the answer that the student believes there is only
one indifference curve. There are many – in fact, infinitely many – indifference curves. The
student does not need to explicitly state that there are several in order to receive full credit.
What matters is that the answer does not leave the impression that each person has only
one such indifference curve.

questions.title: Autumn 2023 · Part 2 · Question 2
questions.promptMarkdown:
Question 2:
In competitive markets, the price is determined by both the supply and demand curves.
Some markets experience strong seasonal shifts in the demand curve (e.g., between winter
and summer), but not all such markets show large seasonal changes in prices. Briefly
explain what determines the size of price changes due to seasonal shifts in demand.
rubricChecks: Verify key point: Grading guide: The supply curve shows how much firms wish to produce and sell at different price levels.
Verify key point: The supply curve is often drawn as an upward-sloping curve, which means that supply increases when the price increases.
Verify key point: This must in turn imply that firms’ marginal cost increases as production rises.
hints: Sketch the same outward demand shift against two differently sloped supply curves.
Compare how much quantity can expand following a small price increase. Explain why more responsive supply can accommodate a demand shift with a smaller price change.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Grading guide:
The supply curve shows how much firms wish to produce and sell at different price levels.
The supply curve is often drawn as an upward-sloping curve, which means that supply
increases when the price increases. This must in turn imply that firms’ marginal cost
increases as production rises.
If the demand curve shifts outward (such a shift can correctly be described in several ways:
a positive shift, a shift upward, or a shift to the “right”), the equilibrium price will be pushed
up so that price again balances demand and supply. How large the price increase will be
depends on how steep the supply curve is. If the supply curve is almost flat, a small price
increase will lead to a large increase in supply. In such a situation, the equilibrium price will
vary little between seasons.
If, on the other hand, the supply curve is steep, large price increases are needed for the
supplied quantity to increase significantly. In such a situation, prices will vary a lot between
seasons.
An answer that clearly explains the relationship between the steepness (slope) of the
supply curve and seasonal price variations will receive a very good evaluation. A small
“bonus point” may be given if the student also connects this to marginal costs, although
that is not required for a strong grade.

questions.title: Spring 2024 · Part 2 · Question 1
questions.promptMarkdown:
Question 1: Explain what the marginal rate of substitution tells us about a person’s
preferences.
rubricChecks: Verify key point: It reflects preferences and depends on the current combination of consumption and leisure.
State the utility/budget trade-off (MRS vs. MRT) clearly
Explain the direction of quantity/hours adjustment and intuition
hints: Read MRS as a local willingness to exchange the two goods.
With free time on x and consumption on y, MRS is the magnitude of the indifference-curve slope: consumption willingly given up per extra free hour, holding utility fixed.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Grading Guide:
The marginal rate of substitution (MRS) between consumption and leisure shows how
much consumption a person is willing to give up for one additional hour of leisure while
maintaining the same utility level. It reflects preferences and depends on the current
combination of consumption and leisure.

questions.title: Spring 2024 · Part 2 · Question 2
questions.promptMarkdown:
Question 2: Explain what we mean by the economic value of having a job ('employment
rent').
rubricChecks: Verify key point: Grading Guide: Employment rent is the difference between the net value of being employed and the next- best alternative, usually unemployment.
Verify key point: A job provides benefits such as income, social contact, and fulfillment, but also costs like effort and stress.
Verify key point: Unemployment provides more leisure but comes with disadvantages like uncertainty.
hints: Compare net wellbeing in the job with the next-best available alternative.
Include wages and job benefits, effort/stress costs, and the benefits and costs of unemployment. Explain how benefits or the ease of finding a new job alter the difference.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Grading Guide:
Employment rent is the difference between the net value of being employed and the next-
best alternative, usually unemployment. A job provides benefits such as income, social
contact, and fulfillment, but also costs like effort and stress. Unemployment provides more
leisure but comes with disadvantages like uncertainty. Employment rent equals the
difference between these net values. It decreases if unemployment benefits rise, if work
becomes more demanding, or if job prospects improve.

The indifference curve shows the lowest level of consumption you can manage on, i.e. the income that just covers your basic needs.

One indifference curve represents one utility level. Its slope describes the local willingness to trade the two goods; other curves represent other utility levels.

questions.title: Autumn 2024 · Part 2 · Question 2
questions.promptMarkdown:
Question 2:
In the course we have studied a person's optimal choice between two goods — consumption and
free time. Explain what is meant by the concept of indifference curves, and what these say about a
person's preferences.
rubricChecks: Verify key point: An indifference curve illustrates all combinations of two goods that a person regards as equally good.
Verify key point: The slope of the indifference curve tells us how much consumption the person is willing to give up to obtain one more unit of free time.
Verify key point: The slope varies depending on the situation the person is in, i.e.
hints: Think of several bundles of consumption and free time that someone judges equally good.
One indifference curve represents one utility level. Its slope describes the local willingness to trade the two goods; other curves represent other utility levels.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Examiner guidance:
An indifference curve illustrates all combinations of two goods that a person regards as equally
good.
The slope of the indifference curve tells us how much consumption the person is willing to give up to
obtain one more unit of free time. The slope varies depending on the situation the person is in, i.e.
how much free time and consumption the person has. The slope of the indifference curve is also
called the marginal rate of substitution (MRS).
Since preferences are personal, different people will have different indifference curves.
A good answer demonstrates understanding by mentioning some of the central properties of
indifference curves:
• The indifference curve between consumption and free time slopes downward because the
person likes both goods — both free time and consumption — and because more of one
good can compensate for less of the other. All else equal (ceteris paribus), the person will
value more free time (which means less work), but this also means they can manage with
less consumption without their level of utility falling.
• Each indifference curve shows a particular level of utility. Indifference curves that lie
“further out” represent a higher level of utility, while indifference curves that lie further in
towards the origin give a lower level of utility. Free time and consumption are two goods, i.e.
something we like and will always like to have more of (“the more the better”).

• As we move to the right along an indifference curve, it becomes flatter. This is because the
scarcer one good becomes relative to the other, the less willing one is to trade away
consumption for yet more free time.

questions.title: Autumn 2024 · Part 2 · Question 3
questions.promptMarkdown:
Question 3:
Explain what is meant by the concept of marginal cost. Why will a firm in a competitive market
produce the quantity that makes marginal cost equal to the price?
rubricChecks: Verify key point: A good answer defines marginal cost precisely, and brings out the significance of the firm having to take the market price as given.
Verify key point: Marginal cost means the cost of increasing production “a little”, e.g.
Verify key point: A firm in a competitive market must take the market price as given (is a price-taker) and cannot influence it.
hints: Marginal cost concerns producing a little more, rather than total cost or average cost.
Compare the extra unit’s revenue with its cost when P > MC and when P < MC. Use those comparisons to explain the profit-maximising stopping point.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Examiner guidance:
A good answer defines marginal cost precisely, and brings out the significance of the firm having to
take the market price as given.
Marginal cost means the cost of increasing production “a little”, e.g. by one unit. A firm in a
competitive market must take the market price as given (is a price-taker) and cannot influence it.
The firm can sell as many units as it wishes at the market price p*.
If the market price is higher than the marginal cost, it means the firm can increase its profit by
producing more. Why? Because the increase in revenue from producing one more unit (which equals
the market price) is greater than the increase in cost from producing one more unit (which equals
the marginal cost).
If, on the other hand, the market price is lower than the marginal cost, it means the firm can
increase its profit by producing less. Why? Because the reduction in costs from producing one unit
less is greater than the reduction in revenue from producing one unit less. In other words — for all
the units where marginal cost is higher than price, the cost of producing those units is higher than
the revenue.
The firm can therefore maximise its profit only by producing up to the quantity that makes marginal
cost equal to the price.

questions.title: Autumn 2024 · Part 3 · d)
questions.promptMarkdown:
d) Discuss the validity of the following claim: “Trade unions play an important role in the Norwegian
model, but even strong unions with many members are unable to push up the real-wage level in the
economy.”
questions.contextMarkdown:
Part 3
This part consists of several sub-questions. All sub-questions must be answered. You have one text
field per sub-question. No word limit is set in this part, but that does not mean you necessarily have
to write a lot to give good answers.
In the course we have described the supply side of the economy using a so-called price-setting curve
and a wage-setting curve. The figure below illustrates both of these, as well as the equilibrium in the
economy.
rubricChecks: Verify key point: 2.5 of CORE Macroeconomics.
Verify key point: Figure 2.16 is intended only as support, and the student does not have the opportunity to explain using figures.
Verify key point: Bargaining effect: Trade unions have power because they can take their members out on strike, something firms want to avoid.
hints: Treat the union’s bargaining effect and its voice/motivation effect separately.
Consider how each affects WS, then find the new intersection with unchanged horizontal PS. Distinguish changes in nominal wage demands from the equilibrium real wage.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Suggested solution:
This claim is correct. A good answer brings out the two effects we have studied in the course, the
“bargaining effect” and the “motivation effect / voice effect”, which are explained in ch. 2.5 of CORE
Macroeconomics. Figure 2.16 is intended only as support, and the student does not have the
opportunity to explain using figures.
Bargaining effect:
Trade unions have power because they can take their members out on strike, something firms want
to avoid. They thus have the power to push wages above what is required to get workers to exert
effort. That would give a wage-setting curve higher up than the original one. In the model, this gives
a new equilibrium with an unchanged real wage and higher structural unemployment in equilibrium.
“Motivation effect”:
Trade unions contribute to cooperation on things other than just wages, for example the working
environment, working hours, strategy, and solutions for downsizing. This suggests that unions give
workers a say in decision-making, which can produce a so-called “voice effect”. In Norwegian this
can be translated as a “motivation effect” that can increase job satisfaction. The workers will then

exert effort for a lower wage than before, which shifts the wage-setting curve down. If this effect
dominates, we get a new equilibrium with lower unemployment, but here too an unchanged real
wage.
The explanations the model gives us are thus that strong unions can affect wage-setting, and
thereby structural unemployment, but not the real wage in equilibrium. The claim therefore holds.
A good answer brings out both of these effects and the fact that the real wage in equilibrium remains
unchanged. Some credit is given if only one of the effects is mentioned. Good credit is also given if it
is explained that unions can force through nominal wage increases, but that these are “eaten up” by
price increases in firms that bring the economy back to the real wage determined by the price-setting
curve.

questions.title: Autumn 2024 · Part 3 · e)
questions.promptMarkdown:
e) Based on your understanding of the model illustrated above with the price- and wage-setting
curves, what can produce a higher real wage in the economy's equilibrium? Justify your answer.
questions.contextMarkdown:
Part 3
This part consists of several sub-questions. All sub-questions must be answered. You have one text
field per sub-question. No word limit is set in this part, but that does not mean you necessarily have
to write a lot to give good answers.
In the course we have described the supply side of the economy using a so-called price-setting curve
and a wage-setting curve. The figure below illustrates both of these, as well as the equilibrium in the
economy.
rubricChecks: Verify key point: In the model there are two factors that determine the level of the real wage in equilibrium.
Verify key point: 1) Productivity If workers become more productive, total value creation (output) per worker increases.
Verify key point: The price- setting curve shows how this value is distributed between the worker (as the real wage) and the firms' owners (as profit).
hints: In the standard diagram, which curve determines the equilibrium real wage?
Think about output per worker and firms’ pricing margin. Hold competition fixed when analysing higher productivity; distinguish a margin or share from a total profit amount.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Suggested solution:
In the model there are two factors that determine the level of the real wage in equilibrium.
1) Productivity
If workers become more productive, total value creation (output) per worker increases. The price-
setting curve shows how this value is distributed between the worker (as the real wage) and the
firms' owners (as profit). For a given competitive situation (i.e. the same profit share as before),
increased productivity will cause the price-setting curve to shift up, and thereby cause the real wage
to increase. Reduced costs (as a result of increased productivity) will lead firms to reduce prices, and
this is what explains the rise in the real wage: a lower price level gives higher real wages.
2) Competition
Increased competition among firms in the economy squeezes firms' margins — they will compete
more intensely. This reduces the share of value creation per employee that goes to owners as profit,
and the price-setting curve therefore shifts up, which causes real wages to increase. Firms reduce
prices as a result of increased competition, and this is what explains the rise in the real wage: a
lower price level gives higher real wages.
A good answer brings out both of these, and half credit is given if one of them is mentioned.

questions.title: Spring 2025 · Part 2 · Question 1
questions.promptMarkdown:
Question 1:
You are considering spending three hours studying for an exam. Your next-best alternative is to work
these 3 hours and earn NOK 600. You value the work effort as a cost of NOK 200, and studying gives
you a perceived gain of NOK 1,000 but has a mental cost that you value at NOK 300. Briefly explain
what is meant by opportunity cost and economic rent. What is the economic rent from choosing to
study in this example?
rubricChecks: Verify key point: A good answer defines opportunity cost and economic rent precisely.
Verify key point: To receive full credit, the student must in addition correctly explain how they arrive at the economic rent being NOK 300.
Verify key point: The net gain from studying is: 1,000 − 300 = NOK 700.
hints: Compute the net payoff from the forgone work, subtracting effort cost from pay.
For studying, compare its net value with that forgone net payoff. In the short-answer calculation also subtract the mental cost from the study benefit.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Examiner guidance:
A good answer defines opportunity cost and economic rent precisely. To receive full credit, the
student must in addition correctly explain how they arrive at the economic rent being NOK 300.
The economic rent is the difference between the net gain of the chosen option (studying) and the
opportunity cost (the value of the best option that was given up, i.e. working).
The net gain from studying is: 1,000 − 300 = NOK 700.
The net gain from working is: 600 − 200 = NOK 400.
The opportunity cost of studying is therefore NOK 400, and the economic rent is 700 − 400 = NOK
300.

obsidianLink.heading: 2.1 Opportunity Cost, Reservation Options, and Economic Rent

questions.title: Spring 2025 · Part 2 · Question 2
questions.promptMarkdown:
Question 2:
In firms there is generally a separation between the owners and the employees. Explain why this
separation can create challenges for how well the firm performs.
rubricChecks: Verify key point: In a firm, the owners care about employees working hard and contributing to the firm performing well.
Verify key point: This is because employment contracts are incomplete, and because employees have more information about their own effort than the owners do (asymmetric information).
Verify key point: Employees may therefore have incentives to work less than desired, especially if they are not monitored or rewarded for their effort.
hints: Owners and employees can have different objectives, and effort can be difficult to verify.
Use principal, agent, asymmetric information and incomplete contracts to explain why desired effort cannot simply be guaranteed by writing a contract.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Examiner guidance:
In a firm, the owners care about employees working hard and contributing to the firm performing
well. But since effort is often difficult to observe, a principal–agent problem can arise: the owners
(the principal) want particular behaviour from the employees (the agents) but cannot fully ensure
this through a contract. This is because employment contracts are incomplete, and because
employees have more information about their own effort than the owners do (asymmetric
information). Employees may therefore have incentives to work less than desired, especially if they
are not monitored or rewarded for their effort.
A good answer clearly explains what is meant by the separation between owners and employees, and
demonstrates a good understanding of the principal–agent problem, ideally using relevant concepts
such as asymmetric information and incomplete contracts, and how this can create challenges for
companies' performance.

questions.title: Spring 2025 · Part 2 · Question 3
questions.promptMarkdown:
Question 3:
Explain what is meant by gross domestic product (GDP), and reflect on some central challenges with
this measure that we have discussed in the course.
rubricChecks: Verify key point: GDP (gross domestic product) is the value of all finished production of goods and services in a country during a period, usually a year, valued at market prices.
Verify key point: It is a standard measure for tracking economic developments over time and for making comparisons of economic development.
Verify key point: The answer should further reflect on weaknesses of GDP as a measure of welfare.
hints: Start by distinguishing recorded production from overall wellbeing.
Consider environmental damage, unpaid work, income distribution and how public services are valued. Explain the limitation rather than just naming it.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Examiner guidance:
GDP (gross domestic product) is the value of all finished production of goods and services in a
country during a period, usually a year, valued at market prices. It is a standard measure for tracking
economic developments over time and for making comparisons of economic development.

The answer should further reflect on weaknesses of GDP as a measure of welfare. In the course we
have discussed several factors, and a good answer should include several of these.
GDP says nothing about how income and wealth are distributed in the population, or about the
environmental consequences of production — polluting activity can increase GDP even though it in
practice reduces quality of life. Another point is that unpaid work, such as childcare in the home or
voluntary work, is not captured in GDP, even though it creates value. It can also be pointed out that
value creation in the public sector is measured at production costs, not market values, which makes
it difficult to assess actual value creation.

questions.title: Spring 2025 · Part 3 · b)
questions.promptMarkdown:
b) Give an economic explanation of why the wage-setting curve is drawn as an upward-sloping curve
in this way.
questions.contextMarkdown:
Part 3
In this part you are given several questions related to the same theme. All questions must be
answered. There is no upper limit on the number of words per question, as there was in Part 2. That
does not mean it is necessary to write a long text to answer well, but you should emphasise
justifying your answers as well as you can.
You have already seen the figure below in Part 1; it shows an economy with an equilibrium point A:
The vertical axis shows the real wage and the worker's productivity (“output per worker”), while the
horizontal axis shows the level of employment and thereby also unemployment.
rubricChecks: Verify key point: The wage-setting curve shows the level of real wage that firms must offer in order for workers to have an incentive to exert effort, for each level of employment.
Verify key point: It is based on the idea that workers compare the wage they receive in the job with the alternative, i.e.
Verify key point: the value of being unemployed.
hints: Start with what happens to the worker’s fallback when unemployment falls.
Trace lower unemployment → easier replacement job → smaller loss from dismissal at a given wage → higher wage needed to secure effort. This explains WS’s slope.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Examiner guidance:
A good answer reflects that the student understands that the wage-setting curve shows the real
wage required for workers to exert effort, and how the degree of unemployment or employment
affects this.
The wage-setting curve shows the level of real wage that firms must offer in order for workers to
have an incentive to exert effort, for each level of employment. It is based on the idea that workers
compare the wage they receive in the job with the alternative, i.e. the value of being unemployed.
This alternative is called the reservation wage and includes, among other things, unemployment
benefits, free time, and the probability of getting a new job.
When unemployment is high, it is difficult to find a new job, and the reservation wage is therefore
low. Then firms can offer a relatively low real wage and still get workers to exert effort, because the
cost of losing the job is high. But when unemployment is low, it is easy to find a new job, and the
reservation wage increases. To avoid employees quitting or shirking, firms must in such situations
offer a higher real wage. Therefore the real wage required to ensure effort from workers increases
as unemployment falls, which is reflected in the upward-sloping wage-setting curve.

unchanged if unemployment benefit increases.
questions.contextMarkdown:
Part 3
In this part you are given several questions related to the same theme. All questions must be
answered. There is no upper limit on the number of words per question, as there was in Part 2. That
does not mean it is necessary to write a long text to answer well, but you should emphasise
justifying your answers as well as you can.
You have already seen the figure below in Part 1; it shows an economy with an equilibrium point A:
The vertical axis shows the real wage and the worker's productivity (“output per worker”), while the
horizontal axis shows the level of employment and thereby also unemployment.
rubricChecks: Verify key point: If unemployment benefit increases, the economic loss from being unemployed becomes smaller.
Verify key point: It must then be briefly explained that firms must respond by offering a higher real wage to keep workers sufficiently motivated to exert effort.
Verify key point: The WS curve shows, as explained in b), the real-wage level that is just sufficient to get workers to exert effort.
hints: Higher benefits change how costly losing a job is to the worker.

questions.solutionMarkdown:
Examiner guidance:
If unemployment benefit increases, the economic loss from being unemployed becomes smaller. It
must then be briefly explained that firms must respond by offering a higher real wage to keep
workers sufficiently motivated to exert effort. The WS curve shows, as explained in b), the real-wage
level that is just sufficient to get workers to exert effort. If unemployment benefit increases, the WS
curve will therefore shift up: for a given level of employment, the real wage will be higher than

questions.title: Autumn 2025 · Part 2 · Question 1
questions.promptMarkdown:
Question 1:
Explain how a wage increase gives rise to an income effect and a substitution effect.
rubricChecks: Verify key point: When the wage increases, both a substitution effect and an income effect arise.
Verify key point: At the same time, a higher wage gives greater purchasing power for a given amount of work, so one can afford more free time.
Verify key point: This is the income effect, which pulls in the opposite direction and reduces the labour supply.
hints: Separate becoming able to afford more consumption/free time from the change in free time’s opportunity cost.
A higher net wage creates an income effect toward more normal free time and a substitution effect toward less. Explain the net outcome through their relative strengths.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Examiner guidance: When the wage increases, both a substitution effect and an income effect arise.
The substitution effect means that free time becomes relatively more expensive — each hour of free
time costs more in forgone wages — and therefore the person will want to work more. At the same
time, a higher wage gives greater purchasing power for a given amount of work, so one can afford
more free time. This is the income effect, which pulls in the opposite direction and reduces the labour
supply. The overall effect on the labour supply depends on which of the effects dominates. If the
substitution effect is stronger, the labour supply increases, whereas if the income effect is stronger, it
decreases.

obsidianLink.heading: 3.3 Income and Substitution Effects of Wage and Tax Changes

questions.title: Autumn 2025 · Part 2 · Question 2
questions.promptMarkdown:
Question 2:
Maria earns NOK 120 per hour in her current job and works 35 hours per week. The discomfort /
stress cost of working corresponds to a cost of NOK 20 per hour. If she loses her job, she will receive
unemployment benefit equivalent to NOK 40 per hour. In addition, unemployment has psychological
and social costs equivalent to NOK 10 per hour. Assume that Maria's planning horizon is 156 weeks,
and that if Maria becomes unemployed she expects to find a new job with the same hourly wage
and the same effort cost after 44 weeks. Explain what is meant by the economic value of the job
(employment rent). What is the economic value of the current job for Maria?
Important: Explain how you arrived at this. You can in fact receive credit even if you arrive at the
wrong number, provided we can see that you have “reasoned correctly”.
rubricChecks: Verify key point: The economic value of the job shows the gain one obtains from being in work, compared with the next-best alternative.
Verify key point: Employment rent: NOK 70/hour × 35 hours × 44 weeks = NOK 107,800.
Identify the incomplete-contract / asymmetric-information mechanism
hints: Calculate the net hourly value in employment and in unemployment separately.
Find their difference, multiply by 35 hours/week and the 44 weeks before the identical replacement job. Ask why the payoffs after that point cancel despite the longer horizon.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Examiner guidance:
The economic value of the job shows the gain one obtains from being in work, compared with the
next-best alternative. To find the economic value of the current job for Maria, we must compare the
net value of being in the job with the net value of her next-best alternative, which is to be
unemployed and search for a new job:
Step 1: The net value of having a job
Maria earns NOK 120 per hour, but experiences an effort cost of NOK 20 per hour.
Net income in work per hour = 120 − 20 = NOK 100
Step 2: The net value of being unemployed
She receives NOK 40 per hour in benefits, but has psychological and social costs of NOK 10 per hour.
Net income when unemployed per hour = 40 − 10 = NOK 30
Step 3: The difference (employment rent per hour)
The value of having the job = 100 − 30 = NOK 70 per hour
Step 4: Total value of the job (over the whole period)
Maria works 35 hours per week and has a planning horizon of 156 weeks, but expects to be
unemployed for 44 weeks if she loses her job. She therefore compares the present value of continuing
in work for 156 weeks with the value of being unemployed for 44 weeks + then being in a new job (at
the same net wage) for 112 weeks.
Employment rent: NOK 70/hour × 35 hours × 44 weeks = NOK 107,800.

obsidianLink.heading: 4.2 Employment Rent and the Cost of Job Loss

questions.promptMarkdown:
Question 3:
Earlier this autumn, NRK reported that the prices of nuts have shot up, with sharp price jumps. The
price per kilo is said to have reached almost NOK 900. Assume that the market for nuts can be
described as a perfectly competitive market. You are not expected to demonstrate knowledge of the
nut market itself, but, based on what you have learned in this course, briefly explain possible causes
of the price jump. There may be several causes — not just one.
rubricChecks: Verify key point: In a perfectly competitive market, the price is determined by supply and demand.
Verify key point: A sharp price increase for nuts may be due to supply having fallen (i.e.
Verify key point: the supply curve shifts to the left in a quantity–price diagram), demand having risen (i.e.
hints: Start from the competitive-market intersection of supply and demand.
Sketch a possible demand increase and a possible supply decrease separately. Give plausible drivers of each, and explain why the price rise alone cannot identify the cause.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Examiner guidance: In a perfectly competitive market, the price is determined by supply and demand.
A sharp price increase for nuts may be due to supply having fallen (i.e. the supply curve shifts to the
left in a quantity–price diagram), demand having risen (i.e. the demand curve shifts to the right), or
both. Poor harvests and/or higher production costs can cause the supply curve to shift to the left. At
the same time, increased demand — for example, due to seasonality or changing consumer trends
(nuts are healthy!) — can move the demand curve to the right. Both types of change will lead to a

higher equilibrium price. A strong price jump often indicates that both supply and demand have
contributed to the change.

In the course we have described the supply side of the economy using a so-called price-setting curve
and a wage-setting curve. The figure below illustrates both of these. We have often referred to this
as the “WS–PS model”.
rubricChecks: Verify key point: In the WS–PS model, the effect of coordinated wage-setting can be illustrated by the wage-setting curve (WS) shifting downward.

questions.solutionMarkdown:
Examiner guidance: In the WS–PS model, the effect of coordinated wage-setting can be illustrated by
the wage-setting curve (WS) shifting downward. When wages are set in a coordinated manner, as in
the frontfag model, the parties take into account competitiveness and unemployment in the
economy as a whole. This gives more moderate wage growth at each level of unemployment, so that
equilibrium unemployment falls. The PS curve, which reflects productivity and firms' price-setting,
does not change. The result is a new equilibrium point where WS and PS cross at higher employment
and lower unemployment. Thus countries with coordinated wage-setting can achieve lower
unemployment than countries with uncoordinated wage-setting.

questions.promptMarkdown:
Problem 3
Below you see figure 1.8b from Core Microeconomics. It shows a production function.
a) Explain what is meant by the concept of a production function.
b) How many thousand kilograms of grain are produced when the number of farmers is 800
and 1600, respectively?
c) Explain what is meant by average productivity. At which of the points, A or B, is the
average productivity highest?
d) In your own words, explain what is meant by diminishing average productivity.
Exercise 1.11 fra CORE
Exercise 1.11 in CORE is intended for individual exploration and reflection. Question 1 has a definitive
answer, but question 2 will vary from person to person.
rubricChecks: Address a) Explain what is meant by the concept of a production function
Address b) How many thousand kilograms of grain are produced when the number of farmers is 800 and 1600, respectively
Address c) Explain what is meant by average productivity
Address d) In your own words, explain what is meant by diminishing average productivity
hints: Read total output from the height of the production function, then divide by labour for average productivity.

Compare output/labour at A and B; the slope from the origin measures that ratio. Falling average productivity can occur while total output continues rising. Use the textbook for the separately referenced CORE task.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Exercise 3
a) A production function describes the relationship between input (resources used in
production) and output (results). In this case, the function shows the relationship between
number of farmers and kilograms of grain produced. From the figure:
- At 800 farmers, 500,000 kg of grain is produced.
- At 1,600 farmers, 778,000 kg is produced.
b) Average productivity is the output per unit of input—in this case, kg per farmer:
- At Point A: 500,000 / 800 = 625 kg per farmer
- At Point B: 778,000 / 1,600 = 486.25 kg per farmer
So average productivity is higher at A than at B.
c) Diminishing average productivity means that as we add more input (e.g., more farmers),
each additional input contributes less output per unit. Total output increases, but
productivity per worker decreases.
This is evident here: total grain increases, but the grain per farmer falls as the number of
farmers rises from 800 to 1,600.

Excercise 1.11 from CORE
Note: This answer is based on the online version available in August 2024 and uses Norway as an
example. Answers will vary by country and data.
1. Earth Overshoot Day is the day of the year when humanity has consumed all the resources
that Earth can regenerate in a year. The rest of the year we live on "natural credit"—
depleting resource stocks.
The calculation is based on data about demand for:
- Plant-based food and fiber
- Meat and fish
- Timber and other forest products
- Land for infrastructure (roads, buildings)
- Forests’ ability to absorb CO₂ emissions
This is called the ecological footprint, which is compared to the planet’s renewable resource capacity.
If we use more than Earth can regenerate, Overshoot Day comes earlier in the year.
Example:
- If our ecological footprint equals Earth's renewable resources → Overshoot Day =
December 31
- If Earth's capacity is only 25% of our use → Overshoot Day ≈ day 91 (early April)
Norway:
- Norway’s Overshoot Day is April 12, meaning if everyone lived like Norwegians, we’d use up
the planet’s yearly capacity by April.
Developing countries tend to have Overshoot Days later in the year.
Higher CO₂ emissions are linked to:
- Diets rich in meat
- More carbon-intensive transport
- Higher consumption levels
2. Personal reflection:
Answers will vary. You can reflect on factors that contribute to your own ecological footprint.

questions.promptMarkdown:
Exercise 1
Let’s assume you pay 80,000 NOK to study at BI for one year. There are two alternatives to studying
at BI:
You can either:
A: Take a job that pays you 450,000 NOK per year
B: Work as a volunteer (unpaid) for the Red Cross
a) Explain why the opportunity cost of attending BI is not 80,000 NOK. How would you estimate the
opportunity cost?
b) Assume the best alternative is option A. What determines whether you choose to study at BI?
c) Assume only the job option (A) is available in addition to the BI option. What is the opportunity
cost of studying at BI?
d) Assume only alternative (B) is available as an option to BI. What is the opportunity cost of studying
at BI for one year?
e) CORE also defines another concept—economic costs. What is the economic cost of studying at BI?
f) What about the concept of economic rent? What is the economic rent (or economic gain) of
studying at BI?
rubricChecks: Address a) Explain why the opportunity cost of attending BI is not 80,000 NOK
Address b) Assume the best alternative is option A
Address c) Assume only the job option (A) is available in addition to the BI option
Address d) Assume only alternative (B) is available as an option to BI
hints: List BI’s direct costs separately from the value of its best forgone alternative.

For each scenario compare net payoffs, allowing nonmonetary benefits of volunteering. Economic cost combines relevant direct cost with opportunity cost; economic rent compares the chosen payoff with the best alternative.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Exercise 1
a) We must stick to the definition of opportunity cost, found in ch. 2.2 in CORE
Microeconomics.
Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative you must forgo—the value of what you
miss out on by making a choice. It is therefore not affected by how much you value studying
at BI or the cost of studying there, but solely by the value of the best alternative to attending
BI.
If you study at BI, you cannot also take the job that pays 450,000 NOK, nor can you work for
the Red Cross. You thus have three mutually exclusive alternatives.
To estimate the opportunity cost of studying at BI, we must determine which of the two
other options you would have chosen if not studying at BI. That is personal and will vary by
student.
Example:
- Value of Option A (job): 450,000 minus possible job disadvantages (stress, night shifts)
- Value of Option B (Red Cross): Joy of helping others minus disadvantages of volunteering
The opportunity cost of attending BI will be the higher of the two.
If value of A > value of B, then opportunity cost = 450,000 – Job stress.
b) Studying at BI also has value—social benefits, learning, and personal development.
If the value of being a student minus 80,000 is greater than the opportunity cost,
one may choose BI.
Remember: opportunity cost is independent of the value of the choice made; it’s based on
the best forgone alternative.
c) If only A is an alternative, the correct answer is the same as in a)
d) If only B is an alternative, the answer is “Joy of helping others minus disadvantages
of volunteering”
e) Economic cost includes both the direct cost of the chosen option and the
opportunity cost:
- 80,000 + (Joy of helping – volunteering drawbacks) if volunteering is preferred to
paid job
- 80,000 + (450,000 – Job stress) if paid job is preferred

f) Economic gain = Value of choice made – value of best forgone alternative
E.g.:
- (Joy of being a student – 80,000) – (Joy of helping – volunteering drawbacks) if
volunteering preferred
- (Joy of being a student – 80,000) – (450,000 – Job stress) if job preferred

Exercise 4: Based on CORE exercise 2.5
Assume, for simplicity, that a company uses two inputs: labor and energy.
Also assume that the hourly wage for employees is 100 NOK and the price of one unit of energy (100
kWh of electricity) is 50 NOK.
a) What is the relative price of labor?
b) Explain in a few words how you interpret the number you found in a). What information does this
number give about the firm's costs?
c) Draw the isocost line for this company that shows all combinations of inputs that result in a total
cost of 6,000 NOK.
In the figure, plot labor hours on the horizontal axis and units of energy on the vertical axis.
Since the energy price is given per 100 kWh, interpret the vertical axis as units of “100 kWh.” For
example, the number 3 on the vertical axis means the company uses 300 kWh.
d) Add two more isocost lines to the same figure: one for a total cost of 3,000 NOK and another for
9,000 NOK.
e) Now assume the electricity price has increased from 100 to 200 NOK per 100 kWh.
How does this change the isocost lines compared to the ones you just drew?
rubricChecks: a) Relative price of labour: w/p = 100/50 = 2 energy units per labour hour.
b) Interpretation: At the stated prices, using one additional labour hour while keeping total cost unchanged requires giving up two energy units.
c) Cost of 6,000 NOK: 100L + 50E = 6,000, hence E = 120 − 2L.
d) Other cost levels: For C = 3,000: E = 60 − 2L, with intercepts (0,60) and (30,0).
hints: With labour L on x and energy units E on y, begin with C = wL + pE. One energy unit means 100 kWh.
Rearrange to E = C/p − (w/p)L. Use w = 100 and p = 50 for a–d; read the warning about the conflicting starting price in e before explaining the rotation.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**AI-written worked solution · no official solution was available for this exercise**
- **a) Relative price of labour:** w/p = 100/50 = 2 energy units per labour hour. Each energy unit is 100 kWh, so one hour of labour costs the same as 200 kWh.
- **b) Interpretation:** At the stated prices, using one additional labour hour while keeping total cost unchanged requires giving up two energy units. This is a cost trade-off between inputs; it does not say they are technically interchangeable in production.
- **c) Cost of 6,000 NOK:** 100L + 50E = 6,000, hence E = 120 − 2L. With labour on x and energy units on y, the slope is −2. The intercepts are (L = 0, E = 120) and (L = 60, E = 0). Draw the straight line between them. E = 120 means 12,000 kWh.
- **d) Other cost levels:** For C = 3,000: E = 60 − 2L, with intercepts (0,60) and (30,0). For C = 9,000: E = 180 − 2L, with intercepts (0,180) and (90,0). All three lines are parallel because the input prices are unchanged.
- **e) Energy-price change and the source inconsistency:** The original question first sets the energy price at 50 NOK per 100 kWh, then describes an increase “from 100 to 200”. Preserve that discrepancy explicitly. At a new price of 200, the line for C = 6,000 is E = 30 − 0.5L: intercepts (0,30) and (60,0). Relative to p = 50, the absolute slope falls from 2 to 0.5 and the energy intercept from 120 to 30. If the intended comparison was p = 100 to p = 200, the previous line would instead be E = 60 − L. Either way, increasing the energy price flattens the line and reduces the energy intercept, holding C and w fixed, while leaving the labour intercept unchanged. State which starting price you use.

questions.solutionMarkdown:
Exercise 1
We will use the same dataset for all the sub-questions, so the first step is to find the correct dataset.
To do this:
• Open OECD Data Explorer
Navigate to Employment → Employment indicators → Average annual hours actually worked per
worker.
a) To find the number of working hours in the selected countries for 2023, do the following:
1. Choose the correct parameters
• Time period: Select 2023
• Reference area: Check the relevant countries
• Worker status: Leave it set to Total (the difference between Total and Employees is that Total also
includes the self-employed, who are not employees but still workers, so we can include them as well)
2. Look at the results. Here are two options:
• Table: Click on Table to view the data in table form
• Chart: Click on Chart → Column to display the data as a chart
• You may also click on Customise to change the color of the bars
• Hover your mouse over the bars to see the exact numbers.
•

b)
1. Choose the correct parameters
• Time period: Start: 1990, End: 2023
• Reference area: Make sure only Norway is selected
2. Interpret the results. It’s appropriate here to view the results in a chart that shows the
development over time.
• Click on Chart → Timeline to display the data as a time series chart
• Click on Customise to adjust the chart. I have chosen:
• Horizontal axis: Step for labels: 1. This means each step represents one year.
• Vertical axis: Minimum: 1000. Maximum: 1500. Step: 50.
This means the axis starts at 1000 working hours and increases by 50 at each step up to 1500 working
hours.

We see that the average number of working hours in Norway has decreased from 1990 to 2023.
From 1992 to 2003, the reduction was particularly notable, with an average drop of about 100 hours
(1500 in 1992 vs. 1401 in 2003). To put this into perspective, we can assume that a typical full-time
workweek is 37.5 hours. Dividing 100 hours by 37.5 gives us 2.67, meaning that, on average, a worker
worked more than 2.5 fewer workweeks in 2003 than in 1992. After 2003, the average has increased
slightly, reaching 1418 hours in 2023.Her kan det igjen være nyttig å visualisere utviklingen i et
diagram hvor man ser utviklingen over tid.
c)
1. Choose the correct parameters
• Time period: Start: 1970, End: 2023
• Reference area: Norway, United States, United Kingdom
2. Interpret the results.
• Click on Chart → Timeline to display the data as a time series chart
• Click on Customise to adjust the chart. I have chosen:
• Horizontal axis: Step for labels: 1. This means each step represents one year.

• Vertical axis: Minimum: 1300. Maximum: 2000. Step: 50.
This means the axis starts at 1300 working hours and increases by 50 at each step
up to 2000 working hours.
All countries share the common trend of a decline in average working hours over the period. We can
see that Norway experienced a particularly sharp reduction from the 1970s until 2003, while the
decline in the United States was more moderate. The U.S. has had higher working hours than both of
the other countries throughout the entire period. We can also observe a sharp drop in all three
countries in 2020, a year heavily affected by the COVID-19 pandemic and lockdowns. It is clear that
the United Kingdom experienced the most significant decline in average working hours during the
pandemic. Possible reasons for the differences include variations in labor market measures
implemented in each country, the feasibility of working from home, the strictness of infection control
measures, and so on.
d) Several factors can explain the differences in working hours between countries. Individual
preferences for work and leisure vary, and these are influenced by societal norms, economic

incentives, and labor market laws and regulations. In some countries, work–life balance is
highly valued, while in others, long working hours are more emphasized. Women’s
participation in the labor market also plays a role, as women are more likely to work part-
time, which can lower the overall average number of working hours. Working time is
influenced by political decisions such as vacation policies, working time regulations, and tax
systems, all of which can affect individuals’ choices about how much they want to work.

questions.promptMarkdown:
> **Note:** Source discrepancy preserved: statement 4 in the question set uses 16 hours / 446 consumption; the solution document uses 15 hours / 540. Treat that subpart cautiously.

Exercise 2
a) Explain what is meant by indifference curves and what they reveal about a person’s
preferences between consumption and leisure.
b) In the figure below you see 3 indifference curves with some marked points. Evaluate each of
the following statements. Are they true or false?
1. The person is indifferent between alternatives A and B, and between D and C.
2. Moving from B to A gives a greater increase in utility than moving from C to B.
3. Alternative C must be the worst among the options.
4. The person is equally satisfied with 16 hours of leisure and 446 in consumption as
with 20 hours of leisure and 250 in consumption.
5. We can conclude that alternative F must be the best choice, as it represents a middle
ground.
6. If you calculated the marginal rate of substitution (MRS) at A and D, you would find
that the MRS is constant.
c) Explain what is meant by the budget constraint and the opportunity set. What determines
the slope (steepness) of the budget constraint? You can use the figure below to support your
explanation.
rubricChecks: Address a) Explain what is meant by indifference curves and what they reveal about a person’s preferences between...
Address b) In the figure below you see 3 indifference curves with some marked points
Address c) Explain what is meant by the budget constraint and the opportunity set
hints: Separate utility, willingness to trade, and affordability before judging the statements.

Same curve means equal utility; a higher curve ranks bundles more highly. MRS is a local slope, whereas the budget slope comes from wages. Watch the flagged difference between statement 4 and its solution.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Exercise 2
a) An indifference curve is drawn in a coordinate system where the axes measure the quantities
of two goods. In this course, we are particularly focused on the two goods: leisure and
consumption. The measure of leisure is the number of hours, while the measure of
consumption is the amount of money (in kroner) spent on consumption. An indifference
curve shows all combinations of the two goods that provide the same level of satisfaction or
utility to a person. This means that along an indifference curve, a person is indifferent
between different combinations of the two goods, because each combination gives the same
utility level.
There are two key things you should explain in a task like this:
• The curves usually slope downward (i.e., have a negative slope), which reflects the
assumption that when a person has more of one good (e.g., leisure), they must give up
some of the other good (consumption) to maintain the same level of satisfaction. If they
don’t reduce consumption slightly, their utility would increase because they now have
more leisure. The steepness of the indifference curve tells us how much consumption the
person is willing to give up to gain one additional unit of the other good—leisure.
• We often draw these curves bowed inward toward the origin, meaning the slope varies
depending on the person's situation, i.e., how much leisure and consumption they
already have. As we move to the right and down along an indifference curve, it becomes
flatter. How much a person is willing to sacrifice in terms of consumption for one extra
hour of leisure depends on how much leisure they already have. This slope of the
indifference curve is also called the marginal rate of substitution (MRS).
• Each indifference curve represents a specific utility level. Indifference curves that lie
“further out” represent higher levels of utility or satisfaction, while those closer to the
origin represent lower utility levels. Leisure and consumption are both goods, meaning
they are things we like and always want more of ("the more, the better").
Also remember that preferences are personal, so different individuals have different
indifference curves.
b)
1. The person is indifferent between alternatives A and B, and between D and C.
This statement is incorrect. We see that A and D lie on higher indifference curves than B and
C. The higher the indifference curve, the higher the utility level. It is clear that A provides a
higher level of utility than B (and C), and that D provides a higher level of utility than C (and
B).
This also makes logical sense:
In alternatives A and B, the person has the same level of consumption, but more hours of
leisure in A than in B. Since people generally prefer more leisure to less, alternative A must

be better than B.
In alternatives D and C, the person has the same number of leisure hours, but higher
consumption in D than in C. Since people generally prefer more consumption to less,
alternative D must be better than C.
2. Moving from B to A will give a greater increase in utility than moving from C to B.
Each indifference curve represents a utility level—a number expressing how satisfied a
person is. Along an indifference curve, the utility level is the same, but the higher the
indifference curve, the higher the utility.
We cannot observe the exact utility levels of the three indifference curves from the figure,
but we do know that the innermost curve represents the lowest of the three, the middle one
a moderate level, and the outermost the highest utility.
Therefore, we cannot conclude that moving from B to A gives a greater increase in utility
than moving from C to B.
3. Alternative C must be the worst of the options.
Yes, among the listed alternatives, C must be the worst, because it lies on the lowest
indifference curve.
4. The person is equally satisfied with 15 hours of leisure and 540 in consumption as with
20 hours of leisure and 250 in consumption.
Yes. Since these two points (E and D) lie on the same indifference curve, the person considers
these two alternatives equally good.
5. We can conclude that alternative F must be the best option, since it represents a middle
ground.
Incorrect. We do not have enough information to determine which alternative is best. To do
that, we would need information about the budget constraint and where it touches (is
tangent to) the highest possible indifference curve.
6. If you calculated the marginal rate of substitution (MRS) at A and at D, you would find
that the MRS is constant.
This statement is incorrect. The MRS reflects the slope of the indifference curve, and the
slope is steeper at point A than at point D. This means the person is willing to give up more
consumption for one extra hour of leisure at point A (and still be equally satisfied) than at
point D. This is because the scarcer leisure is relative to consumption, the less willing one is
to trade consumption for even more leisure.
c) The budget constraint shows the relationship between the number of hours of leisure and
how much consumption the person can afford. In the figure provided in the task, the red line
represents a budget constraint. For example, if the person has 10 hours of leisure per day—
that is, works (24 – 10 = 14 hours)—how much consumption can the person afford?
According to the budget line in the figure, it appears the person can afford about 400 euros
in consumption.
Consumption is made possible by income, and income depends on how many hours one
works and what the hourly wage is. The slope of the budget line shows how much
consumption must fall if leisure increases—it represents the opportunity cost of increasing

leisure. The higher the wage rate, the steeper the budget line, because one gives up more
consumption when choosing more leisure.
The person can at most afford combinations of leisure and consumption that lie on the
budget line. All combinations within the budget line are possible. This shaded area is called
the feasible set (or opportunity set).
• Point A lies within the feasible set, meaning the person can increase either leisure
and/or consumption up to the budget line. For example, they could increase
consumption without working more, up to the budget limit.
• Point B is outside the feasible set. Given this person's wage and the number of hours
in a day, they cannot afford the combination of leisure and consumption in point B.
To reach point B, the person would need a higher wage.
• Point C is attainable, as it lies on the budget line. Here, the person has used up their
entire budget, meaning they cannot increase either consumption or leisure without
reducing the other.

questions.title: Topic 3 · Set A · Exercise 3
questions.promptMarkdown:
Exercise 3
A key learning objective this week is to 'explain what indifference curves and the marginal rate of
substitution express, and apply this to describe individual preferences for leisure and consumption.'
This assignment gives you an opportunity to test that ability. We continue to work with consumption
and leisure, starting gently:
a) Based on the figure and table above, when a person has 18 hours of leisure and an income
(for consumption) of 323 euros, what is their marginal rate of substitution (MRS)?
b) What if the person has 19 hours of leisure and an income of 282 euros? What is the new
level of MRS?
c) Forget that person. Now consider another individual who enjoys both leisure and
consumption, but only if they can spend at least a few hours working. If leisure (including
sleep) exceeds 20 hours, additional leisure actually reduces life quality for a given level of
consumption. Illustrate an indifference curve for such a person. Do you think this is a
reasonable description of preferences? Explain.
d) Assume the person in c) has 21 hours of leisure. Try to explain how much they would have to
be paid to work 1 extra hour.
e) Assume the person in c) has 20 hours of leisure. Explain how this changes the answer to the
previous question.
rubricChecks: Address a) Based on the figure and table above, when a person has 18 hours of leisure and an income (for consumption)...
Address b) What if the person has 19 hours of leisure and an income of 282 euros
Address c) Forget that person
Address d) Assume the person in c) has 21 hours of leisure
hints: Use the original table in the shared setup and compare neighbouring bundles on the same curve.
Calculate |Δconsumption|/Δfree time for the next hour. For c–e, consider whether an extra free hour is desirable once free time exceeds 20 hours; the curve’s usual shape can change.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Exercise 3
a) The marginal rate of substitution (MRS) is equal to the slope of the indifference curve. The slope
of the indifference curves we work with in this course (with leisure and consumption) tells us exactly
how much consumption must be reduced to keep utility unchanged when leisure increases by a small
(i.e., marginal) amount.
Here, we can practically think of “small” as one hour, so the MRS expresses how much consumption
must be reduced if leisure increases by one hour without changing the level of utility.
We can then use the table from the problem above to calculate this.

Point G on the indifference curve is the “starting point.” If we increase leisure marginally, i.e., by 1
hour, and adjust consumption so that utility remains unchanged, we move to point H on the same
indifference curve. In the table, we see that consumption has been reduced to 282. That gives us the
answer: MRS is approximately 41 euros. This means the person is willing to go from 323 to 282 in
consumption if leisure increases from 18 to 19 hours.
Why only "approximately"? Because 1 hour is quite a bit more than a marginal increase in the
mathematical sense.
b) Now we’ve reached point H. We see that if the person gets 1 more hour of leisure—from 19 to 20
hours—they can manage with 250 euros in consumption without experiencing a lower level of utility
than at H. MRS is therefore 32 euros, much lower than the MRS of 41 when the person had 18 hours
of leisure.
c) To draw this indifference curve, we really need to remember that utility is constant along the
curve. Suppose you have 20 hours of leisure. That’s so much that if you're given even more, say 21
hours, it might feel like a burden (you miss colleagues and work tasks). So how can you maintain the
same utility if you are forced to take one more hour of leisure? You’ll need more consumption, not
less!
The enjoyment from the extra consumption (which we still assume is a good) compensates for the
loss of utility from the additional unwanted leisure.
That means the indifference curve becomes upward-sloping when we pass 20 hours on the
horizontal axis. We’ve illustrated that below:
More leisure shifts from being a good to being a bad if we get more than 21 hours of free time.
When reflecting on this, it's important to remember that we are only talking about preferences—not
about what we can actually afford or not.

d) The person has now passed the critical threshold of 20 hours of leisure. The 21st hour of leisure
was unpleasant. Suppose that, in such a situation, you are offered by your employer to work 1 more
hour, so that your leisure decreases from 21 to 20 hours.
The person is actually willing to reduce their consumption to get this opportunity! In other words,
the person is willing to pay to work an extra hour.
e) Once the person has reached 20 hours of leisure, the situation changes. At that point, leisure
switches back from being a bad to being a good. You are no longer willing to pay to work even more.
If you are to work one more hour, reducing your leisure from 20 to 19 hours, you will need a bit
more consumption to compensate for the loss of one hour of free time.

questions.title: Topic 3 · Set A · Exercise 4
questions.promptMarkdown:
Exercise 4 (Inspired by CORE Exercise 3.2 )
You are offered a job after your BI studies, with an hourly wage (after tax) of 200 NOK. The contract
states that you will work 40 hours per week, giving you 128 hours of leisure per week.
a) Draw a diagram with hours of leisure per week on the horizontal axis and weekly wage on
the vertical axis and plot the point that represents this job offer—how many hours you work.
Call this point A. Assume you need about 10 hours per day for sleep and meals, so it makes
sense to start the horizontal axis at 70 hours.
b) Now draw (freehand) an indifference curve that passes through point A.
c) Suppose you are offered another job that requires 45 hours of work per week. Use the
indifference curve you drew in b) to illustrate the weekly wage that would make you
indifferent between the new job and the original contract.
d) Do the same for another job that requires 35 hours of work per week. Is the wage increase
required to accept 45 hours (5 hours more) equal to the wage reduction you would accept
for working 35 hours (5 hours less)? Explain.
rubricChecks: Address a) Draw a diagram with hours of leisure per week on the horizontal axis and weekly wage on the vertical axis...
Address b) Now draw (freehand) an indifference curve that passes through point A
Address c) Suppose you are offered another job that requires 45 hours of work per week
Address d) Do the same for another job that requires 35 hours of work per week
hints: A week has 168 hours. Convert each proposed work schedule into free time and plot the original wage first.
Use ONE indifference curve through the original offer to find equally attractive alternatives. Diminishing MRS determines whether equal changes in hours require equal wage changes.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Exercise 4 (Inspired av Exercise 3.2)
a) og b)
In one week, there are a total of 24⋅7=168 hours, so the horizontal axis can extend to 168.
Number of hours of leisure per week when working 40 hours:
168−40=128 hours
Weekly income when working 40 hours per week:
200 ⋅ 40 hours = 8,000 NOK
This point can be marked as Point A.
Then, we sketch an indifference curve that passes through Point A. This means that all other
combinations of leisure time and weekly income that lie as points on this indifference curve are
considered equally good as alternative A.
c)
Number of hours of leisure per week if you are to work 45 hours:
168−45=123 hours
To find the level of weekly income that would make you indifferent between the new job and the
original contract, we need to identify what income level lies on the same indifference curve at 123
hours of leisure.

We do this by drawing a dashed line upward from 123 hours of leisure until it intersects the
indifference curve, and we mark this point as Point B.
In this figure, you can see that if the weekly income increases by x kroner (we use x because we
can’t determine the exact amount from the figure), so that the new weekly income becomes 8000 +
x, the person will consider working 45 hours per week to be just as good as in Point A, where the
income was 8000 and they worked 40 hours.
d)
Number of hours of leisure per week if you are to work 35 hours:
168−35=133 hours
To find the level of weekly income that would make you indifferent between the new job and the
original contract, we need to identify what income level lies on the same indifference curve at 133
hours of leisure.
We do this by drawing a dashed line upward from 133 hours of leisure until it intersects the
indifference curve, and we mark this point as Point C:

In this figure, we have reduced working hours by 5 hours from 40 hours, and we see that the person
would accept a pay cut of y kroner, so that the new weekly income becomes 8000 – y. From the
figure, we observe that the pay cut (y kroner) that can be accepted for working 5 fewer hours is
smaller than the pay increase (x kroner) required to accept working 5 more hours.
If you understand why, you have every reason to be proud of yourself!
The reason is the diminishing marginal rate of substitution (MRS) (and thus the curved shape of
indifference curves).
When you are asked to work more, you get less leisure. With less leisure, leisure becomes relatively
more valuable to you—and this is reflected in the higher wage you demand to give up more of it.
Conversely, when you get the chance to work less (35 hours), you get more leisure, which makes
each extra hour of leisure less valuable to you. This is reflected in your lower willingness to accept a
pay cut.

questions.promptMarkdown:
Exercise 5
Draw a diagram with hours of leisure per day on the horizontal axis and daily wage on the vertical
axis.
a) First, draw a budget line (budget constraint) for a worker who earns a fixed hourly wage and
is free to choose how many hours to work each day.
b) The worker negotiates a higher hourly wage. Draw the new budget line on the same diagram.
c) The employer regrets the wage increase and proposes that the worker receive the original
wage for the first 8 work hours, with a higher wage for hours worked beyond 8 (i.e., overtime
pay). If the worker works enough hours, this overtime scheme will yield a higher daily income
than in b). Draw the budget constraint for this alternative contract with “overtime pay” in
the same figure.
rubricChecks: Address a) First, draw a budget line (budget constraint) for a worker who earns a fixed hourly wage and is free to...
Address b) The worker negotiates a higher hourly wage
Address c) The employer regrets the wage increase and proposes that the worker receive the original wage for the...
hints: For each arrangement, express earnings as a function of work hours and then use work = 24 − free time.
A uniform wage increase changes the whole slope. Overtime changes the slope only beyond eight work hours; take care to place that kink at the correct free-time value.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Oppgave 5
a) og b)
Den heltrukne blå linjen viser budsjettlinjen før lønnsøkning. Hvis vedkommende ikke jobber, og
dermed har 24 timer fri i døgnet, vil inntekten være 0. Jo mer vedkommende jobber (slik at fritiden
blir mindre), desto høyere ser vi inntekten blir. Stigningstallet, eller det vi kan omtale som helningen
(bratt vs. slakk), bestemmes av timelønnen. Jo høyere timelønn, desto raskere stiger inntekten hvis
det jobbes mer. Det er grunnen til at den stiplede linjen er brattere, siden denne viser
budsjettbetingelsen når timelønnen er økt.
c)
Dersom personen jobber 8 timer per dag, har hen 16 timer fritid i døgnet og vil ha samme lønn som
tidligere, altså vil den nye budsjettlinjen ligge over den opprinnelige mellom 16 og 24 timer fritid hver
dag. Etter 8 arbeidstimer vil timelønnen øke og den skal øke såpass mye at inntekt per dag blir
høyere enn i oppgave b, altså høyere enn den blå stiplede budsjettbetingelsen.
Derfor kan vi mellom 16 og 0 timer fritid tegne en budsjettbetingelse som krysser den blå stiplede på
ett eller annet punkt. Den høyere overtidslønnen vises ved at budsjettlinjen blir brattere når vi
passerer 8 arbeidstimer, altså ved 16 timer fritid i døgnet.
Alt etter hvor bratt du tegnet den nye budsjettkurven, kan du anslå hvor mange timer personen må
jobbe for å oppnå en høyere lønn per dag enn det som var tilfelle i oppgave b. I min skisse ser det ut
til at budsjettkurvene krysser hverandre ved ca. 10 timer fritid, noe som betyr at dersom personen
jobber mer enn 14 (24 – 10) timer per dag, vil lønnsalternativet i denne oppgaven være bedre enn
lønnsalternativet i oppgave b. Samlet inntekt i overtidsmodellen blir altså høyere dersom
vedkommende vil jobbe mer enn 14 timer i døgnet.
