Exercise 1
Explain the difference between the marginal rate of transformation (MRT) and the marginal rate of
substitution (MRS) between two goods.
A person has the following indifference curves and budget constraint:
Use the figure to answer the following sub-questions:
a) The person is considering a combination of leisure and consumption on the lowest
indifference curve. Could one of these combinations be an optimal choice?
b) Comment on the statement: “Since point E is on the highest indifference curve, the optimal
choice must be the combination of leisure and consumption at point E.”
c) Comment on the statement: “Moving from point D to F gives a greater utility gain than
moving from point D to B.”
d) Based on the figure, which combination of consumption and leisure will the person choose?
rubricChecks: Address a) The person is considering a combination of leisure and consumption on the lowest indifference curve
Address b) Comment on the statement: “Since point E is on the highest indifference curve, the optimal choice must be...
Address c) Comment on the statement: “Moving from point D to F gives a greater utility gain than moving from point D...
Address d) Based on the figure, which combination of consumption and leisure will the person choose
hints: Distinguish the consumption a person is willing to surrender from what their opportunities require.

Rank points by indifference curves, then check whether they are affordable. The best attainable bundle is on the highest reachable curve; ordinal utility does not measure the numerical size of utility gains.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Exercise 1
a) The marginal rate of substitution (MRS) expresses how many units of one good a
person is willing to give up to obtain one more unit of the other good. It is
determined by the person’s individual preferences, and thus by the slope of the
indifference curve. The marginal rate of transformation (MRT), on the other hand,
expresses how many units of one good a person must give up to obtain one more
unit of the other good. This is determined by the slope of the budget constraint.
In this course, we study the choice between the two goods: consumption (enabled
by income) and hours of leisure. In that case, the MRS tells us how much
consumption the person is willing to give up for one additional hour of leisure. This
will vary depending on the person’s situation: if the person has relatively little leisure,
they will be more willing to sacrifice consumption for more leisure than if they
already have a lot of leisure.
In the same example, the marginal rate of transformation (MRT) expresses how
much consumption the person actually must give up to obtain one more hour of
leisure—and this depends on the person’s hourly wage.
With an hourly wage of 200 NOK, it means that for each additional hour of leisure
(i.e., for each hour less worked), the person loses 200 NOK in income, and thus 200
NOK in consumption. MRT is therefore determined by the budget constraint.
b) No, none of the combinations on the lowest indifference curve can be an optimal
choice for the person. We can comment on each of the points A, C, and G to better
understand why:
Point A: This point lies on the budget constraint, so it is a feasible combination.
However, we see that the slope of the indifference curve (MRS) is steeper than the
slope of the budget constraint (MRT), which means the person is willing to give up
more consumption for one more hour of leisure than they actually have to.
Therefore, point A cannot be optimal.
Point C: This point is within the feasible set, but we can see that there are other
combinations that provide higher utility and are still within the feasible area. All
combinations in the area between the lowest indifference curve and the budget
constraint yield higher utility than points C, A, and G.
Point G: Here we see the opposite of point A. The slope of the indifference curve
(MRS) is flatter than the slope of the budget constraint (MRT), which means the

person is willing to give up less consumption for an additional hour of leisure than
what they actually must give up. Therefore, point G cannot be an optimal choice
either.
c) This statement is incorrect. It is true that the combination at point E would give the highest
utility level, but it is unattainable because the point lies outside the feasible set. Therefore,
it cannot be an optimal choice for this person.
d) This statement is correct. If the person chooses to move from combination D to B, it will not
increase utility, as both points lie on the same indifference curve. However, if the person
moves from D to F, this will increase utility, as point F lies on a higher indifference curve
than D (and B).
e) The person will choose point F, where they have approximately 17 hours of leisure and a
little over 200 euros in consumption. The reason we can determine this is because we see
that the point lies on the highest possible indifference curve, given the budget constraint.
At point F, we say that the indifference curve is tangent to the budget constraint. This
means that the slope of the indifference curve (MRS) is equal to the slope of the budget
constraint (MRT)—meaning that the person is willing to give up exactly as much
consumption as they have to.
In general, we can say that the combination that maximizes utility is the point on the budget
constraint where MRS = MRT, which point F satisfies.
Note: We often say that “MRS is equal to the slope of the indifference curve” and “MRT is equal
to the slope of the budget constraint.” But both MRS and MRT are positive numbers, while the
slopes themselves are negative, since both indifference curves and the budget constraint slope
downward. So, strictly speaking, MRS and MRT are equal to the absolute values of the slopes,
meaning we disregard the negative sign.

obsidianLink.heading: 3.2 The Feasible Frontier and Optimal Choice ($MRS = MRT$)

questions.title: Topic 3 · Set B · Exercise 2
questions.promptMarkdown:
Exercise 2
a) Explain what is meant by the income and substitution effects in the context of an income
increase.
b) What determines whether an increase in income leads to a higher or lower labor supply?
Below you see Figure 3.1 from CORE Microeconomics:
•
c) Summarize briefly the characteristics of the development in these three countries.
d) Are there any periods in the figure where GDP per capita declined? If so, in which periods?
e) Over the long time span covered by the figure, real wages in these countries have also
increased (even though you cannot see this in the figure)—not just GDP per capita. How
would you explain the fact that workers are working less and less even though they are paid
much more per hour (real wage)? Use the concepts of income and substitution effects in
your explanation.
rubricChecks: Address a) Explain what is meant by the income and substitution effects in the context of an income increase
Address b) What determines whether an increase in income leads to a higher or lower labor supply
Address c) Summarize briefly the characteristics of the development in these three countries
Address d) Are there any periods in the figure where GDP per capita declined
hints: A wage increase changes both purchasing power and the opportunity cost of leisure.
For the historical-country comparisons, read hours and GDP axes and dates carefully. Use the stated assumption that real wages rose to infer which effect dominated when work hours fell.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Exercise 2
a) The income effect describes how a change in income affects the demand for a good,
solely as a result of changed purchasing power. When income increases, a person
can afford more, as their opportunity set expands. Leisure is considered a normal
good—a good we demand more of as income increases. The income effect of a wage
increase therefore tends to increase leisure (i.e., reduce work).
The substitution effect, on the other hand, is about how a change in relative
prices affects the demand for a good. If the income increase is due to a higher
hourly wage, the opportunity cost of leisure rises. Each hour of leisure now
means more forgone income than before. This makes leisure relatively more
expensive, which creates an incentive to work more and reduce leisure.
b) Whether labour supply increases or decreases depends on which effect dominates.
If the income effect is stronger, the person will choose more leisure and work less.
If the substitution effect is stronger, the person will work more because leisure has
become relatively more expensive.

c) The figure shows trends in income (measured as GDP per capita) and working hours
since 1870 in three countries—USA, France, and the Netherlands.
The figure illustrates that GDP per capita has increased significantly since 1870,
while average working hours have fallen in all three countries. This suggests that as
incomes rise, people choose to work fewer hours.
In the USA, annual working hours have stabilized at a somewhat higher level than in
the other two countries.
d) GDP per capita is shown on the horizontal axis.
If we look at the graph for the USA, we can see that GDP per capita declined
between 1929 and 1938, as the red curve moves leftward. The same is true for
France during a period from 1929, and for the Netherlands (though exact years are
not marked).
Anyone interested in history may know that this was the time of The Great
Depression, which started in 1929 and had global consequences.
Note: The Great Depression is not part of the syllabus, but the ability to read and
interpret graphs is.
e) As explained in task a, the substitution effect describes the effect of a change in
relative prices. When the real wage increases, the price of leisure increases (one
extra hour of leisure costs more than before), which in isolation encourages more
work (less leisure).
The income effect is about the change in purchasing power. When the real wage
increases, a person can work the same amount or less than before and still afford the
same level of consumption. This effect alone suggests that a person would choose to
work less (more leisure).
Since we observe that we work less despite increasing real wages, this suggests that
the income effect has dominated the substitution effect.

obsidianLink.heading: 3.3 Income and Substitution Effects of Wage and Tax Changes

Exercise 3
In the video «Why do we work so hard» sociologist Juliet Schor discusses what affects our work
effort. When you have seen it, answer the following questions (feel free to discuss with fellow
students):
a) How did working hours develop before 1870?
b) From 1970 there are changes. Two countries stand out from the rest after 1970. Which two
countries, and in what way?
c) Does Schor agree with the central assumption in the analysis of choice of working time,
namely that the employee chooses the preferred working time?
d) How does Schor describe the connection between a country's greenhouse gas emissions and
the development in working hours?
rubricChecks: Address a) How did working hours develop before 1870
Address b) From 1970 there are changes
Address c) Does Schor agree with the central assumption in the analysis of choice of working time, namely that the...
Address d) How does Schor describe the connection between a country's greenhouse gas emissions and the development in...
hints: Use Schor’s argument in the assigned video rather than substituting the model’s free-choice assumption.
Organise the answer by historical hours, post-1970 country differences, bargaining power over hours, and the use of productivity growth for either output or leisure.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Exercise 3
a) Working hours increased for all of these countries up until 1870.
b) While other countries continued to see a decline in average working hours after 1970, the
decline stopped in the USA and the UK. In fact, the data shows that working hours have
increased in these two countries compared to the 1970 level.
c) She argues that the reason is that companies (employers) have gained more power—
greater bargaining strength. Trade unions have been weakened. Companies benefit from
longer working hours, and when workers’ bargaining power is weakened, it becomes difficult
to resist demands for longer workdays.
She claims that firms choose working hours (unlike what we’ve assumed in this week’s
model), and workers choose jobs.
d) She argues that we have a choice in how to use productivity growth: either in the form of
more leisure or more "goods and stuff." Companies prefer to take it out in the form of
increased production, and with today’s technology, this leads to greater environmental
impact and greenhouse gas emissions.

questions.promptMarkdown:
Exercise 4
In this problem, we will continue working with problem 5 from plan 4. The problem text is pasted
below here, and you may find it beneficial to refer to your solutions for this task as a starting point
when addressing the tasks.
Problem 5 (Plan 4)
Draw a diagram with hours of leisure per day on the horizontal axis and daily wage on the
vertical axis.
a) First, draw a budget line (budget constraint) for a worker who earns a fixed hourly wage
and is free to choose how many hours to work each day.
b) The worker negotiates a higher hourly wage. Draw the new budget line on the same
diagram.
c) The employer regrets the wage increase and proposes that the worker receive the
original wage for the first 8 work hours, with a higher wage for hours worked beyond 8
(i.e., overtime pay). If the worker works enough hours, this overtime scheme will yield a
higher daily income than in b). Draw the budget constraint for this alternative contract
with “overtime pay” in the same figure.
a) Start from exercise 5 b) from last week. How will the increased salary affect how much the
employees want to work? Will they work more or less? Draw one or more figures with
budget lines (before and after the wage increase) and indifference curves to support your
answer.
b) Now we take with us the information in 3 c), also that from last week, and look further at the
two alternatives:
1) The increased salary, as explained in b)
2) Original salary, but combined with a high overtime salary per hour after 8 hours.
Now imagine that Per and Anne work in this company. If the company gets approval to
change to overtime payment (option 2) rather than a general higher salary (option 1), we
assume that Per will work even less - and less than 8 hours. Anne, on the other hand, wants
to work much more - and get paid overtime. Draw two figures - one figure for Per and one
figure for Anne - showing their preferences and adaptation in alternatives 1) and 2).
rubricChecks: Address a) First, draw a budget line (budget constraint) for a worker who earns a fixed hourly wage and is free to...
Address b) The worker negotiates a higher hourly wage
Address c) The employer regrets the wage increase and proposes that the worker receive the original wage for the...
Address a) Start from exercise 5 b) from last week
hints: First draw the uniform higher wage and the alternative contract with overtime beyond eight hours.

Then draw each person’s preferred affordable tangency before and after the contract change, using the stated directions for Per and Anne. Keep each person’s indifference curves consistent and non-crossing.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Oppgave 4
a) It is uncertain how an increase in wages will affect labour supply. It depends on which effect
is stronger: the income effect or the substitution effect.
Substitution effect dominates
Here, we have illustrated a situation where the substitution effect is stronger (the higher wage
increases the price of leisure, making you want less leisure—and therefore to work more).
You can see that after the wage increase, the person works more, since the number of hours of
leisure is lower at point B than at point A, despite the higher wage.

Income effect dominates
Below, we have illustrated a situation where the income effect is stronger (a higher wage increases
income for a given amount of work, and then you want to “buy” more leisure—and work less—if
leisure is a normal good).
You can see that after the wage increase, the person works less at point C, since the number of
leisure hours is higher at C than at A, despite the higher wage.
Note: Students often interpret this as if we either have a substitution effect or an income effect. This
is a misinterpretation.
Both effects are always at play, but what determines the change in labour supply is which of the two
effects is stronger.

b)
Per:
When transitioning to alternative 2 from alternative 1, we are told that Per works fewer hours
than before, and less than 8 hours. In the illustration, we assume that under alternative 1, he
initially worked 8 hours per day. We label this adjustment as Point A, and see that the
indifference curve we sketch should be tangent to the budget constraint for alternative 1 at 16
hours of leisure (8 hours of work) per day.
After the introduction of alternative 2, Per chooses to work less. We then draw a new
indifference curve that is tangent to the budget constraint for alternative 2 (the red one) at a
point with more leisure than before (i.e., less work). This point can be labeled as Point B.
Anne:
After the introduction of alternative 2, Anne chooses to work significantly more and thereby
receives overtime pay. We draw an indifference curve that is tangent to the budget
constraint for alternative 1, and label this point as Point A. In the illustration, we assume that
she initially chose to work about 11 hours per day.
After the introduction of alternative 2, we are told that she chooses to work much more, so
we must draw a new indifference curve that is tangent to the budget constraint for
alternative 2 at a point corresponding to substantially more work. This point is labeled Point
B.

Note: When sketching the indifference curves, be careful that they do not cross each other.
Each indifference curve represents a specific utility level, so no two indifference curves can
ever intersect.

questions.title: Topic 3 · Set B · Exercise 5
questions.promptMarkdown:
Exercise 5
This article was published in Aftenposten, 18/6 2024.
- I am very happy that we can still work at least 20 per cent for full salary, says retired midwife Ellen
Puntervold.
The 65-year-old did not like the fact that the government proposed a law that would make it less
lucrative for her to work a little alongside her pension.
In an interview with Aftenposten last autumn, the experienced midwife said she was considering
stopping taking shifts because of the government's proposal.
She has been able to work in a 19.9 percent position with regular hourly wages. Without deductions
in the pension.
The government's proposal would mean a significant reduction in her salary. She would receive a so-
called "pensioner's salary": NOK 233 an hour for working in a position of up to 20 per cent.
- It is lousy pay. Then it's probably over for me, the midwife told Aftenposten at the time.
But now the government has turned around.
The Storting asked the government to turn around
The government would make it less profitable for early retirees to take extra shifts. The Storting asked
the government to do the opposite: to make it possible for retired nurses to work a little on the side.
Now the government is in favor of allowing retired nurses to work up to 20 per cent without the
pension being reduced.
Labor and Inclusion Minister Tonje Brenna acknowledges that there is a great need for the experience
and workforce of retired nurses. In a press release, she expresses that she is happy that together with
the parties they have reached a solution.
- It is good for people and good for our welfare, says Brenna.
Glad to be heard
- This is very good, says Lill Sverresdatter Larsen.
She is the union leader of the Norwegian Nurses' Association.
- We are happy that the government has listened to us and the Storting and made this change. We
are short of nurses, so we are happy that the government has turned around, she says.
Larsen emphasizes that retired nurses constitute an important resource that society now has the
opportunity to use.
- If the government had not turned around, the retired nurses would have had to work on
"pensioner's pay". With this change, they can work with full pay in up to 20 positions, Larsen points
out.
Has significance for the students as well
The dire shortage of nurses will only increase in the future. Today, around 700 nurses work alongside
the pension.
Union leader Larsen recalls that 3,000–4,000 retired nurses worked during the pandemic. They could
work as much as they wanted without deductions from their pension.
Now she is also satisfied that the government is in favor of a scheme that will be important for
students.
- Students will be able to earn a pension during their studies, from the first kroner. It is independent of
the vacancy rate, says Larsen.
Retired midwife Ellen Puntervold finds it more interesting to work for full salary.
- I get questions about working all the time. It is nice to come to work where I am received in a good
way. I get to use myself, says Puntervold.
She points out:
- It would be strange if we were not to receive full salary when we are in such demand.
You can base the analysis on the following assumptions:
Number of hours in a year:
365 days × 24 hours = 8,760 hours
Therefore, 8,760 represents the maximum number of leisure hours along the x-axis.
Number of possible work hours with low pay (alongside pension):
A full-time equivalent (100% position) = 1,750 hours
A retired nurse can work 20% without the pension being reduced:
0.2 × 1,750 = 350 hours
a) Illustrate the budget line for a retired nurse under the following three assumptions:
1) The nurse receives a fixed retirement pension of NOK 500,000 a year, of course
without working. As a pensioner, the nurse can work up to 20%, and keep the extra
salary in addition to the pension of NOK 500,000. Assume that 20% amounts to 350
hours a year.
2) The nurse receives a fixed retirement pension of NOK 500,000 a year, of course
without working. As a pensioner, the nurse can work up to 20%, and be paid a
pensioner's salary that is 40% below the ordinary hourly wage in 1). The nurse keeps
the pension of NOK 500,000, as in 1).
3)The nurse receives a fixed retirement pension of NOK 500,000 a year, of course
without working. As a pensioner, the nurse can work up to 20%, and receive an
additional salary as in 1). However, the pension is reduced kroner for kroner
corresponding to the extra salary the nurse receives.
b) The leader of the Nurses' Association states: "We are happy that the government has
listened to us and the Storting and made this change. We are short of nurses, so we are
happy that the government has turned around". Which effect does she assume is stronger –
the income effect or the substitution effect. Remember that you must be able to justify
your answer.
rubricChecks: Address a) Illustrate the budget line for a retired nurse under the following three assumptions: 1) The nurse...
Address b) The leader of the Nurses' Association states: "We are happy that the government has listened to us and the...
hints: Start from a zero-work pension of 500,000 NOK and an annual time endowment of 8,760 hours.

Use 350 work hours as the relevant threshold. Compare additional take-home resources from an hour of work under full extra pay, reduced pay, and a kroner-for-kroner pension offset; then relate the changed slope to substitution and income effects.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Oppgave 5
Det kan være krevende å «oversette» informasjon i artikler som denne fra Aftenposten og oppgave 1
til en grafisk fremstilling. Med en grafisk fremstilling er det forhåpentligvis lettere å se hva som skiller
de ulike lønnsavtalene, og dermed hvilken effekt slike avtaler kan ha på tilpasningen.
a)
Situasjon 1) Pensjonist med full ekstralønn inntil 350 arbeidstimer
If the retired nurse does not work, they will have 8,760 hours of leisure per year and 500,000
NOK in pension income. We can therefore start by drawing a vertical line upward from 8,760
hours of leisure, up to 500,000 NOK in income.
For each hour worked up to 350 hours (which reduces leisure time to 8,410 hours), total income
increases (pension + earned income).
We can mark a point at 8,410 hours of leisure by calculating the income from working 350 hours:
400 𝑘𝑟𝑜𝑛𝑒𝑟⋅350 ℎ𝑜𝑢𝑟𝑠 = 140 000 𝑘𝑟𝑜𝑛𝑒𝑟
The person thus receives a total income of
500,000 + 140,000 = 640,000 NOK
by working 20% (i.e., 350 hours) in addition to receiving their pension.
This point can now be marked at
8,410 hours of leisure (8,760 – 350)
and
640,000 NOK in income
on the graph, illustrating the combined effect of partial work and pension.

Situation 2: Retiree with reduced hourly wage (60% of original) for up to 350 hours of work
Since the hourly wage is reduced by 40%, the person keeps 60% of the original wage.
The new hourly wage for the first 350 hours is
400⋅0,6 = 240 𝑘𝑟𝑜𝑛𝑒𝑟
We can mark a point for 8,410 hours of leisure by calculating the income from 350 hours of
work:
240 NOK×350 hours=84 000 NOK
The person thus receives:
500 000+84 000=584 000 NOK
in total income by working 20% in addition to being a pensioner.
We have plotted Situation 2 in the same diagram, showing a point at:
• 8,410 hours of leisure
• 584,000 NOK in income
This allows a direct comparison with Situation 1, where income at the same number of work
hours (350) was 640,000 NOK.

Situation 3: Full reduction of pension benefits
In this situation, any work income fully reduces the pension, so total income remains 500,000 NOK
regardless of how much the person works.
For example, if the retired nurse works 350 hours and earns an additional 140,000 NOK (as calculated
in Situation 1), the pension will be reduced by 140,000 NOK, leaving total income unchanged at
500,000 NOK.
In other words:
Whatever the person earns from working is offset by an equal reduction in the pension.
So no matter how many shifts they take on, affecting their leisure time, they will always end up with
500,000 NOK in income.
Graphically, this is shown as a horizontal line at 500,000 NOK, stretching leftward from 8,760 hours
of leisure—indicating no income gain from working, only a loss of leisure.

b)
Note: We are now considering the income and substitution effects in the context of a reduction in
income. The effects of substitution and income will then be opposite to those in the case of an
income increase.
If a pensioner who previously has been able to take extra shifts (up to 20%) at the regular
wage gets their extra pay reduced to a “pensioner’s wage,” which is lower than the regular wage,
their willingness to work will be affected by both the substitution effect and the income effect:
• Substitution effect:
The substitution effect concerns how changes in relative prices (here: the hourly wage for
extra shifts) affect the labour supply.
When extra shifts offer lower pay than before, the opportunity cost of leisure is lower—the
person loses less income by declining extra shifts.
This makes leisure relatively more attractive and, in isolation, suggests that the person would
work less if the government’s original proposal to reduce the wage for extra shifts were
implemented.
• Income effect:
The income effect concerns how a change in total income affects the demand for various
goods, including leisure.
When the wage for extra shifts is reduced, the total income (pension + extra income) for the
pensioner who used to take such shifts will decrease.
For a given number of extra shifts, income falls.

If leisure is a normal good, the person will want less leisure when income decreases. With
lower income, this effect pushes in the direction of the pensioner taking on more shifts.
Since the statement in the task argues that maintaining regular pay is important to gain
access to valuable labour, they assume that the substitution effect is stronger.
We can illustrate both a case where the substitution effect dominates and a case where the
income effect dominates.
1) Substitution effect dominates
The person would work less (more leisure) with a lower wage.
2) Income effect dominates
The person would choose to work more (i.e., have less leisure) when faced with a lower
wage.

questions.title: Topic 4 · Exercise 1
questions.promptMarkdown:
Exercise 1
The figure below shows a simplified image of the actors within a firm and its decision-making
hierarchy.
The grey lines represent orders given from superiors to subordinates within the company. The
dashed arrows represent the flow of information.
a) Explain what is meant by asymmetric information and why the dashed green arrows
represent this. Why does this problem arise?
b) The return to shareholders on their investments in a company is determined by the
company’s profit. Decisions made by management and the effort of employees affect how
large the profit will be. Managers have better information about the company than
shareholders. What can shareholders do to incentivize management to make decisions that
benefit them?
rubricChecks: Address a) Explain what is meant by asymmetric information and why the dashed green arrows represent this
Address b) The return to shareholders on their investments in a company is determined by the company’s profit
hints: Identify who knows what inside the firm and who wants which outcome.
Managers and workers know more about their own decisions or effort. Explain how incentives linked to performance and monitoring through the board can address the owners’ information problem.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Exercise 1
a) Asymmetric information arises when one party in an economic transaction has more or
better information than the other. This can create problems because the better-informed
party may act in ways that benefit themselves, but not necessarily the other party.
1. Between owners and managers:
Owners (shareholders) hire managers to run the company but cannot fully observe the
managers’ efforts or decisions. Managers may therefore pursue their own interests, for
example by focusing on short-term profits or personal gain, rather than the owners’ goal of
long-term value creation.
2. Between managers and employees:
Managers do not always know how hard employees are working or how productive they
are. Employees may therefore have incentives to exert less effort than expected, especially if
they know the chance of being caught is low or if it won’t affect their pay.
These problems arise due to incomplete contracts. A contract is incomplete when it does not
specify all possible actions and outcomes—either because it is too complex or too costly to do
so. In employment relationships, it is often very expensive or even impossible to describe,
monitor, or measure every aspect of a manager’s or employee’s performance, which creates
room for behaviour that is not aligned with the best interest of the firm.
b) CORE (ch. 6.3) highlights two main ways in which owners can motivate managers to act in
the interests of shareholders:
1. Incentive-based executive compensation:
Owners can design contracts so that managerial pay depends on the company’s
share price. This gives managers a direct financial incentive to increase the
company’s value, since their own income is tied to the firm’s performance.
2. Monitoring by the board of directors:
The board, which represents the shareholders and often holds a significant
ownership stake in the company, can monitor management performance. The board
hires and can dismiss the CEO if their performance is unsatisfactory.

questions.title: Topic 4 · Exercise 2
questions.promptMarkdown:
Exercise 2
a) In the market we can buy goods and services. Small purchases such as clothes and food are
simple transactions that are carried out without a contract being written between buyer and
seller, but larger purchases such as houses and cars normally require a purchase contract.
There are few people who miss a purchase contract at the checkout at Rema, while most
would be skeptical about buying a house without a purchase contract. Explain what this
could be due to. What is the difference between the two types of purchase?
b) Describe an important difference between a purchase contract and an employment contract.
rubricChecks: Address a) In the market we can buy goods and services
Address b) Describe an important difference between a purchase contract and an employment contract
hints: Compare how quickly the exchange finishes and how easily its quality and terms can be verified.
Large purchases can involve complex future obligations. An employment contract also covers future behaviour and effort that cannot all be specified or enforced like a clearly defined purchased item.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Exercise 2
a)
This is an assignment without a single correct answer, but the idea is that what you read in Chapter 6
of CORE about incomplete contracts and information gives you important clues.
When I buy simple groceries, I know exactly what I’m getting. We are well familiar with what’s inside
a carton of milk, how those particular apple varieties taste, and what’s inside a box of frozen pizza.
We know this from previous purchases and from government regulations on labeling and shelf life.
If the product does not match the information provided, you have the right to cancel the purchase
and get your money back. This right is already protected by the Sales Act. A separate contract for a
large grocery purchase at Rema is therefore completely unnecessary—and would be very time-
consuming.
It’s different with large one-time purchases, such as buying a house. In such cases, it’s much harder
to uncover all aspects of the product—asymmetric information exists, and it is therefore useful to
write a contract where buyer and seller clarify the house’s quality and condition. The cost of entering
such a contract is small compared to the value at stake.
Still, disputes arise because such contracts may be incomplete (see, for example, the Firestone case
in ch. 6.6)). Everything about a house’s condition and features cannot be described precisely enough
for a court to clearly determine whether the contract terms have been fulfilled.
b)
A purchase contract transfers ownership from the seller to the buyer, whereas an employment
contract only gives the paying party the right to direct the employee’s work within an agreed time
frame and to assign tasks as specified in the employment contract. See how CORE summarizes the
differences in the subsection Contracts and relationships:
“A contract for the sale of a car transfers ownership, meaning that the new owner can now use the
car and exclude others from its use and sell it to someone else. Under an employment contract, by
contrast, an employee gives the employer the right to direct them to be at work at specified times,
and authority over the use of their time while at work. The contract does not give the employer
ownership of the employee—that would be slavery. To summarize:
• Contracts for products sold in markets permanently transfer ownership of the good from the
seller to the buyer.
• Contracts for labour temporarily transfer authority over a person’s activities from the
employee to the manager or owner.”

questions.title: Topic 4 · Exercise 3
questions.promptMarkdown:
Exercise 3
A newly graduated economist, Berit, is considering a job offer. She has applied for several positions
and has received a concrete offer of 5,500 NOK per week. She knows that if she waits a bit, she might
find a job that pays 6,000 NOK per week, but she is uncertain about how long that will take. While
unemployed, she receives unemployment benefits of 3,500 NOK per week.
a) Explain what is meant by the concept of reservation wage.
b) Mention factors that would influence Berit’s reservation wage in this case.
c) How might increased unemployment benefits affect the reservation wage and Berit’s
decision?
d) The employer becomes impatient and increases the offer to 5,800 NOK. How is the
reservation wage affected?
rubricChecks: Address a) Explain what is meant by the concept of reservation wage
Address b) Mention factors that would influence Berit’s reservation wage in this case
Address c) How might increased unemployment benefits affect the reservation wage and Berit’s decision
Address d) The employer becomes impatient and increases the offer to 5,800 NOK
hints: The reservation wage comes from Berit’s next-best alternative, including waiting for another job.
Compare benefits, expected search time, future job prospects and effort costs. A better offer changes the attractiveness of the current job; it need not itself change the outside option.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Exercise 3
a)
The reservation wage is the lowest wage a person is willing to accept to take a job. It is determined
by the value of the next best alternative to accepting the job.
If unemployment is the next best alternative, the reservation wage includes unemployment benefits,
the value of having more leisure time (which varies by individual), and the expected income the
person anticipates from eventually finding another job.
b)
Berit’s reservation wage will be influenced by several factors:
• Unemployment benefits: The level of unemployment benefits gives her an income while
unemployed and will help determine how high her reservation wage is. In this case, it's 3,500
NOK per week, which means her reservation wage must be higher than that.
• Expected future wage: If she is confident that she can soon get a better-paid job at 6,000
NOK per week, this will affect her willingness to accept a job with lower pay.
• How long it will take to find a new job: Berit doesn’t know how long it will take to land a job
paying 6,000 NOK per week. If she thinks the wait will be long and not worth it, her
reservation wage will be lower. If she expects to get the better-paying job soon, her
reservation wage will be higher. Thus, the reservation wage is influenced by the expected
waiting time, which is uncertain and depends on her expectations.
• Other factors affecting her well-being while unemployed, such as the value of more free
time for hobbies or interests that increase her life satisfaction. On the other hand, negative
effects like the psychological strain of being unemployed may lower her overall utility.
c)
If unemployment benefits increase, Berit’s financial situation as an unemployed person improves.
This will raise her reservation wage, because her alternative to working has become better.
She can now afford to wait longer for a better-paying job.
Higher unemployment benefits may lead workers to become more selective and take more time to
find a better job match, but they may also lead to longer periods of unemployment.
d)
The wage in the job offer does not determine the reservation wage.
The reservation wage is based on the value of what Berit considers her best alternative to taking the
job.
However, the offered wage does affect her decision:
If the wage (after subtracting the cost of effort on the job) is higher than her reservation wage, she
will accept the job. If it is lower, she will reject it and wait for a better offer.

questions.title: Topic 4 · Exercise 4
questions.promptMarkdown:
Exercise 4
In Norway, there is strong employment protection legislation intended to protect workers from
unfair dismissals. A dismissal must be objectively justified, either due to the company’s financial
difficulties or documented serious violations of the employment agreement.
Lack of effort from employees can often be difficult to document in a way that supports dismissal.
a) Explain how such strong employment protection, like Norway’s, affects the incentive to exert
effort and thereby the value of the job (“employment rent”).
b) Read section 6.9 in CORE carefully and explain how we can argue that strong employment
protection imposes an additional cost on firms.
Hint: Study Figure 6.9 and think about what happens to “s” (the number of expected weeks one can
get away with shirking) when employment protection increases.
c) In what way can increased use of remote work affect the wage level in the company?
Exercise 6.7 from CORE
rubricChecks: Address a) Explain how such strong employment protection, like Norway’s, affects the incentive to exert effort and...
Address b) Read section 6.9 in CORE carefully and explain how we can argue that strong employment protection imposes...
Address c) In what way can increased use of remote work affect the wage level in the company
hints: Compare the time gaining from shirking with the time suffering the consequences of dismissal.

If effective detection/dismissal takes longer, s rises: avoided effort lasts longer and the remaining punishment period h − s is shorter. For remote work, explain the monitoring assumption rather than presuming a universal wage effect.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Exercise 4
a)
Employment rent is the economic value of keeping your job. The worse your alternative is, the higher
the value of your current job.
In Chapter 6, this value is explained in detail, including what affects it—such as how long you expect
to be unemployed if you lose your job, the level of unemployment benefits during that period, and
job stress or disutility of work.
If your current job is clearly better than the alternative—being unemployed for a while—this gives
you a strong incentive to exert effort. If you don’t, your employer may fire you.
Job protection, in isolation, makes it more difficult to fire someone, which means you have less to
fear even if you don’t exert effort.
If, on the other hand, your employer doesn’t need to give any reason for termination—just say
“you’re fired”—you need to work hard every day to keep your job.
For a given value of the job, job protection reduces the incentive to exert effort, meaning that the
economic value of the job (employment rent) has decreased.
b)
In Chapter 6.9, effort and wage decisions are modeled as follows:
• The employer sets the wage level based on how they expect the employee to respond (in
terms of effort) to a given wage.
• The employee chooses an effort level based on the wage, the cost of losing the job, and the
probability that the employer will detect insufficient effort (and thus fire the worker).
When job protection increases, the probability of being fired decreases.
In Figure 6.9, we can think of “s”—the number of weeks it takes before someone loses their job—as
increasing when this probability drops. On average, it will take longer to detect shirking, and so s
increases.
To illustrate this clearly, we can set up a simple example to show the effect this has on the net value
of working with effort vs. shirking, and how this may lead to higher costs for the firm.
Note: The explanation below is meant to support your understanding of the model. A calculation like
this is not necessary to answer such a question well.
Example setup:
Let’s assume a situation where the value of working with effort is initially equal to the value of
shirking.
When the difference between the two is zero, the model assumes that the person will just choose to
work with effort.
(Note: In practice, the value of effort would have to be slightly higher than shirking for the person to
choose effort, but here we simplify and assume equal values mean effort is chosen.)

We assume:

shirking, and how increased job protection (increased sss) changes the outcome.

Let us now see what happens if "s" increases by 5, to 30.
We’ll call the new value s_new, and illustrate again.
The alternative of working with effort remains unchanged.

We now see that the orange shaded area has become larger. It has become more attractive to shirk
than to work with effort, since it takes longer to be discovered if one shirks. Initially, the two shaded
areas were equally large, but now the orange one is bigger.
To give the worker an incentive to once again choose effort over shirking, the employer must
increase the wage. This means the employer incurs an additional cost in the form of a higher wage.
One could now go further and calculate how much the employer would need to raise the wage for
the areas to once again become (at least) equally large, using the “no shirking wage” formula in
Chapter 6.9. Doing so would show that the wage would need to increase to 110 NOK per hour for the
two options to become equally attractive again.
If a question of this type were to appear on an exam, you would be provided with the formula. The
most important thing here is not the calculations, but rather to understand what the model shows,
and what happens when different elements in the model change.
For those especially interested, we’ve calculated below the new economic value of working, as well
as what the new wage must be to once again provide an incentive to exert effort at work:
• Value of working with effort remains unchanged: 4,000
• Value of shirking is:

meaning the individual would prefer to shirk.

c) Several things can happen here.
Increased use of remote work (working from home) may increase the attractiveness of the current
job. For example, we can think of “c”, the cost of working (disutility of work), as decreasing.
That would increase the value of the job. But what could the firm then do?
Well, the firm could reduce the wage (or offer smaller raises) and still get the employee to exert
effort.
What else might happen?
It’s often said that remote work makes it harder to monitor what employees spend their time on.
They might more easily use time for things the company isn’t paying for—like cleaning the house or
going to a café with neighbors.
That makes it easier to get away with low effort at work.
Then “s” (the number of weeks before getting caught shirking) would increase, just like in question
b.
If that happens, the firm must increase the wage to get the employee to exert effort (and postpone
the house cleaning).
There are many other aspects of remote work that are certainly important, but here we have
highlighted two key factors that can influence wage levels in firms.

who are unemployed, then being employed results in a higher payout than being
unemployed. It is also stated that if Maria is unemployed, she will still have her child in

can assume that the child benefit — which we’ll call “b” — is paid weekly.
Therefore, the net weekly benefit of working with effort is:

That is: wage, minus cost of effort, plus child benefit.
Maria receives this amount every week for the entire planning period hhh.

then receives the reservation wage, which represents the value of being unemployed.

As we can see, the value of both working with effort and shirking increases.
However, the value of working with effort increases more than the value of shirking.
Put differently, the value of working with effort increases because b⋅hb \cdot hb⋅h,
which is the added benefit in the work-with-effort scenario,
is greater than b⋅ s, which is the added benefit in the shirking scenario.
Thus, the value of the job increases.
1. If the demand for the company’s products increases because celebrities promote the
product, the answer is not entirely clear-cut.

• If there is no direct link between product demand and wages, then it will not have any effect
in the model.
• If we assume that the firm must hire more workers to meet the increased demand, then
wages might rise, since more hiring pushes up the wage required to attract employees.
In that case, it would have the same effect as in (1)—the value of working with effort
increases.
• A third assumption one might make is that higher demand makes the job busier for current

making shirking more attractive and reducing the job’s overall value.
Graphically, this can be illustrated by increasing c, so that the shaded blue area (the value of working
with effort) becomes smaller, while the shirking option is unaffected—since c = 0 when shirking (no
effort is exerted).
2. New technology that makes the job easier will reduce the cost of working, meaning ccc
decreases.
This increases the value of working with effort.
Graphically, this is shown by reducing c so that the blue shaded area becomes larger,
while the shirking option remains unchanged.

questions.title: Topic 5 · Set A · Exercise 1
questions.promptMarkdown:
Exercise 1
The table below shows the relationship between the price of a basket of strawberries and
the number of baskets demanded and supplied per week in a local market.
Price per basket (kroner) Demand (baskets) Supply (baskets)
80 0 600
60 100 400
40 200 200
20 300 0
0 400 0
a) Draw a diagram with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis.
b) Plot the demand points for the different prices and draw a line through the points to
sketch the demand curve. Briefly explain what the demand curve tells us.
c) Plot the supply points for the different prices and draw a line through the points to
sketch the supply curve. Briefly explain what the supply curve tells us.
d) Find the market equilibrium. What are the equilibrium price and equilibrium
quantity?
e) Explain what is meant by the term seller’s reservation price. What is the lowest
reservation price in this example?
f) Explain what is meant by excess supply and excess demand. At a price of 60 NOK,
will there be excess supply, excess demand, or neither?
rubricChecks: Address a) Draw a diagram with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis
Address b) Plot the demand points for the different prices and draw a line through the points to sketch the demand curve
Address c) Plot the supply points for the different prices and draw a line through the points to sketch the supply curve
Address d) Find the market equilibrium
hints: Plot quantity on x and price on y, then compare supplied and demanded quantity at each listed price.
Find the row where demand equals supply. At other prices, subtract demanded from supplied quantity and interpret the sign. Relate the start of the supply curve to sellers’ reservation prices.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Exercise 1
a, b og c)
The demand curve shows how many baskets of strawberries are demanded at different prices.
For example, at a price of 60 kroner, people in the market want to buy 100 baskets of strawberries.
The supply curve shows how many baskets of strawberries are supplied at different prices.
For example, at a price of 60 kroner, 400 baskets of strawberries are offered for sale.
d) From the table and the diagram we’ve drawn, we can see that at a price of 40 kroner per basket,
200 baskets are demanded and 200 baskets are supplied.
This is the equilibrium price and the equilibrium quantity.
e) The seller’s reservation price is the lowest price a supplier is willing to sell a good for.
In this case, the lowest price someone is willing to sell a basket of strawberries for is 20 kroner.

f)
Excess supply occurs when the quantity supplied is greater than the quantity demanded at a given
price.
Excess demand occurs when the quantity demanded is greater than the quantity supplied at a given
price.
At a price of 60 kroner, 400 baskets of strawberries are supplied, but only 100 baskets are
demanded.
There will therefore be an excess supply of 300 baskets of strawberries at this price.

questions.promptMarkdown:
Exercise 2
Assume that electricity can be produced either in hydropower plants or gas power plants.
Both technologies have limited production capacity. Hydropower plants can together
produce a maximum of 1,000 units of electricity, while gas power plants can produce a
maximum of 500 units.
Hydropower plants have a constant marginal cost of 0.20 NOK, while gas power plants have
a marginal cost of 1 NOK.
a) Explain what is meant by marginal cost.
b) Draw the supply curve for the hydropower plants. Assume there are many
producers who are price-takers.
c) Draw the supply curve for the gas power plants, also assuming many producers and
price-taking behavior.
d) Draw the total supply curve for electricity, showing the relationship between price
and total production (from both hydropower and gas power plants).
e) Calculate the total producer surplus for electricity prices of 0.5 NOK, 1 NOK, and 2
NOK. See Figure 8.8 in CORE for inspiration.
rubricChecks: Address a) Explain what is meant by marginal cost
Address b) Draw the supply curve for the hydropower plants
Address c) Draw the supply curve for the gas power plants, also assuming many producers and price-taking behavior

Exercise 2
In this case, we do not have a smoothly downward-sloping demand curve, as we often draw it.
The reason is that many consumers are assumed to have the same willingness to pay, and that
there are only three price levels.
If the price rises above 3 NOK per kWh, no one will demand electricity for heating jacuzzis.
Therefore, the demand at a price above 3 NOK is zero.
We are told that 250 people have a willingness to pay of 3 NOK per kWh.
We also know that each jacuzzi uses 2,000 kWh per year, which means that if the price is 3 NOK or
lower, demand jumps from 0 to 500,000 kWh (from the 250 people with a willingness to pay of 3
NOK):

250⋅2 000 = 500 000 𝑘𝑤ℎ
Even if the price drops further, demand does not increase as long as the price stays above 2 NOK.
In the diagram, we have kWh in thousands on the x-axis, so demand is marked up to point 500 on the
x-axis, which represents 500,000 kWh.
If the price drops below 2 NOK, however, we see that demand jumps to 1,500,000 kWh.
The reason is that the 500 people with a willingness to pay of 2 NOK will now also turn on their
jacuzzis.
In total, there are now:
(250+500)⋅2 000 = 1 500 000 𝑘𝑤ℎ
If the price falls all the way down to 1.5 NOK, the group with the lowest willingness to pay enters the
market, causing total demand to increase to 2,000,000 kWh.
(250+500+250)⋅2 000 = 2 000 000 𝑘𝑤ℎ
If the price falls below 1.5 NOK, demand does not increase further.
Quite simply, there are no more jacuzzis that need electricity.

Assume a price of 0.5 kroner:
Then only the hydropower plants will produce, since the price is lower than the gas power

For each unit of electricity produced, the hydropower producers earn a contribution margin
(profit) of 0.3 kroner (0.5 – 0.2 = 0.3).
They will produce at full capacity, i.e., 1,000 units of electricity as long as the price is 0.5

which gives a total producer surplus of:
0,3⋅1000 = 300
Assume a price of 1 krone:
The hydropower plants will still produce, since the price is higher than their marginal cost.
The hydropower plants now have a contribution margin of 0.8 kroner per unit of electricity
(1 – 0.2 = 0.8).
The gas power plants have a marginal cost of 1 krone, which is exactly equal to the price, so
they are indifferent between producing and not producing.
Either way, they end up with zero profit.
The total producer surplus is therefore:
0,8⋅1 000 + 0 = 800
Assume a price of 2 kroner:
The hydropower plants will produce since the price is higher than their marginal cost.
The hydropower plants now have a contribution margin of 1.8 kroner per unit of electricity
(2 – 0.2 = 1.8).
The gas power plants, with a marginal cost of 1 krone, have a contribution margin of 1 krone
per unit (2 – 1 = 1).
They will now start producing, so the total supply increases to 1,500 units of electricity.
The total producer surplus is:
(1,8⋅1 000)+(1⋅500) = 1 800 + 500 = 2 300

questions.solutionMarkdown:
Exercise 1
a)
This means that each individual producer is too small an economic player to influence
the market price—in this case, the price of wooden furniture. No matter how much
or how little the producer chooses to produce and sell, the market price for the
furniture will remain unchanged. If the furniture price is $500, it will stay at that level
regardless of the individual producer’s production decision. This does not mean that
the sum of all these production decisions doesn’t affect the price. And of course, it
doesn’t mean that the price will always be $500 in our example. Many factors can
cause the price to change—such as tariffs—but not the production decision of a
single firm in a perfectly competitive market.
b)
Before the tariff war, the marginal cost for all producers was $500. They all adjusted
their production levels to this price, meaning they earned an additional revenue of
$500 for every piece of furniture sold. This gives producers a simple production
decision:
If the marginal cost (i.e., the cost of producing one more unit) is lower than $500, it
pays to increase production.
If the marginal cost is higher than $500, they are producing too much, since $500
does not cover the cost of the last unit.
Thus, they will all adjust their production levels so that marginal cost equals $500,
which is the price they receive in the market.
c)
If they keep production unchanged, marginal cost will increase by 20%, meaning
marginal cost has risen from $500 to $600.

d)
e)
We see that the price in the new equilibrium is lower than 600. If we imagine that the producer
maintained production and the price rose from 500 to 600, there would be an excess supply.
Consumers would not buy as many furniture pieces as before if the price increased to 600. Demand
would drop. In the new equilibrium, the price will rise by less than 100—just enough to once again
create equality between the supply and demand for wooden furniture. How much the price increases
depends on the slope of the demand curve, i.e., on the price sensitivity of the demand side. If

consumers’ demand for wooden furniture is very price sensitive, that means the demand curve is
flat. In that case, the price increase from the tariff will be small, but production will decrease
significantly.
If the demand for wooden furniture is instead not very price sensitive, this means that the demand
curve is very steep. In that case, the increase in the market price will be almost as large as the
increase in marginal cost of 100. The price rises by nearly 20%, and the production volume is only
slightly affected.

questions.title: Topic 6 · Exercise 1
questions.promptMarkdown:
Exercise 1
Explain the meaning of the following terms:
a) Labour force
b) Unemployment rate
c) Employment rate
d) Participation rate
rubricChecks: Address a) Labour force
Address b) Unemployment rate
Address c) Employment rate
Address d) Participation rate
hints: Write the three groups first: employed, unemployed, outside the labour force.
Labour force = employed + unemployed. Unemployment rate divides by labour force; employment and participation rates divide by the relevant working-age population.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Exercise 1
These quantities are defined by CORE in Chapter 1.3 below. Labour market statistics.
a) The labour force consists of all individuals who are either employed or actively
seeking employment. People who are not in the labour force include, for example,
students, pensioners, and individuals who have chosen not to seek work.
b) The unemployment rate shows the proportion of the labour force that is without a
job but actively seeking work. It is calculated as the number of unemployed divided
by the labour force, expressed as a percentage. It's important to note that, to be
counted as unemployed, a person must meet certain criteria: they must have been
without work for a certain period and must have shown interest in working by
actively applying for jobs. A high unemployment rate means many people who want
to work are out of employment.
c) The employment rate measures the proportion of the working-age population
(typically 15–74 or 15–64 years old) who are employed. In other words, it shows how
many of the “adults” are working. It is calculated as the number of employed people
divided by the working-age population, expressed as a percentage. A high
employment rate means that a large share of the working-age population is
employed.
d) The labour force participation rate shows the proportion of the working-age
population—the “adults”—who are either employed or actively seeking employment
(i.e., who are in the labour force). It is calculated as the labour force divided by the
working-age population, expressed as a percentage. High labour force participation
means that a large share of adults want to work. An important factor that varies
between countries is the share of women in the labour force, which is influenced by
factors such as welfare policies and cultural norms.

questions.solutionMarkdown:
Exercise 2
a) The answer depends on whether those who retire are of working age or not when they retire.
We know that:
𝑁𝑢𝑚𝑏𝑒𝑟 𝑜𝑓 𝑒𝑚𝑝𝑙𝑜𝑦𝑒𝑑
𝐸𝑚𝑝𝑙𝑜𝑦𝑚𝑒𝑛𝑡 𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑒 =
𝑁𝑢𝑚𝑝𝑒𝑟 𝑜𝑓 𝑝𝑒𝑟𝑠𝑜𝑛𝑠 𝑖𝑛 𝑤𝑜𝑟𝑘𝑖𝑛𝑔 𝑎𝑔𝑒
If more people of working age retire, the number of employed individuals will decrease, while the
denominator (number of people of working age) remains unchanged. This leads to a decline in the
employment rate.
However, if the increase in the number of retirees is due to more people outside of working age
retiring, the employment rate will not be affected, since these individuals were not included in the
calculation (not even in the numerator) to begin with.

Note: In the figure in the exercise text, everyone aged 20 to 64 is assumed to be of working age. You
can be of working age without actually being able to work. Statistics Norway (SSB) publishes
equivalent figures based on the assumption that those between 15 and 74 years are of working age.
It is not a learning goal to remember whether the age range is 15–74 or 20–64. What’s important is
to understand that the employment rate measures the proportion of “adults” who are in work.
b) No, an increase in the employment rate does not necessarily mean that unemployment has fallen.
Unemployment (as a percentage) measures the share of the labour force that is not employed. The
labour force is not the same as all people of working age. Within the adult population, some may be
unable to work, while others may be full-time students (do you know any?). If you are a full-time
student or unable to work, you are not included in the labour force.
The employment rate can increase without unemployment in the economy falling. To understand
this, let’s look at an example:
Assume we have an economy with:
• Working-age population: 1,000 people
• Employed: 600 people
• Unemployed: 100 people
• Labour force (employed + unemployed) = 700 people
• Inactive (students, disabled, etc.): 300 people
Then we can calculate:
600
𝐸𝑚𝑝𝑙𝑜𝑦𝑚𝑒𝑛𝑟 𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑒: = 60 %
1.000
100
𝑈𝑛𝑒𝑚𝑝𝑙𝑜𝑦𝑚𝑒𝑛𝑡 𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑒: = 14,3 %
700
Now let’s assume that 50 people who were previously students or unable to work start looking for a
job.
Some of them—let’s say 30 people—immediately find employment, while the remaining 20 are
unemployed.
The labour force increases by 50 people.
What has happened to the employment rate and the unemployment rate?
• Working-age population: 1,000 people (unchanged)
• Employed: 630 people (600 + 30)
• Unemployed: 120 people (100 + 20)
• Labour force (employed + unemployed) = 750 people
• Inactive (students, disabled, etc.): 250 people (300 - 50)
We can now again calculate the two indicators:

630
𝐸𝑚𝑝𝑙𝑜𝑦𝑚𝑒𝑛𝑟 𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑒: = 63 %
1.000
120
𝑈𝑛𝑒𝑚𝑝𝑙𝑜𝑦𝑚𝑒𝑛𝑡 𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑒: = 16 %
750
Here we see that both the employment rate and the unemployment rate have increased at the same
time. So, the employment rate can increase without a smaller share of (the now larger) labour force
becoming unemployed, if a large enough share of the new labour market entrants become
unemployed. If, on the other hand, all the new labour force entrants had immediately found jobs,
the employment rate would have increased, and the unemployment rate would have decreased (no
new unemployed, but a larger labour force).
c) The employment rate is calculated as a percentage of the working-age population. The
unemployment rate is calculated as a percentage of the labour force. Thus, the employment rate also
includes those outside the labour force—the “inactive.” Among the inactive are groups such as
students, early retirees, individuals with health issues, people who have given up looking for work,
and those with caregiving responsibilities. Because the inactive are not counted in the labour force,
the employment rate can help reveal whether low unemployment is due to high employment or
simply because many have exited the labour market.
d) We look at the darkest line, which shows the employment rate in Norway during the period and
compare it with other countries. We see that Norway’s employment rate has remained relatively
stable and high throughout the entire period. Until 2014, Norway had the highest employment rate
among the countries included. We can see that the employment rate fluctuates with developments
in the economy. Before the financial crisis that occurred in 2008, the employment rate rose, only to
fall afterward. In autumn 2014, oil prices fell sharply, and during this period, we can see that the
employment rate in Norway dropped, but not in the other countries. In 2020, we also see a drop in
the employment rate across all countries, but the decline in Norway and the Netherlands was smaller
than in the other countries.

questions.title: Topic 6 · Exercise 4
questions.promptMarkdown:
Exercise 4
Explain whether the wage-setting curve or the price-setting curve will shift up, down, or remain
unchanged in the following situations:
1. Unemployment benefits increase.
2. There is less social stigma attached to being unemployed.
3. Price competition in the product market becomes weaker.
4. Work tasks become easier.
5. Workers become less productive.
6. The unemployment rate decreases because other firms increase their demand for labour.
rubricChecks: Verify key point: Unemployment benefits increase If unemployment benefits increase, it means people will have higher income if they lose their job.
Verify key point: The reservation wage—the lowest wage a person is willing to accept to take a new job— will therefore rise.
Verify key point: This means that for each level of employment, firms must offer higher real wages to attract and motivate workers to make an effort.
hints: For each shock, ask whether it changes workers’ effort incentives, firms’ pricing/productivity, or an axis variable.

Work through the list separately: benefits, stigma and effort affect WS; competition and productivity affect PS in this model. A change in employment/unemployment itself is a movement along the existing relationship when the background determinants stay fixed.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Exercise 4
1. Unemployment benefits increase
If unemployment benefits increase, it means people will have higher income if they lose their
job. The reservation wage—the lowest wage a person is willing to accept to take a new job—
will therefore rise. This means that for any given level of employment, workers will demand a
higher real wage than before to be motivated to exert effort, which causes the wage-setting
curve to shift upwards.
2. There is less social stigma associated with being unemployed
If the social stigma of being unemployed is reduced, the quality of life without a job increases
relative to the quality of life with a job, which increases the reservation wage. This means
that for each level of employment, firms must offer higher real wages to attract and motivate
workers to make an effort. Again, the wage-setting curve shifts upward.
3. Price competition in the product market weakens
Weaker competition in the product market means that firms have more power to raise
prices. The less competition, the higher the markup. A higher price level reduces real wages,
which pushes the price-setting line downward.
4. Jobs become easier
If job tasks become easier, this can be interpreted as a reduction in the disutility of effort for
the employee. The reservation wage will not change, since it is not directly affected by the
effort required in the current job. But since the cost of effort has decreased, employers can
offer a lower wage and still provide sufficient incentive for workers to put in effort.
Therefore, the wage-setting curve shifts downward.
5. Workers become less productive
If workers become less productive, the productivity line (output per worker per hour) shifts
downward. As long as market competition remains unchanged, this means the price-setting
curve must also shift downward to keep the markup unchanged. The lower the labor
productivity, the lower the real wage that corresponds to the profit-maximizing markup.
6. The unemployment rate falls because other firms increase demand for labor
If the unemployment rate decreases, workers perceive it as easier to find a new job, which
increases the wage required to prevent shirking. For a given size of the labor force, the wage-
setting curve does not shift, because unemployment is measured on the horizontal axis.
Instead of the curve shifting, we move rightward along the wage-setting curve. Remember:
we measure employment to the right and unemployment to the left (from the labor force),
so the further to the right we move, the lower the unemployment.

questions.title: Topic 7 · Exercise 1
questions.promptMarkdown:
Exercise 1
The Lorenz curve provides a graphical description of how income is distributed in the population.
a) The Lorenz curve shows the relationship between two quantities (variables) in a coordinate
system. Explain what is measured on the horizontal and the vertical axis in this coordinate
system.
b) Draw (freehand) a Lorenz curve for an economy where everyone has the same income.
c) Then draw a Lorenz curve for an economy described as follows: 90% are employees, all with
the same annual income. The remaining 10% are capital owners without wage income but
with capital income that is equal for all. The capital income of each capital owner is assumed
to be much higher than the wage income of the employees. The total income of the capital
owners constitutes 50% of total income in the economy.
d) Same as c), but now assume that the incomes of the capital owners have increased sharply
and now make up 60% of total income. The wage level is as before.
e) Same as in c), but assume the capital owners can be divided into two groups: 90% of the
capital owners (i.e. 9% of the total population) have annual capital income at the same level
as employees. The remaining 10% of the capital owners (1% of the total population) have
capital income that is much higher.
rubricChecks: Address a) The Lorenz curve shows the relationship between two quantities (variables) in a coordinate system
Address b) Draw (freehand) a Lorenz curve for an economy where everyone has the same income
Address c) Then draw a Lorenz curve for an economy described as follows: 90% are employees, all with the same annual...
Address d) Same as c), but now assume that the incomes of the capital owners have increased sharply and now make up...
hints: Order people from poorest to richest, using cumulative population on x and cumulative income on y.

For each equal-income group draw a straight segment. At a kink use the cumulative population share and the TOTAL income share it receives. For e), identify the 99% with the same income before working out the remaining top group’s share.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Exercise 1
a) We will explain this by quoting Lorenz himself. He deserves it, since he is referred to as one of
our most well-known unknown economists. In 1905, at the age of 29, he published an article in
which he introduced a hand-drawn curve that he believed provided a good representation of
income distribution in an economy. The curve later took his name, and it's the one you can now
read about in CORE. He wrote:
“Plot along one axis cumulated per cents, of the population from poorest to richest, and
along the other the per cent, of the total wealth held by these per cents, of the
population.”
For example, the number 25 on the horizontal axis captures the poorest 25% of the
population, all of whom have lower income (or wealth, which Lorenz focused on) than
the remaining 75%. On the vertical axis, we read off the percentage share of total income
(or total wealth, if we are looking at wealth distribution). For instance, if we start from
the 25 mark on the horizontal axis (the poorest 25%) and move straight up to the Lorenz
curve, then read the number directly to the left on the vertical axis, that number tells us
what share of total income the poorest 25% of the population holds.
b) This situation, of course, Lorenz described as a special case – or as a point of comparison:
"To illustrate, take a population in which wealth is distributed equally. ( . . . ). This will give a
straight line."
In other words, like this:
If everyone has the same income, then 25% of the population (we don’t need to say “the
poorest” – since everyone is equally rich or poor) will have 25% of the total income. As you

can see in the figure here. Since the endpoints are the same on both axes (100), the straight
line will be a 45-degree line, with a slope of 1.
c) If the situation is as described here, the Lorenz curve will lie below the straight line, which serves
as a point of comparison. Why? Because the poorest 25% will not have 25% of the total income.
The 10% of the population who are capital owners receive a larger share of the income. The
income difference between the richest 10% and the remaining 90%, who are wage earners,
determines how far below the Lorenz curve will lie. Here is an example:
Lorenz wrote: “With an unequal distribution, the curves will always begin and end in the same points
as with an unequal distribution [i.e. started at 0 and ended at 1], but they will be bent in the middle”
d) The Lorenz curve will now move further away from the 45-degree line and position itself like
this:
Since capital income increases while labor income remains unchanged, the 90% of the population
who are wage earners will receive a smaller share of total income. In part (c), they received 50% of

total income, but now they receive only 40%. How do we know that? Well, the assignment text
states that the capital owners receive 60% of total income, which means 40% is left for the workers.
If we assume that total capital income remains unchanged, so that the change described here only
involves a redistribution of capital income among capital owners (e.g., more concentrated ownership
in companies), then the workers’ share of total income will be the same as in (c), i.e., 50%. The
change happens only within the group of capital owners: 90% of the capital owners (who make up
9% of the total population) have the same income as the workers, while the remaining 10% of capital
owners (who make up 1% of the population) now earn much more. The Lorenz curve shifts to the
new dashed line below.

questions.promptMarkdown:
Exercise 2
Below you see Figure 2.7 from CORE Macroeconomics. If you read the figure description in CORE,
you’ll see that the economy consists of 100 people, of whom 80 are employed.
a) In the figure on the right, CORE assumes there are 10 unemployed people. But what do they
assume about the income level of the unemployed?
b) How would you explain why the labor force in the figure is placed at 90, and not 100, which
would represent all adults?
c) Explain what the number 60 on the vertical axis in the figure on the right tells us.
d) Assume that weaker competition in the markets reduces the labor share from 0.6 to 0.4 in
the figure on the left. Explain and illustrate in a figure how this affects the real wage level,
the Lorenz curve, and the Gini coefficient.
rubricChecks: Address a) In the figure on the right, CORE assumes there are 10 unemployed people
Address b) How would you explain why the labor force in the figure is placed at 90, and not 100, which would...
Address c) Explain what the number 60 on the vertical axis in the figure on the right tells us
Address d) Assume that weaker competition in the markets reduces the labor share from 0.6 to 0.4 in the figure on the...
hints: Keep working-age population, labour force, employment and the population used for the Lorenz curve distinct.

Read the source’s zero-income assumption for unemployed people. A smaller labour share lowers PS’s real wage and redistributes total income away from workers; then trace the Lorenz and Gini consequences.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Exercise 2
a) The figure assumes that the unemployed have an income of zero: The 10 unemployed individuals
receive 0% of the total income.
b) This is because the 10 people who are capital owners are neither employed nor unemployed – and
therefore are not part of the labor force.
c) The number tells us that those who are part of the labor force (90 employed workers and 10
unemployed) receive 60% of the total income. 40% of the income goes to the capital owners.
d) This shifts the price-setting curve downward. Since it does not affect the position of the wage-
setting curve, the new labor market equilibrium will be characterized by lower real wages and higher
unemployment. This pushes the Lorenz curve (the two line segments) further to the right. Both
effects are illustrated below:

As the curve is drawn, it is assumed that the unemployed have zero income. The unemployed portion
of the population (far left) therefore receives 0% of the total national income. Initially, wage earners
receive 60% of total value creation, so when we sum up all workers and unemployed individuals,
they receive 60% of the total income. The remaining 40% goes to capital owners.
When market power increases and workers receive only 40%, the kink in the Lorenz curve will
therefore drop from 60 to 40 in the figure, while the lower part of the curve starts further to the right
on the baseline, since more people have become unemployed and have zero income.

Since the Gini coefficient measures the area between the Lorenz curve and the 45-degree line, it will
increase. You will never be asked to calculate it! You only need to know that a higher Gini coefficient
indicates that the income distribution has become more unequal.
