questions.title: Topic 8 · Exercise 1
questions.promptMarkdown:
Exercise 1
Assume a country produces only one
thing—tourism. We can say the country
lives off tourism. The country has a
beautiful mountain peak that people
from all over the world come to climb.
The tourism economy, which together
makes mountain climbing trips possible
for foreigners, consists of several
industries.
The tour guides, who accompany
tourists to the top, sell the climbing
trips for a total value of 10 million NOK. The tour guides purchase climbing equipment (needed by all
tourists) from local equipment producers for a total value of 5 million NOK. The hotels that
accommodate the tourists sell overnight stays including food for a total value of 50 million NOK. The
food that tourists eat during their stay is produced by local food producers and sold to the hotels for
10 million NOK. All maintenance and cleaning of the hotels is done by firms in the cleaning industry,
which sell their services to the hotels for 10 million NOK.
a) What is the country’s gross domestic product (GDP)?
b) Assume all tourists are foreigners. What is the value of exports?
c) The country’s income (measured by GDP) accrues to its citizens as labor and capital income.
These incomes are used for consumption and investment. Since everyone works in tourism,
all consumption and investment must be imported. Can we determine the size of household
consumption?
rubricChecks: Address a) What is the country’s gross domestic product (GDP)
Address b) Assume all tourists are foreigners
Address c) The country’s income (measured by GDP) accrues to its citizens as labor and capital income
hints: Build a small value-added table for the guides, equipment, hotels, food and cleaning industries.

Subtract intermediate purchases from each industry’s sales, then sum. For exports count final sales to foreigners; for household consumption use the expenditure identity to see what is and is not separately identified.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Exercise 1
a) GDP is equal to the market value of all production in the country, minus the value of
intermediate goods (inputs) used by firms in the production process. CORE defines it in
Chapter 3.2 (Macroeconomics) as follows:
”The sum of the outputs of the different sectors of the economy. Production is measured by
the value added⁠ by each industry: this means that the cost of goods and services used as inputs to
production is subtracted from the value of output. These inputs will be measured in the value
added of other industries, which prevents double-counting when measuring production in the
economy as a whole. The example of the production of a cotton shirt, below, illustrates how this is
done.”
To calculate GDP in this small, simple economy, we must sum the production value from all sectors,
subtracting the value of intermediate goods (inputs). This gives us a GDP of 60 million NOK. See the
table below.
Sector Gross production Inputs, Contributin to GDP,
value, mill. kroner mill.kroner mill.kroner
Tour guides 10 5 5
Equipment 5 0 5
Hotels 50 10+10 30
Food 10 10
Cleaning 10 10
Total 85 25 60
Here, we have listed each sector and the sales price of what they produce, subtracting any
intermediate goods purchased from other sectors. In this way, we avoid double counting.
b) Exports are then equal to 10 million (tour guides) + 50 million (hotels) = 60 million. The entire GDP
of this tourist nation goes to exports!
c) Here, we must bring forward the accounting identity that shows how GDP can be used:
(https://core-econ.org/the-economy/macroeconomics/03-aggregate-demand-03-components-of-
gdp.html)
Disregarding changes in inventories, it can be written as:
GDP = private consumption + government consumption + investment + exports – imports
Since this small tourist country has no public sector, GDP will cover private consumption, investment,
and net exports (exports – imports):
GDP = private consumption + investment + exports – imports.Vi vet altså at
60 mill. = Privat konsum + Investeringer + 60 mill. – Import

This can be reformulated as:
0 = Private consumption + Investment – Imports
And again to:
Imports = Private consumption + Investment
Since the entire GDP goes to exports, all consumption and investment must be imported. It is entirely
possible to run a trade deficit (financed by borrowing). A trade deficit means that imports are greater
than exports. This would occur in this case if the value of what is spent on consumption and
investment (imports) exceeds the value of exports (revenue from tourism). We cannot know how
large or small total consumption and investment in the country are, and therefore cannot determine
the country’s net exports.

questions.title: Topic 8 · Exercise 2
questions.promptMarkdown:
Exercise 2
In descriptions of Norway’s economic development, a distinction is often made between GDP and
Mainland GDP (Fastlands-BNP).
a) Briefly explain the difference between these two measures.
b) In the figure below, you see the development in the annual percentage change in these two
measures from 1999 to 2019, measured in constant prices. Assume that the underlying
growth in GDP (what CORE refers to as “normal GDP”) is 2% during this period.
c) Briefly describe the different business cycle phases in the Norwegian economy.
rubricChecks: Address a) Briefly explain the difference between these two measures
Address b) In the figure below, you see the development in the annual percentage change in these two measures from...
Address c) Briefly describe the different business cycle phases in the Norwegian economy
hints: Separate the coverage of the GDP measures from the definitions of business-cycle phases.
For the chart, compare actual real growth with the stated 2% normal growth AND ask whether output itself falls. Those tests correspond to different recession definitions.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Exercise 2
a) The difference is explained by the production value in oil and gas and maritime
transport. In particular, it is the extraction of oil and gas on the Norwegian
continental shelf that makes up a significant difference. Between 20 and 30% of
Norway’s GDP comes from oil and gas and maritime transport, and this is not
included in the GDP for Mainland Norway.
b) If we stick to the NBER definition, as presented in CORE chapter 3.5, Norway
experienced a recession in 2009. It was short-lived, as GDP returned to positive
growth already in 2010. In the periods 2001–2003, 2008–2011, 2013–2016, and from
2018 onwards, GDP growth was below 2%. When GDP grows less than potential GDP,
we often refer to this as a downturn, and conversely, in the other years from 1999 to
2019, the economy was in an upturn since actual GDP grew faster than potential
GDP. Note that even though we know the GDP growth rate relative to the underlying
growth, we do not have enough information to determine whether this can be
described as a boom or a recession. A recession occurs when actual GDP is lower
than potential GDP (see CORE’s alternative definition).

questions.promptMarkdown:
Exercise 3
We now return to the tourist country from Assignment 1.
Assume that climate change has had macroeconomic consequences for the country. The glacier,
previously a major attraction on the way up to the summit, has suddenly melted. The number of
tourists has almost halved overnight.
a) Has this event brought the country into a recession? You must justify your answer.
b) Illustrate in a figure the income development over time for one of the tour guides. The figure
should cover a period both before and after the news of the melting glacier.
c) Assume the guide realized years ago that the glacier would melt and impact tourism.
Illustrate in the same figure the development in the guide’s consumption. Show the effect of
potential “impatience”, or what is referred to in English as “present bias.”

questions.solutionMarkdown:
Exercise 3
a) In CORE, you will see that several definitions of a recession are used. (https://core-
econ.org/the-economy/macroeconomics/03-aggregate-demand-05-growth-
fluctuations.html#the-business-cycle)
The most common definition says that a country is in a recession if GDP is falling, while
an alternative definition says the country is in a recession if GDP is below its normal level.
The challenge with the alternative definition is that one must also determine what the
“normal” level is.
This becomes important in the example described here:
According to the standard definition, the country enters a recession when the glacier
melts, as GDP falls due to the absence of tourists.
However, the low number of tourists may be considered the new normal, since the

glacier will not return. GDP has fallen to a “new normal,” and in that case, it would not
be defined as a recession if we use the alternative definition.
b)
To illustrate the income of a tour guide over time, before and after the glacier melted, we can
assume that income was at a relatively high level for a period. At a certain point, the glacier melts,
and the number of tourists is nearly halved overnight. As a result, the tour guide’s income will also
drop to nearly half of what it was before the event.
c)
A person or household with present bias places more weight on consumption now than in the future.
They may prefer to spend all of their current income immediately, even if they know that income will
be lower in the future. For a tour guide with present bias, the consumption path will follow the
income path, illustrated by the blue dashed line, which tracks income over time.
If the guide does not have present bias, they will reduce their consumption as soon as they realize
that the glacier will melt and future income will decline. In this case, the guide will start saving
immediately in order to smooth consumption over time. When the glacier melts and actual income
drops, the guide won’t need to reduce consumption as drastically, since they can rely on their
savings. This is similarly illustrated by the red dashed line, showing a smoother consumption path
than income.
See ch. 3.10 - Limits to consumption smoothing, figure 3.19 for explanation.

Bruk av oppsparte midler

We do not provide solution comments for this one. You will not be tested on this index in the exam,
but it is a great way to reflect on what you believe should be included in a ranking of quality of life
and standard of living. You choose how much weight to place on the different aspects of quality of

questions.promptMarkdown:
Exercise 1
When we compare economic figures across different points in time, we must account for inflation to
get an accurate picture of developments.
The figure below shows the development of household consumption per year from 2010 to 2022,
both in current prices and in constant prices. The data is taken from Statistics Norway (SSB).
The blue dashed line shows consumption in current prices, while the solid red line shows household
consumption in constant prices.
a) Which year has been used as the base year?
b) You can see that the graph for constant price consumption lies below the current price graph
after 2015. Briefly explain what this says about inflation after 2015.
c) As you explained in (b), does the fact that the red graph lies below the dashed one mean that
inflation must have been positive in all years after 2015? Justify your answer.
d) Use the table in the figure to calculate the value of the consumer price index (CPI) from 2010
to 2022, in such a way that the base year has a value of 100. This task is meant to help you
understand how indexes are constructed. In the workplace, you may need to adjust economic
figures for inflation, or interpret reports using index values.
e) Use this CPI to estimate the annual inflation from 2011 to 2022.
rubricChecks: Address a) Which year has been used as the base year
Address b) You can see that the graph for constant price consumption lies below the current price graph after 2015
Address c) As you explained in (b), does the fact that the red graph lies below the dashed one mean that inflation...
Address d) Use the table in the figure to calculate the value of the consumer price index (CPI) from 2010 to 2022, in...
hints: Current prices include price changes; constant prices value quantities using base-year prices.

At the base year the two values coincide. Form the index as current/constant × 100, then calculate annual inflation from successive index values. Being above the base-year price level does not imply every year had positive inflation.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Exercise 1
a) We see that 2015 is used as the base year because consumption at current and constant prices is
equal in that year.
b) This means that, on average, the price level for all years after 2015—as measured by the
Consumer Price Index—is higher than prices in 2015. We know this because consumption measured
in constant prices is lower than consumption measured in current prices.
c) No, that is not correct. In principle, we could have had shorter periods of falling prices (deflation)
after 2015, but not large enough declines for prices to fall below the 2015 level. In reality, the CPI has
not fallen after 2015, but the point is that the figure alone does not rule out deflation in a short
period—even if consumption in constant 2015 prices lies below consumption in current prices after
2015.
d) We will go through this step by step, since CORE does not cover this very thoroughly. They explain
how the price index is calculated ( https://core-econ.org/the-economy/macroeconomics/04-
inflation-and-employment-02-measuring-the-economy-inflation.html )
When we go into such detail, it is because everyone studying economics should understand precisely
what is meant when something is reported in “constant prices,” and how this is done in practice.
Statistics Norway (SSB) calculates the Consumer Price Index (CPI). It shows how prices for goods and
services develop on average from year to year (in fact, it is updated every month). It is an index and
therefore requires a reference year. The index value is set to 100 in the reference year, and the price
development determines how the index value evolves before and after the reference year. For
example, if the reference year is 2015 and the Consumer Price Index has a value of 105 at a later
point in time, it means that prices at that later time are on average 5% higher than prices in 2015. Let
CPIₜ represent the value of the Consumer Price Index in year t.
Now we need a few formulas:
If we know the Consumer Price Index, we can calculate, for example, consumption in constant prices
as follows:

𝐶𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑢𝑚𝑝𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛 𝑖𝑛 𝑦𝑒𝑎𝑟 𝑡,𝑖𝑛 𝑛𝑜𝑚𝑖𝑛𝑎𝑙 𝑣𝑎𝑙𝑢𝑒
= ∙𝐶𝑃𝐼
𝐶𝑃𝐼 2015
𝑡
Since we use 2015 as the reference year, CPI₍₂₀₁₅₎ = 100, and we often say that we are measuring

questions.title: Topic 9 · Exercise 2
questions.promptMarkdown:
Exercise 2
The figure below is taken from CORE, figure 4.5.
a) What is the inflation rate if the economy is located at point A?
b) Assume the economy experiences a sudden drop in demand, e.g., due to a fall in exports.
Explain what happens to unemployment, the real wage level, and prices (CPI) in the short
and long run.
rubricChecks: Address a) What is the inflation rate if the economy is located at point A
Address b) Assume the economy experiences a sudden drop in demand, e.g., due to a fall in exports
hints: The WS–PS diagram does not by itself give a numerical inflation rate at its equilibrium.

A demand fall changes employment first. Trace the bargaining gap, wage and price adjustments, and the return toward the structural equilibrium under the course model’s assumptions; distinguish lower inflation from falling prices.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Exercise 2
a) We cannot know what the inflation rate is at point A. What we do know is that the real wage
remains constant, which in turn means that inflation equals the growth in nominal wages.
b) What happens in the short term is that employment falls due to a drop in demand, and
unemployment rises. This is likely the first thing that happens, before prices and wages start to
adjust. We then move to the left of point A, for example to point B: The real wage remains fixed in
the short term, but unemployment increases.
Higher unemployment increases the value of having a job, and firms now experience that the real
wage is higher than what is required to motivate employees to put in effort (as indicated by the
wage-setting curve). This will lead firms to reduce the wage level (or in practice, to push harder in
negotiations to significantly slow down wage growth). Then the real wage begins to fall, but it cannot
fall below point C, because for real wages below the wage-setting curve, workers will not be willing
to make an effort.
When the real wage falls, firms experience improved profitability. Lower costs due to lower real
wages will lead firms to reduce the prices of their products. This begins to lift the real wage back up,
and with that comes increased purchasing power and demand. Increased demand leads to higher
employment, so that in the long run we can return to point A, with unchanged real wages and
employment.

questions.title: Topic 9 · Exercise 3
questions.promptMarkdown:
Exercise 3
The figure below is taken from the National Budget for 2025 (White Paper No. 1 (2024–2025)). It
shows the development in house prices from January 2020 to August 2024.
a) Both curves start at 100 (January 2020). That doesn’t mean the price per square meter was
100 kroner, but what does it mean?
b) The red curve shows real housing prices, while the blue shows nominal price development.
How would you explain the terms “real” and “nominal” in this context?
rubricChecks: Address a) Both curves start at 100 (January 2020)
Address b) The red curve shows real housing prices, while the blue shows nominal price development
hints: An index of 100 is a normalisation relative to the starting period.
Read nominal house prices in money terms and real prices relative to the chosen price deflator. The starting index does not reveal a price per square metre.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Exercise 3
a) This means that the curves show the level of housing prices from month to month
relative to the price level in January 2020. This makes it easier to assess the
percentage change in prices. For example, it appears that the blue curve (nominal
housing prices) passed the value 104 in September 2020. This means that the price
per square meter in September 2020 was 4% higher than the price level in January
2020. If we follow the red curve, we see how the real price development has been,
month by month. Note: If the blue and red curves cross in a given month—such as in
late 2020—it does not mean that the real price (red) and the nominal price (blue) are
equal. It means that both the real and nominal prices are approximately 7% higher
than their respective levels in January 2020.
b) The difference is that the real curve shows price development adjusted for inflation,
while the nominal price shows how much homes are sold for each month (in NOK per
square meter). The higher the inflation, the greater the distance between these two
curves.

questions.title: Topic 9 · Exercise 4
questions.promptMarkdown:
Exercise 4
The figure below is taken from NOU 2024:11 ("Low Wage Commission").
The abbreviation “h.a.” refers to the right vertical axis, while “v.a.” refers to the left vertical axis.
Below the figure, you can see what the various lines in the diagram represent.
a) Explain what is meant by the term “real wage” (reallønn in Norwegian)
b) Based on the figure, describe the growth in real wages in Norway over the past 10 years,
from 2014 to 2023.
c) What about real wage development in the previous 10-year period, from 2005 to 2014? How
would you describe it?
d) Use the figure to estimate inflation in the years 2000, 2010, and 2023.
rubricChecks: Address a) Explain what is meant by the term “real wage” (reallønn in Norwegian)
Address b) Based on the figure, describe the growth in real wages in Norway over the past 10 years, from 2014 to 2023
Address c) What about real wage development in the previous 10-year period, from 2005 to 2014
Address d) Use the figure to estimate inflation in the years 2000, 2010, and 2023
hints: Check which series uses each vertical axis and distinguish nominal wage growth from real wage growth.
Purchasing power depends on wages relative to prices. Approximate inflation by nominal wage growth minus real wage growth for the named years, making clear these are estimates read from the chart.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Exercise 4
a) Real wages show what we can actually buy with our salary—that is, our nominal wages adjusted
for the price level. If we receive a wage increase of 5% while prices rise by 3%, then real wages
increase by 2% (5% - 3%). You can buy more than before because your wage has increased more than
prices. If, on the other hand, prices increase more than your wage, your purchasing power will
decrease—even if your wage appears higher on paper (your nominal wage is higher, but your real
wage has fallen).
b) Real wages are represented by the red, rising curve, which can be read on the right axis. The axis
starts at 60 and ends at 110. This is not the real wage in kroner per hour, but—as stated in the figure
caption—an index (as you read about in ch. 1.4 regarding the use of indexes). Using indexes is
common when showing development over time. A well-known example is the Consumer Price Index
(CPI).
Here, we are looking at the real wage index. It is indexed to 100 in 2015. What does that mean? It
means that real wages in all other years are measured relative to the real wage in 2015. For example,
you can see that the real wage index is around 95 in 2011. That means real wages in 2011 were 95%
of the 2015 level.
𝑅𝑒𝑎𝑙 𝑤𝑎𝑔𝑒
2011
⋅100 = 95
𝑅𝑒𝑎𝑙 𝑤𝑎𝑔𝑒
2015
or
𝑅𝑒𝑎𝑙 𝑤𝑎𝑔𝑒 =0,95∙𝑅𝑒𝑎𝑙 𝑤𝑎𝑔𝑒
2011 2015
We can see from the figure that the red curve flattens out after 2013. This means that real wages
have remained almost unchanged over the 10 years since 2014. Since real wages reflect the

purchasing power of our income (what we can afford to buy with our salary), and real wage growth
thus shows the development of our purchasing power, this indicates that purchasing power has
changed very little over the past 10 years.
c) The previous 10-year period was different. Real wages rose steadily from 2005 to 2014, so
that the real wage level in 2005 was about 20% below the 2015 level. Why? The index was
around 80 in 2005.
d) Real wage growth is defined as nominal wage growth (i.e., the increase in hourly wages in
kroner) minus inflation (price growth). This means that inflation equals nominal wage growth
minus real wage growth.
From the figure, we can determine both nominal and real wage growth. The difference
between the blue line (top) and the green line (bottom) is therefore inflation. By estimating
visually, we can approximate inflation to be about 3.2 in 2000, 2.7 in 2010, and 5.3 in 2023.
See the figure below for how this has been estimated visually.

questions.title: Lecture 7 · Nora / tax and transfers · Question 1
questions.promptMarkdown:
1. The budget constraint.
a) Write down Nora’s budget constraint as an equation, with consumption c on the left-hand side
and hours of free time t on the right. Take a look at Chapter 3.4 in the textbook if you need
guidance on how to write down the budget constraint. Make sure that you understand what the
equation describes.
b) Explain why the line passes through the point where free time is 24 hours and consumption is
zero.
c) What is the highest daily consumption that is feasible for her, and what does she have to give up
to reach it?
questions.contextMarkdown:
Problem 1: Nora decides how much to work
Nora is a freelance translator in Oslo. She finds assignments through an online platform and decides
for herself how many hours she works each day. After tax and platform fees she keeps 250 kroner for
every hour she works, and the rate is the same whether she works two hours or twelve. She spends
everything she earns the same day, so her daily consumption is equal to her daily earnings.
In the diagrams, free time means every hour of the day she does not work, so it includes the roughly 8
hours she needs for sleep and meals. She would never work more than 16 hours in a day, and the
horizontal axis therefore starts at 8 hours of free time. The axis along the top shows hours of work,
which is always 24 minus free time.
Figure 1 shows Nora’s budget constraint and three combinations she is considering: B, E and D. The
orange curves are indifference curves with one through each of the three points. The number next to
each point is Nora’s marginal rate of substitution (MRS) in these points. Remember that the MRS is
the amount of consumption she would just be willing to give up in exchange for one more hour of free
time.
Figure 1

Part A. The budget constraint and the opportunity cost of free time
rubricChecks: Address a) Write down Nora’s budget constraint as an equation, with consumption c on the left-hand side and hours of...
Address b) Explain why the line passes through the point where free time is 24 hours and consumption is zero
Address c) What is the highest daily consumption that is feasible for her, and what does she have to give up to reach it
hints: Free time plus work hours must equal 24. Nora earns only when working.
Use consumption = 250 × (24 − free time) and the stated maximum workday. Evaluate the zero-work endpoint and the maximum feasible work-hours endpoint.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
1. The budget constraint.
Suggested answer:
a) c = 250(24 − t) for 8 ≤ t ≤ 24. Equivalently c = 250h, where h = 24 − t is hours of work. The
equation is just “income = wage × hours” rewritten with free time on the right-hand side, which
is how the textbook sets it out in Chapter 3.4.
b) At t = 24 she does no work at all. She earns nothing, and since consumption equals earnings
she can consume nothing. Worth noticing: this is the one point in the diagram that a change in
the wage does not move, which is why the line pivots about it in Part C.
c) 250 × 16 = 4,000 kroner. To reach it she has to give up every waking hour outside sleep and
meals and work all 16 of them. It is a theoretical end point rather than a realistic choice, but it
fixes where the budget constraint crosses the y-axis.

questions.title: Lecture 7 · Nora / tax and transfers · Question 2
questions.promptMarkdown:
2. The slope of the budget constraint.
a) What is the slope, and why is it negative?
b) Explain in your own words what the slope tells us about the opportunity cost of one more hour of
free time. Is this an amount Nora pays to anybody?
c) The slope is also called the marginal rate of transformation (MRT). Why is the MRT the same at
every point on this particular line? Describe a pay arrangement under which it would not be.
questions.contextMarkdown:
Problem 1: Nora decides how much to work
Nora is a freelance translator in Oslo. She finds assignments through an online platform and decides
for herself how many hours she works each day. After tax and platform fees she keeps 250 kroner for
every hour she works, and the rate is the same whether she works two hours or twelve. She spends
everything she earns the same day, so her daily consumption is equal to her daily earnings.
In the diagrams, free time means every hour of the day she does not work, so it includes the roughly 8
hours she needs for sleep and meals. She would never work more than 16 hours in a day, and the
horizontal axis therefore starts at 8 hours of free time. The axis along the top shows hours of work,
which is always 24 minus free time.
Figure 1 shows Nora’s budget constraint and three combinations she is considering: B, E and D. The
orange curves are indifference curves with one through each of the three points. The number next to
each point is Nora’s marginal rate of substitution (MRS) in these points. Remember that the MRS is
the amount of consumption she would just be willing to give up in exchange for one more hour of free
time.
Figure 1

Part A. The budget constraint and the opportunity cost of free time
rubricChecks: Address a) What is the slope, and why is it negative
Address b) Explain in your own words what the slope tells us about the opportunity cost of one more hour of free time
Address c) The slope is also called the marginal rate of transformation (MRT)
hints: Imagine shifting one hour from work to free time while the hourly wage stays fixed.
Work out the lost earnings and the sign of the slope. For a different pay arrangement, ask whether each additional work hour still earns the same net amount.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
2. The slope of the budget constraint.
Suggested answer:
a) The slope is −250. It is negative because the two goods compete for the same scarce resource,
her time. She can have more of one only by having less of the other.

b) One more hour of free time is one hour less of work, which is 250 kroner less to spend. The
opportunity cost of an hour of free time is therefore 250 kroner of consumption. It is not a bill
she pays anyone. It is the value of the best thing she gives up, exactly the concept we have
discussed in Lectures 3 and 5. The MRT is the same number seen from the other side. It says how
many kroner of consumption the market lets her transform one hour of free time into, at the
margin.
c) Because she is paid the same 250 kroner for every hour, whether it is her first or her twelfth.
The trade-off on offer does not change as she moves along the line, so the line is straight. It
would not be constant if she were paid a higher rate for hours beyond eight, that is, overtime
pay, or if the platform took a larger cut above some earnings threshold, or if her marginal tax
rate rose with income. The budget constraint would then have a kink, and the MRT would be
different on the two sides of it.

questions.solutionMarkdown:
3. The feasible set.
Suggested answer:
The feasible set is everything on and below the budget constraint between
t = 8 and t = 24, the shaded area in Figure 1 above.
a) At 18 hours of free time the line allows 1,500 kroner, so at (18, 1,000) she is throwing away
500 kroner of consumption without buying a single extra minute of free time. Since more of both
goods is better, she can always move straight up onto the line and reach a higher indifference
curve. A point strictly inside the feasible set is never optimal.
b) At 18 hours of free time she works 6 hours and earns 1,500 kroner, so 2,000 is simply not
available to her. The budget constraint marks the boundary of what is possible, and points above
it lie outside her feasible set.

questions.title: Lecture 7 · Nora / tax and transfers · Question 4
questions.promptMarkdown:
4. Reading the indifference curves.
a) At B the MRS is about 650. Explain in words what the number 650 means. Is it something Nora is
willing to do, or something she is able to do?
b) At D the MRS is only about 70. Why is her MRS so much smaller there? Refer to how much free
time and how much consumption she has at each of the two points.
c) Use your answer to (b) to explain why indifference curves become flatter as we move to the right.
questions.contextMarkdown:
Problem 1: Nora decides how much to work
Nora is a freelance translator in Oslo. She finds assignments through an online platform and decides
for herself how many hours she works each day. After tax and platform fees she keeps 250 kroner for
every hour she works, and the rate is the same whether she works two hours or twelve. She spends
everything she earns the same day, so her daily consumption is equal to her daily earnings.
In the diagrams, free time means every hour of the day she does not work, so it includes the roughly 8
hours she needs for sleep and meals. She would never work more than 16 hours in a day, and the
horizontal axis therefore starts at 8 hours of free time. The axis along the top shows hours of work,
which is always 24 minus free time.
Figure 1 shows Nora’s budget constraint and three combinations she is considering: B, E and D. The
orange curves are indifference curves with one through each of the three points. The number next to
each point is Nora’s marginal rate of substitution (MRS) in these points. Remember that the MRS is
the amount of consumption she would just be willing to give up in exchange for one more hour of free
time.
Figure 1

Part A. The budget constraint and the opportunity cost of free time
rubricChecks: Address a) At B the MRS is about 650
Address b) At D the MRS is only about 70
Address c) Use your answer to (b) to explain why indifference curves become flatter as we move to the right
hints: MRS describes willingness to give up consumption at unchanged utility, rather than earnings.
Compare the scarcity of free time and consumption at B and D. Explain why extra free time can be more valuable when it is scarce and why this changes the curve’s slope.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
4. Reading the indifference curves.
Suggested answer:
a) At B, Nora would be just willing to hand over 650 kroner of consumption in exchange for one
more hour of free time, and would be exactly as well off afterwards as before. She would stay on
the same indifference curve. It is what she is willing to trade, not what she is able to trade. What
she is able to trade is the MRT, and that is a separate number.
b) At B she works 12 hours and has 3,000 kroner to spend. Free time is very scarce for her and
consumption is plentiful, so an hour off is worth a great deal in kroner. At D she already has 20
hours of free time and only 1,000 kroner. Free time is abundant and consumption scarce, so one
more hour is worth very little consumption to her.
c) Moving to the right along a single indifference curve means steadily more free time and
steadily less consumption. Each additional hour is therefore worth less to her than the one
before, so the amount of consumption she will part with for it falls. The slope of the curve falls in
absolute value, which is exactly what “flatter” means. Behind this is the assumption that people
prefer balanced combinations to extremes.

questions.title: Lecture 7 · Nora / tax and transfers · Question 5
questions.promptMarkdown:
5. Point B. Here Nora works 12 hours a day and consumes 3,000 kroner.
a) Compare her MRS at B with the MRT. Which of the two is larger?
b) Suppose she moves one hour from work to free time. Exactly what does she gain, and exactly
what does she give up? Is she better or worse off, and roughly by how much?
c) Can B be an optimal choice? Explain, and say what this looks like in the figure.

hints: At B compare MRS ≈ 650 with the market trade-off set by the 250 kroner wage.
For a small increase in free time, compare willingness to give up consumption with earnings actually lost. A full-hour numerical comparison uses a local approximation: MRS can change along the move.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
5. Point B, where she works 12 hours and consumes 3,000 kroner.
Suggested answer:
a) MRS ≈ 650 against MRT = 250, so the MRS is much larger.
b) She gains one hour of free time. She gives up 250 kroner of consumption, which is the
opportunity cost. But she would have been willing to give up as much as 650 kroner for that
hour, so she is getting it far more cheaply than it is worth to her. She is better off, by something
in the order of 650 − 250 = 400 kroner’s worth of consumption. The exact gain is a little smaller,
because her MRS falls as she moves, but the direction is what matters.
c) No. So long as MRS > MRT there is a move along the budget constraint that makes her better
off, so she cannot already be doing the best she can. In the figure this shows up as the
indifference curve through B cutting the budget constraint instead of touching it. The points on
the line just to the right of B lie above that curve.

6. Point D, where she works 4 hours and consumes 1,000 kroner.
Suggested answer:
a) MRS ≈ 70 against MRT = 250, so now the MRS is much smaller.
b) She should work more, that is, move to the left. Giving up an hour of free time needs only
about 70 kroner of consumption to compensate her, and working that hour brings in 250. She
comes out ahead by roughly 180 kroner’s worth. She keeps doing this as long as MRS < MRT.
c) She prefers B. The indifference curve through B lies above and to the right of the one through
D throughout the diagram, so it represents a higher level of utility. Both points are on the budget
constraint and so both are affordable, which is the point worth taking away. Being feasible, and

questions.title: Lecture 7 · Nora / tax and transfers · Question 7
questions.promptMarkdown:
7. Point E.
a) Write down the condition that holds at E but not at B or at D.
b) How many hours does Nora work at E, and what is her consumption?
c) Explain why she cannot reach a higher indifference curve by moving along the budget constraint,
in either direction.
d) A fellow student says: “E must be the best point because it lies exactly halfway along the line.” Is
that a good argument? Explain what actually makes E optimal.
questions.contextMarkdown:
Problem 1: Nora decides how much to work
Nora is a freelance translator in Oslo. She finds assignments through an online platform and decides
for herself how many hours she works each day. After tax and platform fees she keeps 250 kroner for
every hour she works, and the rate is the same whether she works two hours or twelve. She spends
everything she earns the same day, so her daily consumption is equal to her daily earnings.
In the diagrams, free time means every hour of the day she does not work, so it includes the roughly 8
hours she needs for sleep and meals. She would never work more than 16 hours in a day, and the
horizontal axis therefore starts at 8 hours of free time. The axis along the top shows hours of work,
which is always 24 minus free time.
Figure 1 shows Nora’s budget constraint and three combinations she is considering: B, E and D. The
orange curves are indifference curves with one through each of the three points. The number next to
each point is Nora’s marginal rate of substitution (MRS) in these points. Remember that the MRS is
the amount of consumption she would just be willing to give up in exchange for one more hour of free
time.
Figure 1

Part A. The budget constraint and the opportunity cost of free time
rubricChecks: Address a) Write down the condition that holds at E but not at B or at D
Address b) How many hours does Nora work at E, and what is her consumption
Address c) Explain why she cannot reach a higher indifference curve by moving along the budget constraint, in either...
Address d) A fellow student says: “E must be the best point because it lies exactly halfway along the line.” Is that...
hints: Look for the relation between willingness to trade and the available market trade-off.
An interior optimum reaches the highest attainable indifference curve where the slopes match. Read the hours and consumption from E; being halfway along a line has no independent optimality meaning.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
7. Point E.
Suggested answer:
a) MRS = MRT, that is, MRS = 250 = the net hourly wage. Equivalently, the indifference curve is
tangent to the budget constraint rather than cutting it.
b) Free time 16 hours, so she works 8 hours, and consumption is 250 × 8 = 2,000 kroner.
c) Move to the right of E and her MRS falls below 250, so each extra hour of free time is worth
less to her than the 250 kroner it costs and she loses. Move to the left and her MRS rises above
250, so the consumption she picks up is worth less to her than the free time she gives up and she
loses again. Both directions take her onto a lower indifference curve, which is what tangency
means. E is the point on the line that reaches the highest indifference curve she can afford.
d) No, the argument is worthless. Where the tangency falls has nothing to do with the midpoint
of the line and everything to do with the shape of Nora’s indifference curves, that is, with her
preferences. Someone who cared more about consumption would have a tangency further to the
left, and that would be their optimum. What makes E optimal is that it is feasible and lies on the
highest indifference curve she can reach, which happens precisely where MRS = MRT. In this
figure that point just happens to fall in the middle.

questions.promptMarkdown:
8. The new budget constraint.
a) Why does the line pivot around the point (24, 0) instead of shifting outwards in parallel?
b) What is her highest feasible consumption now?
c) What has happened to the opportunity cost of one hour of free time, and to the MRT?
d) Has the feasible set become larger or smaller? Is there any combination that was available to her
before but is not available now?
questions.contextMarkdown:
Problem 1: Nora decides how much to work
Nora is a freelance translator in Oslo. She finds assignments through an online platform and decides
for herself how many hours she works each day. After tax and platform fees she keeps 250 kroner for
every hour she works, and the rate is the same whether she works two hours or twelve. She spends
everything she earns the same day, so her daily consumption is equal to her daily earnings.
In the diagrams, free time means every hour of the day she does not work, so it includes the roughly 8
hours she needs for sleep and meals. She would never work more than 16 hours in a day, and the
horizontal axis therefore starts at 8 hours of free time. The axis along the top shows hours of work,
which is always 24 minus free time.
Figure 1 shows Nora’s budget constraint and three combinations she is considering: B, E and D. The
orange curves are indifference curves with one through each of the three points. The number next to
each point is Nora’s marginal rate of substitution (MRS) in these points. Remember that the MRS is
the amount of consumption she would just be willing to give up in exchange for one more hour of free
time.
Figure 1

Part A. The budget constraint and the opportunity cost of free time

Part C. The effects of changing wages
Nora’s platform introduces an AI-assisted translation tool. She can now deliver twice as many words
per hour at the same quality, and her net pay rises from 250 to 500 kroner per hour. Nothing else
changes. In particular, her preferences are exactly what they were before.
Figure 2 shows the old budget constraint (dashed) and the new one (solid), together with her old
choice E and her new choice F.
Figure 2
rubricChecks: Address a) Why does the line pivot around the point (24, 0) instead of shifting outwards in parallel
Address b) What is her highest feasible consumption now
Address c) What has happened to the opportunity cost of one hour of free time, and to the MRT
Address d) Has the feasible set become larger or smaller
hints: Recalculate c = wage × (24 − t) with the new wage.
At zero work, earnings remain zero. Compare the new slope and the consumption possible at other time choices, keeping the time endowment and preferences fixed.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
8. The new budget constraint, after the wage rises from 250 to 500.
Suggested answer:
a) A higher wage changes the rate at which she can turn hours into kroner. It does not hand her
any money. At 24 hours of free time she works nothing and earns nothing, before and after alike,
so that point stays put and the line pivots about it. A parallel shift would mean more
consumption at every level of free time including zero hours of work, and that only happens
when she has income that does not come from working.
b) 500 × 16 = 8,000 kroner.
c) Both have doubled. The opportunity cost of an hour of free time is now 500 kroner of
consumption, and the MRT is 500. Free time has become twice as expensive relative to
consumption as it was.
d) Strictly larger. The new feasible set contains the whole of the old one and more besides, so
every combination that was available before is still available. The only point that is unchanged is
(24, 0). Since she can now reach indifference curves that were out of reach before, she is
unambiguously better off.

Address c) From Figure 2, which of the two effects must be the stronger one
hints: Separate becoming able to afford more consumption/free time from the change in free time’s opportunity cost.
A higher net wage creates an income effect toward more normal free time and a substitution effect toward less. Explain the net outcome through their relative strengths.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
10. The two effects.
Suggested answer:
a) The substitution effect is the part of the change that comes from the change in the relative
price of the two goods. When the wage rises, an hour of free time costs 500 kroner instead of
250, so free time has become relatively expensive and she is pulled towards taking less of it. The
income effect is the part that comes from the fact that the higher wage has made her better off.
The feasible set has expanded, and with more resources she wants more of both goods, including
more free time.
b) Substitution effect: less free time, so more hours of work. Income effect: more free time, so
fewer hours of work. If she were simply handed money, the slope of the budget constraint would
not change and there would be no substitution effect at all. Only the income effect would
remain, pointing towards more free time. That is the sense in which the income effect is the one
that is always in play when the constraint moves outwards.
c) The income effect must be the stronger. The net movement is towards more free time, 17
hours instead of 16, and the only force pushing that way is the income effect, so it must have

outweighed the substitution effect pulling the other way. We say that the income effect
dominates.

questions.promptMarkdown:
11. Splitting the move from E to F. Sketch Figure 2 onto paper. Draw a line that has the same slope
as the old budget constraint and push it outwards until it just touches the indifference curve that
runs through F. Call the point where it touches G.
a) Which part of the move from E to F is the income effect, and which part is the substitution effect?
b) Read off roughly how many hours of free time each of the two effects accounts for, and check
that they add up to the total change you found in Question 9a). It is probably helpful to know
that G lies on 19.9 hours of free time.
c) The new budget constraint you drew lies about 1,450 kroner above the old budget constraint.
Describe a change in Nora’s circumstances that would have made that line her real budget
constraint, while still keeping the old wage of 250 kroner an hour.
questions.contextMarkdown:
Problem 1: Nora decides how much to work
Nora is a freelance translator in Oslo. She finds assignments through an online platform and decides
for herself how many hours she works each day. After tax and platform fees she keeps 250 kroner for
every hour she works, and the rate is the same whether she works two hours or twelve. She spends
everything she earns the same day, so her daily consumption is equal to her daily earnings.
In the diagrams, free time means every hour of the day she does not work, so it includes the roughly 8
hours she needs for sleep and meals. She would never work more than 16 hours in a day, and the
horizontal axis therefore starts at 8 hours of free time. The axis along the top shows hours of work,
which is always 24 minus free time.
Figure 1 shows Nora’s budget constraint and three combinations she is considering: B, E and D. The
orange curves are indifference curves with one through each of the three points. The number next to
each point is Nora’s marginal rate of substitution (MRS) in these points. Remember that the MRS is
the amount of consumption she would just be willing to give up in exchange for one more hour of free
time.
Figure 1

Part A. The budget constraint and the opportunity cost of free time

Part C. The effects of changing wages
Nora’s platform introduces an AI-assisted translation tool. She can now deliver twice as many words
per hour at the same quality, and her net pay rises from 250 to 500 kroner per hour. Nothing else
changes. In particular, her preferences are exactly what they were before.
Figure 2 shows the old budget constraint (dashed) and the new one (solid), together with her old
choice E and her new choice F.
Figure 2
rubricChecks: Address a) Which part of the move from E to F is the income effect, and which part is the substitution effect
Address b) Read off roughly how many hours of free time each of the two effects accounts for, and check that they add...
Address c) The new budget constraint you drew lies about 1,450 kroner above the old budget constraint
hints: Distinguish the actual choices E and F from the hypothetical old-slope tangency G.
Read the free-time changes E→G and G→F separately and add them with their signs. A parallel shift of the old budget line can be produced by non-labour income at the unchanged wage.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
11. Splitting the move from E to F.
Suggested answer:
a) The income effect is E → G and the substitution effect is G → F. The hypothetical line has the
old slope, so along it relative prices are exactly what they were, and moving from E to G
therefore reflects nothing but the fact that she is better off. G and F lie on the same indifference
curve, so moving from G to F leaves her utility unchanged, and that move reflects nothing but the
change in relative prices.
b) G lies at 19.9 hours of free time. The income effect runs from 16 to 19.9 hours, roughly +3.9
hours of free time. The substitution effect runs from 19.9 back to 17, roughly −2.9 hours. They
sum to +1 hour, the total change from E to F. Notice how large each of the effects are relative to
the total effect. They nearly cancel. That is one good reason why it is hard to predict what
happens to hours worked when wages change, and why the question has to be settled with data
rather than with theory.
c) It would be her budget constraint if, at the old wage of 250 kroner an hour, she also received
about 1,450 kroner a day that did not depend at all on how much she worked, such as rental
income, an inheritance or a fixed benefit. In other words, the income effect of doubling her wage
is exactly as large as the effect of handing her that much unearned income at the old wage.

questions.promptMarkdown:
12. The model, the lecture and the data.
a) In Lecture 6, the same kind of wage increase made Arne work more hours, not fewer. Is one of
the two figures wrong? Explain.

employed person in Norway have fallen from about 2,000 around 1962 to roughly 1,400 today,
while real wages have risen many times over. Which of the two effects appears to have
dominated over the long run?

Figure 1

Part A. The budget constraint and the opportunity cost of free time

Part C. The effects of changing wages

rubricChecks: Address a) In Lecture 6, the same kind of wage increase made Arne work more hours, not fewer
Address b) According to statistics available in the OECD database, average annual hours worked per employed person in...
hints: A higher real wage creates two opposing pressures on free time. Use the observed change in working hours to judge their net effect.
The income effect encourages more free time if it is normal; substitution encourages less. State which must be stronger in the case described, without assuming it is always stronger.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
12. The model, the lecture and the data.
Suggested answer:
a) Neither is wrong. The model does not say which effect wins, because that depends on the
shape of the indifference curves, which is to say on preferences. Arne’s preferences are such that
the substitution effect dominates and he works more. Nora’s are such that the income effect
dominates and she works less. Both are optimal choices satisfying MRS = MRT, and both are
drawn correctly. What the model does is to organise the two opposing forces and tell us what to
measure. Which one is bigger is an empirical question, not something theory can settle.
b) The income effect. Wages rose enormously and hours fell, which is Nora’s pattern rather than
Arne’s. It is worth adding the qualification textbook makes in Chapter 3.9. In the nineteenth
century, when wages first began to rise from very low levels, hours rose, and there the
substitution effect dominated. Which effect dominates is not a fixed fact about human beings. It
can depend on how well off people already are.

questions.title: Lecture 7 · Nora / tax and transfers · Question 13
questions.promptMarkdown:
13. The two budget constraints. Sketch a diagram with hours of free time from 8 to 24 along the
horizontal axis and consumption along the vertical. It does not have to be to scale.
a) Draw Nora’s original budget constraint, and then the budget constraint under each of the two
proposals. For each proposal, say what happens to the slope and to the two end points of the
line.
b) One of the two proposals changes the opportunity cost of an hour of free time and the other does
not. Which is which, and what is the opportunity cost of an hour of free time under each of
them?
c) Look at the two new lines you have drawn. If Nora works many hours, which of the two proposals
is worth more to her? What if she works very few hours? Point to what in the figure tells you this.
questions.contextMarkdown:
Problem 2: Two ways of getting people to work more
Nora is back on her original net wage of 250 kroner an hour, and back at point E, working 8 hours a
day. The government would like people in her position to work more, and two proposals are on the
table.
Proposal 1: a tax cut. The tax on labour income is reduced, so Nora keeps 300 kroner for every
hour she works instead of 250. She receives nothing if she does not work.
Proposal 2: a cash benefit. Nora receives 400 kroner a day whether she works or not, and
however many hours she works. Her net hourly pay stays at 250 kroner.
Note before you start that the two proposals cost the state the same amount per day, so long as Nora
goes on working the 8 hours she worked at E: 50 extra kroner an hour for 8 hours is 400 kroner.
rubricChecks: Address a) Draw Nora’s original budget constraint, and then the budget constraint under each of the two proposals
Address b) One of the two proposals changes the opportunity cost of an hour of free time and the other does not
Address c) Look at the two new lines you have drawn
hints: Write each policy’s budget line using net wage and non-labour income as separate terms.
A tax cut changes the net wage and the line’s slope; a fixed transfer changes its level in parallel. Compare the two lines at high and low work hours and locate their crossing.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
13. The two budget constraints.
Figure 3 to go with question 13
Suggested answer:
a) Original: from (24, 0) to (8, 4,000), slope −250.
Proposal 1: the same starting point (24, 0), because with no work there is no labour income to
tax and no transfer either. The line is steeper, slope −300, reaching (8, 4,800).
Proposal 2: the slope is unchanged at −250, since she still gains or loses 250 kroner for each hour
at the margin. The whole line shifts up by 400 kroner, running from (24, 400) to (8, 4,400). Even
with no work at all she now has 400 kroner to spend.
The single most important thing to see in the figure is that Proposal 1 tilts the line while Proposal
2 moves it without tilting it.
b) Proposal 1 changes the opportunity cost of free time and Proposal 2 does not. Under Proposal
1 an hour of free time costs her 300 kroner of consumption rather than 250, because 300 kroner
is what she now gives up by not working that hour. The MRT rises from 250 to 300, which is why
the line gets steeper. Under Proposal 2 the opportunity cost of an hour of free time is still 250
kroner, exactly as before. The transfer arrives whether she works or not, so it does not change
what an hour of work is worth to her at the margin. It changes where the line sits, not how steep
it is.
c) If Nora works many hours, Proposal 1 is worth more to her. If she works very few hours,
Proposal 2 is worth more. What tells you this in the figure is that the two new lines cross. To the
left of the crossing point, where she is working a lot, the Proposal 1 line lies above the Proposal 2
line, and to the right of it, where she is working little, the Proposal 2 line lies above. The reason is

straightforward. A tax cut is worth 50 kroner for every hour she actually works, so it is worth
nothing at all to someone who does not work, whereas the cash benefit is worth the same 400
kroner however many hours she puts in.

questions.title: Lecture 7 · Nora / tax and transfers · Question 14
questions.promptMarkdown:
14. Proposal 2: the cash benefit.
a) Which of the two effects from Problem 1 is at work here, and which one is not? Explain using the
slope of the budget constraint.
b) What happens to the number of hours Nora chooses to work? Can you be certain of the
direction?
c) What does your answer in (b) assume about free time? What would have to be true about her
preferences for the answer to go the other way?
questions.contextMarkdown:
Problem 2: Two ways of getting people to work more
Nora is back on her original net wage of 250 kroner an hour, and back at point E, working 8 hours a
day. The government would like people in her position to work more, and two proposals are on the
table.
Proposal 1: a tax cut. The tax on labour income is reduced, so Nora keeps 300 kroner for every
hour she works instead of 250. She receives nothing if she does not work.
Proposal 2: a cash benefit. Nora receives 400 kroner a day whether she works or not, and
however many hours she works. Her net hourly pay stays at 250 kroner.
Note before you start that the two proposals cost the state the same amount per day, so long as Nora
goes on working the 8 hours she worked at E: 50 extra kroner an hour for 8 hours is 400 kroner.
rubricChecks: Address a) Which of the two effects from Problem 1 is at work here, and which one is not
Address b) What happens to the number of hours Nora chooses to work
Address c) What does your answer in (b) assume about free time
hints: A fixed cash benefit does not change the net earnings lost when taking another hour off.
The unchanged slope removes the substitution effect. The direction of the remaining income effect depends on whether free time is normal or inferior; state that assumption.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
14. Proposal 2, the cash benefit.
Suggested answer:
a) Only the income effect. The slope of the budget constraint is unchanged at −250, so the
relative price of free time and consumption is exactly what it was, and there can be no
substitution effect without a change in relative prices. All that has happened is that she has been
made better off at every level of free time. If the slope does not change, only the income effect
operates.
b) She works fewer hours, and here we can be certain of the direction. The income effect moves
her towards more of both goods, and more free time means fewer hours of work. There is
nothing pulling the other way, so the prediction is unambiguous.
c) It assumes free time is a normal good, that is, that being better off makes her want more of it.
In Lecture 6, we said that the income effect is always positive. If free time were an inferior good
for her, so that becoming richer made her want less of it, she would work more. That is not how
we normally model it, and it is not what the long-run data on working hours suggest.

questions.title: Lecture 7 · Nora / tax and transfers · Question 15
questions.promptMarkdown:
15. Proposal 1: the tax cut.
a) Which effects are at work, and in which direction does each of them push her choice of hours
worked?
b) Can you say for certain, from the model alone, whether she will work more or fewer hours?
Explain what the answer depends on.
c) A politician says: “Proposal 1 is clearly the better of the two if the goal is to get people to work
more hours.” Is that right? Use your answers to questions 14 and 15, and be precise about what
the model does and does not let you claim.
questions.contextMarkdown:
Problem 2: Two ways of getting people to work more
Nora is back on her original net wage of 250 kroner an hour, and back at point E, working 8 hours a
day. The government would like people in her position to work more, and two proposals are on the
table.
Proposal 1: a tax cut. The tax on labour income is reduced, so Nora keeps 300 kroner for every
hour she works instead of 250. She receives nothing if she does not work.
Proposal 2: a cash benefit. Nora receives 400 kroner a day whether she works or not, and
however many hours she works. Her net hourly pay stays at 250 kroner.
Note before you start that the two proposals cost the state the same amount per day, so long as Nora
goes on working the 8 hours she worked at E: 50 extra kroner an hour for 8 hours is 400 kroner.
rubricChecks: Address a) Which effects are at work, and in which direction does each of them push her choice of hours worked
Address b) Can you say for certain, from the model alone, whether she will work more or fewer hours
Address c) A politician says: “Proposal 1 is clearly the better of the two if the goal is to get people to work more...
hints: Separate becoming able to afford more consumption/free time from the change in free time’s opportunity cost.
A higher net wage creates an income effect toward more normal free time and a substitution effect toward less. Explain the net outcome through their relative strengths.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
15. Proposal 1, the tax cut.
Suggested answer:
a) Both are at work. The substitution effect: an hour of free time now costs 300 kroner instead of
250, so free time is relatively more expensive and she is pulled towards working more. The
income effect: at any positive number of hours she is better off than before, so she is pulled
towards more free time and fewer hours.
b) No. The two effects work against each other, and which is larger depends on the shape of her
indifference curves. The model tells us what forces are at work and how to measure them, but it
cannot deliver the answer without knowing preferences, and in practice those have to be
estimated from data on how people actually respond to tax changes.
c) The conclusion is right, but not for the reason the politician probably has in mind. Proposal 2
cannot possibly raise her hours, because it is a pure income effect and it unambiguously lowers
them. Proposal 1 at least contains a force pushing towards more work, so it may raise hours, but
it may also lower them if the income effect dominates. So the honest statement is that Proposal
2 will certainly not achieve the goal while Proposal 1 might. This is the reasoning behind the
scepticism some economists expressed about the tax-lottery proposal discussed in Lecture 6. A
tax cut on labour income is not guaranteed to raise labour supply, and whether it does is an
empirical question that the experiment is designed to shed more light upon.

questions.title: Lecture 7 · Nora / tax and transfers · Question 16
questions.promptMarkdown:
16. From the model to the real world. (Discussion questions)
a) GDP per capita is roughly similar in Norway and in the United States, but an employed American
works around 1,800 hours a year and an employed Norwegian around 1,400. The model holds
everything but the wage constant. Name at least two of the things it holds constant that could
account for a difference of this size.
b) The model assumes that the worker chooses her hours freely. For which groups in the Norwegian
labour market is that assumption least convincing? For which is it most convincing?
c) Does that make it a bad model? Answer using the textbook’s own discussion in Chapter 3.8.
questions.contextMarkdown:
Problem 2: Two ways of getting people to work more
Nora is back on her original net wage of 250 kroner an hour, and back at point E, working 8 hours a
day. The government would like people in her position to work more, and two proposals are on the
table.
Proposal 1: a tax cut. The tax on labour income is reduced, so Nora keeps 300 kroner for every
hour she works instead of 250. She receives nothing if she does not work.
Proposal 2: a cash benefit. Nora receives 400 kroner a day whether she works or not, and
however many hours she works. Her net hourly pay stays at 250 kroner.
Note before you start that the two proposals cost the state the same amount per day, so long as Nora
goes on working the 8 hours she worked at E: 50 extra kroner an hour for 8 hours is 400 kroner.
rubricChecks: Address a) GDP per capita is roughly similar in Norway and in the United States, but an employed American works...
Address b) The model assumes that the worker chooses her hours freely
Address c) Does that make it a bad model
hints: List assumptions the model holds fixed besides wages, including whether work hours can actually be chosen.
Consider taxes, preferences, norms, paid leave, contracts and institutions. Explain which causal trade-off the simplified model helps isolate and which real-world differences it leaves open.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
16. From the model to the real world.
Suggested answer:
a) Everything that is not the wage is held constant, and several of those things differ sharply
between the two countries. Institutions: collective agreements, statutory limits on hours,
negotiated reductions in the standard working week, and holiday entitlement, which is five
weeks by law in Norway and not guaranteed federally at all in the United States. Taxes and public
provision: marginal tax rates differ, and so do publicly funded childcare, health cover and

pensions, which change both the net wage and how much income a household needs to buy
what it wants. Household structure and unearned income: how many earners a household has,
and how much income it has that does not come from work. Preferences and culture: how much
people value time against goods, which is shaped by what those around them do, and which is
textbook’s point that the ceteris paribus assumption omits factors such as culture and politics.
Notice that the model is not silent about these. It says they operate by shifting or tilting the
budget constraint, or by changing the shape of the indifference curves. It simply does not explain
them.
b) Least convincing for employees on standard full-time contracts, for shift workers in health care
and retail whose schedules are set by the employer, for anyone covered by a collective
agreement fixing the standard week, and for people in involuntary part-time work who want
more hours and cannot get them. Most convincing for the self-employed and freelancers like
Nora, for people on hourly contracts who can take or decline shifts, for employees with genuine
discretion over overtime, and for the longer-horizon decisions almost everyone does control,
such as whether to take a part-time position, whether to take a second job, and when to retire.
The model tends to work well at whichever margin the worker actually controls.
c) Not necessarily. The textbook’s argument in Chapter 3.8 is that a model should be judged by
whether it captures the essential trade-off and yields useful predictions, not by whether its
assumptions are literally true. Nobody computes a marginal rate of substitution, but people
adjust by trial and error until they are content with the balance, and they behave as if they were
optimising. The model earns its keep in a second way too. It tells us exactly what to look for,
namely a change in the slope of the budget constraint as against a shift in its position, and that
distinction is what allows the sharp prediction in Problem 2, that a lump-sum benefit and a tax
cut have different effects on hours. That is a real, testable claim, and it does not depend on
anyone doing maths in their head. Where the model needs help is over long periods, when the
things it holds constant are themselves changing.

Jonas’ employment contract states his weekly wage, that he works 37.5 hours a week on the night
shift, and that he “shall bake bread of good quality”.

flour from a mill.

Solsiden Bakeri is one of about 50 small bakeries in Trondheim. It is owned by local investors who
have hired a manager, Hilde, to run it. Jonas is one of the bakers. He works the night shift so that the

Address b) Who is the principal and who is the agent in the relationship between Hilde and Jonas
Address c) Solsiden has had a vacancy for a baker for six weeks, even though many people in Trondheim are unemployed

questions.solutionMarkdown:
1. Contracts and conflicts of interest.
Jonas’ employment contract states his weekly wage, that he works 37.5 hours a week on the night
shift, and that he “shall bake bread of good quality”.
a) Which of the three terms could a court verify? Use your answer to explain why the employment
contract is incomplete (Chapter 6.6), and how it differs from the bakery’s weekly purchase of
flour from a mill.
b) Who is the principal and who is the agent in the relationship between Hilde and Jonas? Describe
the conflict of interest, and explain how asymmetric information makes it hard to resolve. What
is the corresponding conflict between the owners and Hilde?
c) Solsiden has had a vacancy for a baker for six weeks, even though many people in Trondheim are
unemployed. Why can vacancies and unemployed job seekers exist side by side (Chapter 6.4)?
Suggested answer:
a) The wage can be verified (payslips, bank transfers), and so can the working hours (time clock,
key-card logs). “Good quality” cannot. It is not defined, and a bad batch could be caused by the
flour, the humidity or the oven. To prove a breach, Solsiden would have to document what Jonas
did during the night, which nobody saw. Hilde’s impression when she tastes the bread is not
evidence a court can use. The contract is therefore incomplete: it does not specify, in a way a
court can enforce, what the bakery really cares about, namely effort and care. The flour purchase
is different. Ownership of the flour is transferred, its weight and quality can be specified and
checked on delivery, and the transaction is then completed. The employment contract transfers
no ownership. Solsiden buys the right to direct Jonas’ work for a number of hours, in a
relationship that goes on over time.
b) Hilde (on behalf of the owners) is the principal and Jonas is the agent. The bakery wants
careful, high effort, but effort is costly for Jonas, so unless something is at stake he would prefer
to take it easy. Asymmetric information (relevant information that only some parties have) is
what makes this a problem. Jonas knows whether he let the dough rise long enough, while Hilde
only sees a result that also depends on things he does not control. If she could observe his effort
at no cost, she could simply instruct and check. The owners and Hilde have a similar conflict (the
separation of ownership and control). The owners are residual claimants and receive the profit,
while Hilde receives a salary and may prefer an easier working life or pursue her own goals, and
the owners cannot see everything she does.
c) The labour market is a matching market: both sides care about whom they end up with.
Workers differ in skills and preferences (night work is not for everyone), and jobs differ in tasks,

hours and location. Finding a good match takes time and resources for both the bakery
(advertising, interviews, training) and the job seekers (searching, applying). That is why vacancies
and unemployed job seekers exist at the same time. It also means that losing a worker is costly
for the firm, and losing the job is costly for the worker.

2. What is Jonas’ job worth?
Jonas plans ahead over h = 100 weeks. At Solsiden he earns w = 10,500 kroner a week, and the
disutility of the effort the job requires is equivalent to c = 1,500 kroner a week. If he loses the job, he
receives an unemployment benefit of 6,000 kroner a week and expects it to take 20 weeks to find a
new job. That job is in another sector and is worth 8,500 kroner a week to him, after taking effort into
account.
a) Calculate the total value over the 100 weeks of keeping the job, the total value of his reservation
option (losing the job today), and his employment rent. Explain what the employment rent
means, and show it as an area in a figure like the one from Lecture 8 (Chapter 6.8).
b) Divide the value of the reservation option by the number of weeks to find his reservation wage,
w, per week.
r
c) The labour market improves, and the expected time to find a new job falls to 10 weeks. What
happens to Jonas’ employment rent? What weekly wage would Solsiden have to pay to keep the
employment rent as large as before?
Suggested answer:
a) Keeping the job: (10,500 − 1,500) × 100 = 900,000 kroner. The cost of effort is subtracted
because it is a real cost to Jonas that he avoids if he is unemployed. Reservation option: 6,000 ×
20 + 8,500 × 80 = 120,000 + 680,000 = 800,000 kroner. Employment rent: 900,000 − 800,000 =
100,000 kroner. The employment rent is what Jonas loses if he loses the job today: the net value
of the job minus the net value of his next best alternative. In the figure it is area A (the 20 weeks
of unemployment, 3,000 × 20 = 60,000) plus area B (the remaining 80 weeks in a slightly worse
job, 500 × 80 = 40,000).
Figure to go with question 2a
b) w = 800,000 / 100 = 8,000 kroner per week (net of effort). A job with the same cost of effort
r
must therefore pay at least 8,000 + 1,500 = 9,500 kroner for Jonas to accept it.

c) Reservation option: 6,000 × 10 + 8,500 × 90 = 825,000, so w rises to 8,250. The employment
r
rent falls to 900,000 − 825,000 = 75,000 kroner. Losing the job is less costly when it is easier to
find a new one. To keep the rent at 100,000, the job must be worth 925,000, that is 9,250 a week
net of effort, so w − 1,500 = 9,250 and w = 10,750 kroner. The wage has to rise by 250, exactly as
much as the reservation wage: a tighter labour market pushes wages up even though nobody has
negotiated.

3. Working hard or shirking.
Hilde cannot observe Jonas’ effort. If he shirks, he avoids the cost of effort, but he expects to be found
out and dismissed after s = 25 weeks, and after that he gets w = 8,000 kroner a week (Chapter 6.9).
r
Figure 1 shows what he gets each week if he works hard (blue) and if he shirks (red).
a) At the current wage of 10,500 kroner, calculate the total value of working hard and of shirking.
Which does Jonas choose?
b) Hilde wants to pay the lowest wage at which Jonas still works hard. Use the no-shirking condition
to find this wage (see Chapter 6.9). Calculate areas A and B in Figure 1 at this wage, and explain
why they are equal.
c) Jonas would accept the job at 9,500 kroner (Question 2b). Why does Hilde not pay him 9,500?
d) Suppose the labour market improves as in Question 2c, so that w = 8,250. Find the new no-
r
shirking wage.
Suggested answer:
a) Working hard: 100 × (10,500 − 1,500) = 900,000. Shirking: 25 × 10,500 + 75 × 8,000 = 262,500 +
600,000 = 862,500. He works hard, which pays 37,500 kroner more. Shirking saves him 1,500 ×
25 = 37,500 in effort, but once he is fired he loses 10,500 − 1,500 − 8,000 = 1,000 a week for 75
weeks, that is 75,000.
b) Every krone above this wage is a cost that buys no extra effort. The no-shirking condition is
h(w − c) ≥ sw + (h − s)w. With equality: 100(w − 1,500) = 25w + 600,000, so 75w = 750,000 and w
r
= 10,000 kroner. This is w + c + an employment rent of 500 a week (CORE: sc/(h − s) = 25 × 1,500
r
/ 75 = 500). A = c × s = 1,500 × 25 = 37,500, the gain from shirking. B = (w − c − w) × (h − s) = 500
r
× 75 = 37,500, the gain from working hard. They are equal because that is what defines the no-
shirking wage: Jonas is just willing to work hard. Area A does not depend on the wage, but B
does, so the bakery raises the wage until B is as large as A, and no further.

Figure 1 at the no-shirking wage
c) At 9,500 there is no employment rent. Working hard, net of the cost of effort, is worth 100 ×
8,000 = 800,000, while shirking is worth 25 × 9,500 + 75 × 8,000 = 837,500, so he would shirk.
With nothing to lose, the threat of dismissal has no bite. The wage that gets someone to accept a
job is lower than the wage that gets them to work hard in it (exert effort), and the difference is
the employment rent. This also gives Hilde power over Jonas, because, when he receives an
employment rent, he fears losing the job.
d) w = w + c + employment rent gives w = 8,250 + 1,500 + 500 = 10,250 kroner. When
r
unemployment falls, the reservation wage rises and firms must pay more to keep getting effort.

4. Where do the curves come from?

b) Suppose the market price is 20 kroner. Why can Solsiden not charge more? Use Figure 2a to

c) Use Figure 2a to find how many loaves Solsiden would bake at a price of 40 kroner. Explain why
