questions.contextMarkdown:
Problem 2: The market for bread in Trondheim
We now look at the market where Solsiden sells its bread, focusing on a standard loaf of kneippbrød.
There are 50 identical bakeries and thousands of customers, and we assume they are all price-takers.
Figure 2a shows Solsiden’s marginal cost (MC) of baking one more loaf, for different numbers of
loaves per day. We assume that the marginal cost is increasing. Since the bakeries are identical, they
all have this MC curve. Figure 2b shows the market demand curve (D) and the market supply curve (S)
for bread in the city.

Figure 2
rubricChecks: Address a) Read off Figure 2b how many loaves are demanded at a price of 50 kroner
Address b) Suppose the market price is 20 kroner
Address c) Use Figure 2a to find how many loaves Solsiden would bake at a price of 40 kroner
hints: Use the individual bakery’s MC graph for its output choice and the market graph for total demand and supply.
At a given price compare that price with the cost of the next loaf. Then multiply an identical bakery’s supplied quantity by 50 to obtain market supply.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
4. Where do the curves come from?
a) Read off Figure 2b how many loaves are demanded at a price of 50 kroner. What does this point
on the demand curve tell us about the buyers’ willingness to pay? Why does the demand curve
slope downward?
b) Suppose the market price is 20 kroner. Why can Solsiden not charge more? Use Figure 2a to
decide whether Solsiden should bake loaf number 50 and loaf number 150. How many loaves
does it bake?
c) Use Figure 2a to find how many loaves Solsiden would bake at a price of 40 kroner. Explain why
the MC curve is the bakery’s supply curve. How many loaves do the 50 bakeries supply together
at 20 kroner and at 40 kroner? Check that your answers lie on the supply curve in Figure 2b
(Chapter 8.4).
Suggested answer:
a) At 50 kroner, 5,000 loaves a day are demanded. There are buyers for 5,000 loaves whose
willingness to pay is at least 50 kroner, and the buyer of the 5,000th loaf (the marginal buyer) is
willing to pay exactly 50. The demand curve lines up the buyers from the highest to the lowest
willingness to pay. When the price falls, more buyers find that their willingness to pay is at least
as high as the price, so the demand curve slopes downward.
b) The other bakeries sell an identical loaf at 20 kroner and customers know it, so at a higher
price Solsiden would sell nothing. In Figure 2a, the marginal cost of loaf 50 is 15 kroner, which is
less than the price, so baking it adds 5 kroner to profit. Bake it. The marginal cost of loaf 150 is
25 kroner, more than the price, so baking it reduces profit by 5 kroner. Don’t. The bakery bakes
as long as the price is at least as high as the marginal cost and stops where the price line crosses
the MC curve: 100 loaves a day. The 100th loaf provides no extra profit.
c) At 40 kroner the price line crosses the MC curve at 300 loaves. For every price, the bakery
chooses the quantity where the price equals the marginal cost, so the MC curve shows how
much it supplies at each price. That is exactly what a supply curve is. The 50 bakeries together
supply 50 × 100 = 5,000 loaves at 20 kroner and 50 × 300 = 15,000 at 40 kroner, and both points
lie on S in Figure 2b. The market supply curve is therefore the marginal cost curve for all the
bread in the city: its height at each quantity is the sellers’ reservation price for the last loaf.

questions.solutionMarkdown:
5. Competitive equilibrium and gains from trade.
a) Find the equilibrium price and quantity in Figure 2b. How many loaves does Solsiden bake in
equilibrium? Suppose the price were 40 kroner instead. How many loaves are demanded and
supplied, and how would the market get back to equilibrium?

b) Sketch Figure 2b and shade the consumer surplus and the producer surplus. Use the figure to
calculate both, and the total surplus. Why can total surplus not be increased by baking more or
fewer loaves (Chapter 8.5)?
Suggested answer:
a) The curves cross at P* = 30 kroner and Q* = 10,000 loaves a day. In Figure 2a, the price line at
30 kroner crosses Solsiden’s MC curve at 200 loaves, and 50 × 200 = 10,000. At 40 kroner, 7,500
loaves are demanded but 15,000 are supplied, an excess supply of 7,500 loaves. Bakeries left
with unsold bread cut their prices. As the price falls, the quantity demanded rises and the
quantity supplied falls (movements along the curves) until the market clears at 30 kroner.
b) Consumer surplus is the triangle between the demand curve and the price line: ½ × 10,000 ×
(70 − 30) = 200,000 kroner per day. Producer surplus is the triangle between the price line and
the supply curve: ½ × 10,000 × (30 − 10) = 100,000 kroner per day. Total surplus: 300,000 kroner
per day. In equilibrium, every loaf that a buyer values more than it costs to bake is baked, and no
loaf is baked that costs more than a buyer is willing to pay. Baking fewer loaves would leave gains
from trade unused (a deadweight loss), and baking more would add loaves whose cost exceeds
their value. Under the model’s assumptions the equilibrium is Pareto efficient, but that says
nothing about whether the split between buyers and bakeries is fair.

questions.solutionMarkdown:
6. Changing market conditions.
a) The higher wages from Question 3d and a rise in flour prices together raise the marginal cost of
every loaf by 3 kroner. Is this a shift of the supply curve or a movement along it? Draw the
change in a sketch of Figure 2b and show the new equilibrium. What happens to the price and
the quantity? Use your sketch to explain why the price rises by less than 3 kroner.
b) At the same time, a popular low-carb diet makes people want to eat less bread. Show both
changes in a new sketch. Which of the changes in price and quantity can you be sure about, and
which depends on how large the two shifts are?
c) Is the bread market in Trondheim a competitive market? Refer to the assumptions of the model
and to the two questions CORE suggests for checking (Chapter 8.10).

Suggested answer:
a) Costs have risen at every quantity, so the whole supply curve shifts up (inward) by 3 kroner, to
S′ in the figure below. At the old price of 30 kroner there is now excess demand, so the price
rises. As it rises, buyers move up along the demand curve and buy fewer loaves. The new
equilibrium is at a higher price and a lower quantity: about 32 kroner and 9,500 loaves. The
price rises by less than the 3-kroner shift because part of the adjustment happens through a
lower quantity. How much of the cost increase is passed on to buyers depends on how steep the
curves are. The steeper (less price-sensitive) the demand curve, the more the price rises. With a
vertical demand curve, the price would rise by the full 3 kroner, as in the oil market in Lecture 10.
b) The diet shifts the demand curve inward, to D′ in panel b. Both shifts reduce the quantity, so
the quantity falls for certain. The supply shift pushes the price up and the demand shift pushes it
down, so the price effect is ambiguous and depends on how large the two shifts are. In panel b,
the diet lowers every buyer’s willingness to pay by 6 kroner, and the two effects happen to
cancel: the price is back at 30 kroner while the quantity falls to 8,500. With a smaller fall in
demand the price would rise, and with a larger one it would fall. An unchanged price does not
mean nothing has happened: 1,500 fewer loaves are baked each day.
Figure to go with questions 6a and 6b
c) The model assumes many price-taking buyers and sellers, identical products, no frictions and
perfect information. With 50 bakeries and thousands of buyers, price-taking is fairly plausible,
and a bakery can adjust output quickly. But loaves differ in recipe, freshness and location, and
few customers compare the prices of 50 bakeries every morning, which gives each bakery some
room to set its own price. CORE’s two questions are: do all trades take place at the same price
(the law of one price), and is the price equal to marginal cost? The first can be checked by
comparing the prices of comparable loaves. The second is much harder, because marginal cost is
not reported and must be estimated. The bread market lies somewhere between perfect
competition and monopoly. Markets for wheat, coffee or salmon come closer to perfect
competition.

questions.promptMarkdown:
> **Note:** Subpart e is explicitly labelled optional and outside final-exam curriculum in the source.

Problem for Lecture 4 (Exercises session)
Covers curriculum from Topic 2
Carbon pricing, technology choice and innovation
Fjordfrakt AS transports freight by sea along the Norwegian coast, between Bergen and Kristiansund.
Below we look at one standard round trip with 1,000 tonnes of freight. This round trip is the firm’s
output, and it is exactly the same regardless of which technology the firm uses.
Fjordfrakt uses two inputs: marine diesel, measured in tonnes (F), and electricity, measured in MWh
(E). Electricity is used for shore power in port and for charging batteries on board.
The company can choose between four technologies. All four deliver the same round trip:
Technology Marine diesel, F Electricity, E (MWh)
(tonnes)
A : Conventional diesel vessels 10 24
B : Diesel-electric hybrid vessels 6 72
C : An older hybrid design 8 90
D : Battery-electric vessels with fast charging 3 120
Today Fjordfrakt pays 9,000 NOK per tonne of marine diesel and 1,000 NOK per MWh of electricity.
a) Plot the four technologies in the figure below (you will need to redraw the figure yourself), with
diesel on the horizontal axis and electricity on the vertical axis. One of the technologies will
never be chosen, no matter what the two inputs cost. Which one is it? Show in the figure how
you can see this, and state what we called such a technology in Lecture 3 (and in the textbook).
b) What is the relative price of diesel measured in electricity? Explain in one sentence what this
number tells you about the firm’s costs.
c) Calculate the cost of each of the four technologies. Which technology does Fjordfrakt choose?
Draw the isocost line that runs through the technology the firm chooses. What is the slope of
this line, and where does it cross the vertical axis?
d) The government announces that the CO tax will be increased by 2,500 NOK per tonne of CO .
2 2
Burning one tonne of marine diesel releases 3.2 tonnes of CO . The price of electricity is
2
unchanged.
i. What is the new price per tonne of marine diesel, and what is the new relative price of diesel
measured in electricity?
ii. What happens to the isocost lines in your figure? Explain in words before you draw.
iii. Calculate the cost of each technology at the new prices. Which technology is cheapest now?
Draw the isocost line through this technology in your figure.
e) Not strictly curriculum or relevant for the final exam, but fun for those who are curious
(requires algebra). Can be skipped.
How large would the increase in the CO tax have to be, measured in NOK per tonne of CO , for
2 2
Fjordfrakt to switch from technology A to technology B? And how large would it have to be for
the firm to go all the way to technology D?
f) Fjordfrakt is the first shipping company on this route to convert to technology D. The
competitors continue to sail with technology A for a few more years.
i. How much does Fjordfrakt gain per round trip compared with a competitor still using
technology A? What did we call this kind of gain in Lecture 3?
ii. The company sails 100 round trips a year. How large is the gain per year?
iii. What happens to this gain over time, and why? Use the concepts from textbook chapter 2.6
in your answer.
g) Mark in your figure the area that contains technologies which it did not pay to develop before
the tax increase, but which it does pay to develop after it. Describe in one or two sentences
what kind of technologies these are. (Hint: compare the isocost line through the technology
chosen before the tax increase with the isocost line through the technology chosen after it.)
h) Discussion:
i. In textbook chapter 2.7, the same model is used to explain why the Industrial Revolution
started in Britain. What plays the role of the CO₂ tax in that story, and which input did British
firms have an incentive to economise on?
ii. Instead of increasing the tax on diesel, the government could subsidise electricity so that it
becomes cheaper. Would that give Fjordfrakt the same reason to switch to technology D?
What would happen to the isocost lines in your figure? Mention at least one way in which
the two policies are nevertheless not the same.
iii. Name at least two things this model leaves out that could matter for whether Fjordfrakt
actually converts its fleet.
rubricChecks: Address a) Plot the four technologies in the figure below (you will need to redraw the figure yourself), with diesel...
Address b) What is the relative price of diesel measured in electricity
Address c) Calculate the cost of each of the four technologies
Address d) The government announces that the CO tax will be increased by 2,500 NOK per tonne of CO
hints: All technologies produce the same trip, so compare their inputs and total input costs.

First check dominance, then use cost = diesel price × diesel tonnes + electricity price × MWh. Convert the CO₂ tax to a cost per tonne of diesel before recalculating; compare pre/post cost rankings and the innovator’s saving.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Solutions to problem for Lecture 4 (Exercises session)
Covers curriculum from Topic 2
Carbon pricing, technology choice and innovation
a) Plotting the technologies and finding the dominated technology
The four technologies are plotted in Figure 1 below, with diesel (F) on the horizontal axis and
electricity (E) on the vertical axis.
Technology C uses more of both inputs than technology B: 8 tonnes of diesel against 6, and 90 MWh
against 72. C therefore costs more than B no matter what the two inputs cost, and it will never be
chosen. Using the terminology from Lecture 3, C is a dominated technology.
We can see this in the figure by drawing a “box” from B and outwards, up and to the right. Every
technology inside that box uses more of both inputs than B. C lies inside the box; A and D do not.
Which of A, B and D is best cannot be decided from the figure alone — that depends on the relative
price of the two inputs.
Figure 1
b) The relative price of diesel
The relative price of diesel measured in electricity is the ratio between the two prices:
𝑃 9,000
!
= = 9
𝑃 1,000
"
One tonne of marine diesel costs the same as 9 MWh of electricity. Put differently: if Fjordfrakt
wants to use one more tonne of diesel without increasing total costs, it has to use 9 MWh less
electricity.

c) Costs and the isocost line
The cost of a technology is found by multiplying each input by its price and adding up:
𝐶 = 𝑃 ×𝐹+𝑃 ×𝐸
! "
Technology Calculation Cost (NOK) Comment
A 10 × 9,000 + 24 × 1,000 114,000 Cheapest
B 6 × 9,000 + 72 × 1,000 126,000
C 8 × 9,000 + 90 × 1,000 162,000 Dominated
D 3 × 9,000 + 120 × 1,000 147,000
Fjordfrakt chooses technology A which is the conventional diesel vessels. Diesel is cheap relative to
electricity, and A is the technology that uses most diesel and least electricity.
To draw the isocost line we solve the cost equation for E:
𝐶 𝑃
!
𝐸 = − ×𝐹 = 114−9𝐹
𝑃 𝑃
" "
(E measured in MWh, with c = 114,000 NOK)
● The slope is −
#!
= −9. The slope of an isocost line is always minus the relative price.
#"
$ %%&,(((
● The vertical intercept is = = 114 𝑀𝑊ℎ, which is what the firm could buy if it
#" %,(((
spent the whole budget on electricity.
B and D both lie above this isocost line, which confirms that they are more expensive than A at these
prices.
Figure 2

d) A higher CO₂ tax
i. Burning one tonne of marine diesel releases 3.2 tonnes of CO , so an increase in the tax of 2,500
2
NOK per tonne of CO raises the price of diesel by
2
2,500 × 3.2 = 8,000 NOK per tonne of diesel
The new diesel price is 9,000 + 8,000 = 17,000 NOK per tonne, and the new relative price is
17,000/1,000 = 17. One tonne of diesel now costs as much as 17 MWh of electricity.
ii. The isocost lines become steeper: the slope changes from −9 to −17. Since the price of electricity
is unchanged, the vertical intercept for a given total cost (𝐶/𝑃 ) stays where it is, while the
"
horizontal intercept (𝐶/𝑃 ) moves in towards the origin. The lines therefore rotate clockwise around
!
their point on the vertical axis.
iii. Recalculating the costs at the new prices:
Technology Calculation Cost (NOK) Comment
A 10 × 17,000 + 24 × 1,000 194,000
B 6 × 17,000 + 72 × 1,000 174,000
C 8 × 17,000 + 90 × 1,000 226,000 Dominated
D 3 × 17,000 + 120 × 1,000 171,000 Cheapest
Technology D, the battery-electric vessels, is now the cheapest. Note that C is still dominated: a
change in relative prices can never make a dominated technology attractive.
Figure 3

e) Not strictly curriculum or relevant for the final exam, but fun for those who are curious
(requires algebra). Can be skipped.
How high must the tax be?
Fjordfrakt prefers B to A when B is the cheaper of the two:
6𝑃 +72,000 < 10𝑃 → 48,000 < 4𝑃 → 𝑃 > 12,000
! ! ! !
The diesel price must rise by more than 12,000 − 9,000 = 3,000 NOK per tonne, which corresponds to
an increase in the CO tax of 3,000 / 3.2 = 937.50 NOK per tonne of CO .
2 2
Fjordfrakt prefers D to B when:
3𝑃 +120,000 < 6𝑃 +72,000 → 48,000 < 3𝑃 → 𝑃 > 16,000
! ! ! !
That requires an increase of 7,000 NOK per tonne of diesel, that is 7,000 / 3.2 = 2,187.50 NOK per
tonne of CO .
2
So the choice of technology follows a “staircase”: an increase below 937.50 NOK per tonne of CO₂
changes nothing at all and the firm keeps sailing with A. Between 937.50 and 2,187.50 the firm
switches to the hybrids, and only above 2,187.50 does it go all the way to battery-electric vessels.
The announced increase of 2,500 NOK is above the last threshold, which is why D is chosen.
This is a useful point for the green transition: a carbon price that is “a bit higher” may have no effect
whatsoever on which technology firms use. What matters is whether the relative price crosses the
threshold where a different technology becomes the cheapest one.
f) The gain from being first
i. A competitor that keeps technology A pays 194,000 NOK per round trip. Fjordfrakt, on technology
D, pays 171,000 NOK. The gain is
194,000 − 171,000 = 23,000 NOK per round trip
This is an economic rent: the difference between the net benefit of the action taken and the net
benefit of the next best alternative (continuing with A). Because the rent arises from being an early
adopter of a new technology, CORE calls it an innovation rent (also known as a Schumpeterian rent,
not curriculum to know).
ii. With 100 round trips a year: 23,000 × 100 = 2,300,000 NOK per year.
iii. The rent is temporary. When the competitors see that Fjordfrakt is making money, they convert
their own fleets too — the new technology spreads (diffusion). As more and more of the shipping
companies produce at the lower cost, competition pushes freight rates down, and the innovation
rent is competed away. Shipping companies that cannot or will not convert end up with costs above
the market price and are driven out of business. This is what famous economist Schumpeter called
creative destruction (not curriculum to now this term).
The point is that the rent is exactly the incentive that makes someone convert first. Without the
prospect of a temporary gain, no one has any reason to take the risk of being first.

g) Where does it now pay to innovate?
The relevant comparison is between two lines:
● the old isocost line through A (E = 114 − 9F): technologies below this line were cheaper than
A at the old prices, and were therefore already worth developing;
● the new isocost line through D (E = 171 − 17F): technologies below this line are cheaper than
D at the new prices, and are worth developing now.
The shaded green area in Figure 4 lies above the old line and below the new one. Technologies in
this area were too expensive to be of interest before the tax increase, but would now give a firm
lower costs than anyone else has. These are technologies that use relatively little diesel and
relatively much electricity.
The lesson is that the tax does two things at once: it changes which of the existing technologies is
chosen, and it changes the direction in which it pays to innovate. This is the same mechanism as in
Lecture 3, where a change in the relative price both moves the firm along the existing menu of
technologies and redirects the search for new ones.
Figure 4
h) Discussion
i. In CORE 2.7, the role of the CO tax is played by the high wage in Britain relative to the price of
2
energy. In the early 1700s, wages measured against the price of energy were far higher in Newcastle
and London than in Amsterdam, Paris or Beijing, and in England the relative price of labour kept
rising through the eighteenth century. British firms therefore had an incentive to economise on
labour, and to adopt and develop technologies that used a lot of energy and little labour, such as the
spinning jenny, the water frame and the steam engine. In our exercise, the expensive input is diesel
rather than labour, and firms have an incentive to economise on diesel; the mechanism is identical.

ii. Yes! In the model it is only the relative price of the two inputs that decides which technology is
cheapest. Making diesel dearer and making electricity cheaper both raise the price of diesel
measured in electricity, and both therefore make the isocost lines steeper. A large enough subsidy
on electricity can tip the choice from A to D in exactly the same way as the tax does.
There is a difference in how the lines move, and it is worth drawing. When diesel is taxed, the
vertical intercept (what the firm could buy for a given budget if it bought only electricity) is
unchanged, so the lines rotate around their point on the vertical axis. When electricity is subsidised,
it is the horizontal intercept that stays put, so the lines rotate around their point on the horizontal
axis. Either way they get steeper, and that is what matters for the choice.
Outside the model the two policies are not the same:
● The tax raises the total cost of energy; the subsidy lowers it. A firm facing lower energy costs
has a reason to sail more, so total energy use may go up rather than down.
● The tax brings in revenue for the government; the subsidy costs money.
● The tax makes emissions expensive everywhere in the economy, including where there is no
electric alternative at all. A subsidy only makes one particular alternative cheaper.
(For the curious: with diesel back at 9,000 NOK per tonne, electricity would have to fall below 562.50 NOK per
MWh, a subsidy of at least 437.50 NOK per MWh, before D becomes the cheapest technology. The binding
comparison is D against B.)
iii. Things the model leaves out (see CORE 2.12, “How good is the model?”). Any two of these are
enough:
● The cost of the vessels themselves. We have only compared running costs for energy. New
battery-electric vessels are expensive to buy, and that investment cost is not in the isocost
diagram.
● Time and expectations. A ship lasts for decades, so the decision depends on the diesel and
electricity prices the firm expects over the whole lifetime of the fleet, and on whether it
believes the tax will still be there in twenty years.
● Infrastructure. Technology D presupposes charging capacity and a strong enough grid
connection in both ports. If it does not exist, the technology is not actually available.
● The menu of technologies is treated as fixed and known. In reality firms do not have a neat
list of four alternatives.
● Output is assumed constant. Higher transport costs could reduce how much freight
customers want shipped.
● Where the electricity comes from. The model says nothing about emissions in electricity
generation, or about the emissions from building the batteries.

Watch out for the classic trap: An equal percentage increase differs from an equal kroner transfer.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** It is unchanged.

Multiplying numerator and denominator by 1.08 cancels out.
questions.pitfall: An equal percentage increase differs from an equal kroner transfer.

questions.title: M004 · Diminishing average product
questions.promptMarkdown: Farm output rises from 600 to 720 when labour rises from 10 to 15 workers. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Average output per worker rose.
Total output fell because average product fell.
Marginal product must be negative.
Total output rose, while average output per worker fell.
hints: Start from the exact formula for the income ratio, growth rate, or average/marginal product of labour ($APL = Y/L$, $MPL = \Delta Y/\Delta L$).
Watch out for the classic trap: Separate total output from output per worker.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** Total output rose, while average output per worker fell.

Average product changes from 60 to 48. Output still rises by 120, so lower average product does not imply falling total output.
questions.pitfall: Separate total output from output per worker.

questions.title: M005 · Average versus marginal product
questions.promptMarkdown: In a graph of total output Y against labour L, how do you identify average and marginal product at a point?
options: Both are the height Y.
Marginal product is always total output divided by labour.
Average product is the origin-to-point slope; marginal product is the tangent slope.
Average product is the tangent slope; marginal product is Y/L.
hints: Start from the exact formula for the income ratio, growth rate, or average/marginal product of labour ($APL = Y/L$, $MPL = \Delta Y/\Delta L$).
Watch out for the classic trap: A level, a ratio and a derivative are different quantities.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** Average product is the origin-to-point slope; marginal product is the tangent slope.

Average product is Y/L. Marginal product is the additional output from an additional unit of labour, represented by the local slope.
questions.pitfall: A level, a ratio and a derivative are different quantities.

questions.title: M006 · Institutions

questions.title: M011 · Opportunity cost is net
questions.promptMarkdown: An afternoon café shift pays 700 NOK and effort costs the worker 200 NOK in money-equivalent terms. It is the best alternative to attending a lecture. What is the opportunity cost of attending?
options: 200 NOK
500 NOK
700 NOK
900 NOK

questions.title: M012 · Sunk ticket
questions.promptMarkdown: A non-refundable ticket bought last month cost 400 NOK. When deciding whether to attend tonight or work, how should the historical ticket payment enter the comparison?
options: It makes attending automatically optimal.
Treat it as sunk if it cannot be recovered under either choice.
Subtract it from the wage earned by working tonight.
Add it only to the cost of attending tonight.
hints: Write down the total cost equation $C = wL + pR$ (slope $-w/p$) or separate direct cost from the net value of the next-best reservation option.
Watch out for the classic trap: Check whether a cost changes with the decision.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** Treat it as sunk if it cannot be recovered under either choice.

The payment is the same past cost under both current alternatives. Current benefits and avoidable costs decide the choice.
questions.pitfall: Check whether a cost changes with the decision.

questions.title: M013 · Economic rent can be negative
questions.promptMarkdown: An activity gives net benefit 600 NOK; the best alternative gives 850 NOK. What is the economic rent from choosing the activity?
options: −250 NOK
600 NOK
250 NOK

questions.title: M014 · Dominance
questions.promptMarkdown: Two technologies produce the same output. A uses 3 labour hours and 7 energy units; B uses 4 hours and 8 units. Input prices are strictly positive. Which is correct?
options: A strictly dominates B.
Neither can dominate until prices are known.
B dominates A.
B is preferred because it uses more inputs.
hints: Write down the total cost equation $C = wL + pR$ (slope $-w/p$) or separate direct cost from the net value of the next-best reservation option.
Watch out for the classic trap: Dominance compares physical inputs while holding output fixed.

**Correct Answer:** A strictly dominates B.

A uses less of both costly inputs for identical output.

questions.title: M015 · Trade-off is not dominance
questions.promptMarkdown: For the same output, A uses (L=2,R=12), B uses (L=5,R=6). Which is correct?
options: B dominates because 6<12.
Add the two input quantities to decide the cheapest technology.
Neither dominates; cost depends on relative input prices.
A dominates because 2<5.
hints: Write down the total cost equation $C = wL + pR$ (slope $-w/p$) or separate direct cost from the net value of the next-best reservation option.
Watch out for the classic trap: Different input units cannot be added to establish dominance.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** Neither dominates; cost depends on relative input prices.

A saves labour while B saves energy. A common cost comparison requires wL+pR.
questions.pitfall: Different input units cannot be added to establish dominance.

questions.title: M016 · Isocost steepness
questions.promptMarkdown: Labour is on x and energy on y. The wage rises while the energy price stays fixed. What happens to the absolute isocost slope?
options: It stays fixed because output is fixed.
It rises because w/p rises.
It becomes positive.
It falls because p/w falls.
hints: Write down the total cost equation $C = wL + pR$ (slope $-w/p$) or separate direct cost from the net value of the next-best reservation option.
Watch out for the classic trap: Keep the axes fixed when interpreting a price change.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** It rises because w/p rises.

From R=C/p−(w/p)L, slope is −w/p. A higher wage makes it more negative and steeper.
questions.pitfall: Keep the axes fixed when interpreting a price change.

questions.title: M017 · Carbon price and choice
questions.promptMarkdown: A tax increases the price of diesel relative to electricity. For a given transport output, what incentive does this create?
options: An incentive to use a less diesel-intensive technology when its new cost is lower.
Diesel-intensive technology becomes cheaper.
There is no effect because physical input requirements do not change.
Every firm must immediately use zero diesel whatever its costs.
hints: Write down the total cost equation $C = wL + pR$ (slope $-w/p$) or separate direct cost from the net value of the next-best reservation option.
Watch out for the classic trap: An incentive is not a guarantee that every firm switches.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** An incentive to use a less diesel-intensive technology when its new cost is lower.

The tax changes relative input costs and can reverse the ranking of undominated technologies.
questions.pitfall: An incentive is not a guarantee that every firm switches.

questions.promptMarkdown: Studying has net benefit 800 NOK and working has net benefit 650 NOK. A grant of 100 NOK is paid regardless of the afternoon choice. What happens to the rent from studying?
options: It rises to 250 NOK.

questions.title: M025 · Same utility
questions.promptMarkdown: B and C lie on one indifference curve. B has more consumption and less free time than C. What follows?
options: The person is equally satisfied with B and C.
B and C must have identical coordinates.
B must be preferred because consumption is larger.
C must be preferred because free time is larger.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Watch out for the classic trap: Equal utility does not mean equal quantities.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** The person is equally satisfied with B and C.

An indifference curve joins equally preferred bundles. Changes in the two goods compensate each other.
questions.pitfall: Equal utility does not mean equal quantities.

questions.title: M026 · No crossing
questions.promptMarkdown: Why can two distinct standard indifference curves for two desirable goods not cross?
options: Because all indifference curves must be straight.
Because consumption must be identical on every curve.
Because budget lines cannot cross.
A common point would imply equal utility on both, conflicting with preference for a bundle with more of one good and no less of the other.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Watch out for the classic trap: This concerns consistent preferences, not a particular wage.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** A common point would imply equal utility on both, conflicting with preference for a bundle with more of one good and no less of the other.

Indifference is transitive. Crossing would make two bundles equally preferred even when one strictly dominates the other.
questions.pitfall: This concerns consistent preferences, not a particular wage.

questions.title: M027 · Meaning of MRS
questions.promptMarkdown: Free time is on x and consumption on y. What does MRS measure?
options: Minimum consumption needed to survive.
Consumption the market forces the person to sacrifice per hour.
Total utility divided by working hours.
Consumption the person is locally willing to give up per extra hour of free time at constant utility.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Watch out for the classic trap: MRT describes the available market trade-off.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** Consumption the person is locally willing to give up per extra hour of free time at constant utility.

MRS is the magnitude of the indifference-curve slope. It describes preferences at the current bundle.
questions.pitfall: MRT describes the available market trade-off.

questions.title: M028 · Point versus interval
questions.promptMarkdown: Consumption falls by 100 when free time rises by 2 hours along an indifference curve. What is established?
options: The exact derivative at both endpoints is necessarily −50.
Utility fell by 100.
The average trade-off over that interval is 50 consumption units per hour.
The MRS is 100 hours per consumption unit.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Watch out for the classic trap: A table interval does not identify every tangent slope.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** The average trade-off over that interval is 50 consumption units per hour.

The secant slope is −100/2=−50. A local derivative requires additional information.
questions.pitfall: A table interval does not identify every tangent slope.

questions.title: M029 · Diminishing MRS
questions.promptMarkdown: Along a standard convex indifference curve, moving toward more free time and less consumption usually does what?
options: Makes MRS rise without limit.
Makes the budget wage fall automatically.
Raises utility along the same curve.
Reduces willingness to sacrifice consumption for another small increase in free time.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Watch out for the classic trap: Do not confuse moving along preferences with changing market wages.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** Reduces willingness to sacrifice consumption for another small increase in free time.

When free time becomes more abundant relative to consumption, the marginal willingness to exchange consumption for it falls.
questions.pitfall: Do not confuse moving along preferences with changing market wages.

questions.title: M030 · Budget line meaning
questions.promptMarkdown: At a given amount of free time, what does the consumption level on the budget line represent?
options: The person’s utility score.
The amount the government guarantees regardless of work.
Minimum required earnings for happiness.
Maximum affordable consumption under the stated income assumptions.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Watch out for the classic trap: A budget constraint is not a subsistence requirement.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** Maximum affordable consumption under the stated income assumptions.

The line is the affordability boundary. The feasible set includes affordable nonnegative consumption below it.
questions.pitfall: A budget constraint is not a subsistence requirement.

questions.title: M031 · MRS above MRT
questions.promptMarkdown: At an affordable point on the budget line, MRS=420 NOK/hour and net wage=280 NOK/hour. Under standard smooth preferences, which local adjustment improves utility?
options: Double consumption without changing hours.
No adjustment, because the current bundle is affordable.
A little less free time and more work.
A little more free time and less work.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Watch out for the classic trap: Affordability does not prove optimality.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** A little more free time and less work.

The person values extra leisure more than its market cost: MRS>MRT. Moving right can reach a higher utility curve.
questions.pitfall: Affordability does not prove optimality.

questions.title: M032 · MRS below MRT
questions.promptMarkdown: At an interior budget point, MRS=120 and net wage=240 NOK/hour. Which local adjustment improves utility?
options: Work a little more and take less free time.
Take more free time and keep earnings unchanged.
Work less because MRS is positive.
Keep the bundle because consumption is nonnegative.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Watch out for the classic trap: Compare MRS with MRT, not with zero.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** Work a little more and take less free time.

An extra free hour costs 240 while the person values it locally at only 120. Exchanging some leisure for consumption can improve utility.
questions.pitfall: Compare MRS with MRT, not with zero.

questions.title: M033 · Tangency
questions.promptMarkdown: In a smooth interior optimum, why does MRS=MRT?
options: Consumption and free time must be equal numbers.
The highest affordable indifference curve and the budget line have the same slope there.
The two curves must be identical everywhere.
All affordable points give identical utility.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Watch out for the classic trap: Tangency is a condition for the standard interior case.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** The highest affordable indifference curve and the budget line have the same slope there.

At tangency, the marginal willingness to trade equals the feasible trade-off. An endpoint optimum need not satisfy this equality.
questions.pitfall: Tangency is a condition for the standard interior case.

questions.title: M034 · Distance from the origin
questions.promptMarkdown: For U=c+t, compare A=(t=0,c=12) and B=(t=7,c=7). Which is correct?
options: Both must give equal utility.
A gives more utility because its distance is greater.
A budget line is needed to calculate U for a specified bundle.
B gives more utility even though A is farther from the origin.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Watch out for the classic trap: Read the stated preference rule, not physical distance.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** B gives more utility even though A is farther from the origin.

U(A)=12 and U(B)=14. Euclidean distance is not a utility measure. Affordability is a separate question.
questions.pitfall: Read the stated preference rule, not physical distance.

questions.title: M035 · Cash transfer
questions.promptMarkdown: A person receives a lump-sum payment independent of hours worked; net hourly wage stays fixed. What happens to the budget line?
options: It shifts up in parallel; MRT is unchanged.
It pivots inward around the origin.
MRS stays fixed at every possible bundle.
It becomes steeper solely because total income rose.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Watch out for the classic trap: Level and slope are different features.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** It shifts up in parallel; MRT is unchanged.

c=w(24−t)+m. Higher m raises c by the same amount for every t without changing slope −w.
questions.pitfall: Level and slope are different features.

questions.title: M036 · Proportional tax cut
questions.promptMarkdown: A cut in a constant wage-income tax raises the net hourly wage. Other non-labour income is fixed. What follows?
options: Only a parallel shift occurs, with no substitution effect.
Preferences themselves necessarily change.
Working hours must fall for everyone.
The budget line becomes steeper; both income and substitution effects arise.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Watch out for the classic trap: Labour supply can rise or fall when effects oppose.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** The budget line becomes steeper; both income and substitution effects arise.

The lost earnings per extra free hour rise. Greater purchasing power and a changed relative price act together.
questions.pitfall: Labour supply can rise or fall when effects oppose.

questions.title: M037 · Income effect need not win
questions.promptMarkdown: After a wage rise, a person chooses fewer free hours. If leisure is normal, what can explain this?
options: MRT must have fallen.
The income effect must always be larger.
Both effects necessarily reduced leisure.
The substitution effect toward less leisure exceeds the income effect toward more leisure.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Watch out for the classic trap: Do not generalise one diagram’s numerical outcome.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** The substitution effect toward less leisure exceeds the income effect toward more leisure.

For normal leisure, a wage rise creates opposing effects; the final choice reveals which dominates.
questions.pitfall: Do not generalise one diagram’s numerical outcome.

questions.title: M038 · Familiar diagram decomposition
questions.promptMarkdown: In the course diagram, a hypothetical line with the OLD wage slope is shifted until tangent to the NEW indifference curve. What is held fixed when comparing old and hypothetical choices?
options: The new, steeper hourly-wage slope.
Utility at the initial level.
The market trade-off between consumption and free time.
Total consumption.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Watch out for the classic trap: Describe what is fixed rather than relying only on the label Slutsky.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** The market trade-off between consumption and free time.

The old slope holds relative prices fixed while purchasing power changes. The next step compares two points on the final utility curve. This is a Hicks-style (utility-compensated) construction; some notes use a broader decomposition label.
questions.pitfall: Describe what is fixed rather than relying only on the label Slutsky.

questions.title: M039 · Indifference curves after a grant
questions.promptMarkdown: A cash transfer changes income but not tastes. Which describes preferences?
options: The same preference map remains; a higher utility curve can become affordable.
The budget line is an indifference curve.
Every indifference curve shifts upward as a policy rule.
The person must stay on the old utility level.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Watch out for the classic trap: Reach a higher curve rather than assume tastes shifted.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** The same preference map remains; a higher utility curve can become affordable.

Income changes opportunities. The person chooses a different bundle on the existing map of preferences.
questions.pitfall: Reach a higher curve rather than assume tastes shifted.

questions.title: M040 · Budget arithmetic
questions.promptMarkdown: Net wage is 180 NOK/hour, daily non-labour income is 120 NOK, and free time is 15 hours out of 24. What is maximum daily consumption?
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Watch out for the classic trap: The horizontal axis is free time, not work hours.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** 1,740 NOK

Work hours =24−15=9. Consumption =180×9+120=1,740.
questions.pitfall: The horizontal axis is free time, not work hours.

questions.title: M041 · Table MRS
questions.promptMarkdown: Two bundles on one indifference curve are (t=17,c=480) and (t=19,c=360). What is the average MRS over the interval?
options: 2 consumption units/hour
120 consumption units/hour
60 consumption units/hour
0.02 consumption units/hour
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).

Magnitude of slope = |360−480|/(19−17)=120/2=60.

questions.title: M042 · After-tax MRT
questions.promptMarkdown: Gross wage is 400 NOK/hour and the constant wage-income tax rate is 25%. What is MRT in consumption NOK per hour of free time?
options: 400 NOK/hour
300 NOK/hour
0.25 NOK/hour
100 NOK/hour

questions.title: M043 · Two opposing effects
questions.promptMarkdown: A wage rise gives an income effect of +2.4 hours of free time and a substitution effect of −3.1 hours. What is the total change in free time?
options: 5.5 hours
-5.5 hours
-0.7 hours
0.7 hours
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).

questions.title: M044 · Endpoint optimum
questions.promptMarkdown: A person optimally chooses no paid work under a sufficiently large unconditional transfer. Must MRS=MRT hold at that endpoint?
options: Yes, because no work means MRT=0 whatever the wage.
Yes, because every optimum is interior.
No, because utility is necessarily zero.
No; tangency equality need not hold at an endpoint.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Watch out for the classic trap: Separate a corner from a smooth interior solution.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** No; tangency equality need not hold at an endpoint.

The feasible set restricts free time to at most the time endowment. An optimum at that boundary need not have equal slopes.
questions.pitfall: Separate a corner from a smooth interior solution.

questions.title: M045 · Incomplete contract
questions.promptMarkdown: Why can an employment contract be incomplete even if it specifies hours and pay?
options: Managers always know more about each worker’s preferences than the worker does.
It can never state a wage.
It must exclude all legal obligations.
Effort and all future contingencies cannot be fully specified and enforced.

Many aspects of effort, quality and future situations are difficult to observe or verify.

questions.title: M047 · Managers and owners

Assuming all employees own equal shares already.
Giving managers no information about operations and no pay.
Setting consumer prices equal to the unemployment benefit.

questions.title: M048 · Employment rent definition
questions.promptMarkdown: Which best defines employment rent?
options: The net value of keeping a job relative to the next-best alternative.
Rent paid for an employer’s office.
The entire gross wage regardless of effort or alternatives.
The unemployment rate expressed in money.
hints: Separate net hourly value when employed ($w - c$) from net hourly value when unemployed ($b - s$), and multiply only over expected unemployment duration.
Watch out for the classic trap: A high wage alone does not fully determine employment rent.

questions.title: M049 · Higher benefits
questions.promptMarkdown: Other things equal, unemployment benefits increase. How does employment rent at a fixed job wage change?
options: It rises because unemployment pays more.
It falls because the fallback improves.
It must remain unchanged.
It becomes identical to GDP.
hints: Separate net hourly value when employed ($w - c$) from net hourly value when unemployed ($b - s$), and multiply only over expected unemployment duration.
Watch out for the classic trap: Keep the current wage fixed when making this comparison.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** It falls because the fallback improves.

A better alternative narrows the net advantage of the job.
questions.pitfall: Keep the current wage fixed when making this comparison.

questions.title: M050 · Easier job
questions.promptMarkdown: Effort becomes less unpleasant while the wage and outside option remain unchanged. What happens to employment rent?
options: It falls because the worker has less to lose.
It rises because the job’s net value increases.
It is always zero when effort is easy.
The outside option automatically rises by the same amount.
hints: Separate net hourly value when employed ($w - c$) from net hourly value when unemployed ($b - s$), and multiply only over expected unemployment duration.
Watch out for the classic trap: A change inside the current job need not change the outside option.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** It rises because the job’s net value increases.

Lower effort cost raises the difference between job value and fallback value.
questions.pitfall: A change inside the current job need not change the outside option.

questions.title: M051 · Duration matters
questions.promptMarkdown: After dismissal, a worker expects an identical replacement job after 12 weeks. Why not count the wage difference for every remaining working year?
options: An identical replacement job necessarily has a lower wage.
Employment rent must be measured for exactly one week.
All future income is irrelevant from the first day.
Once the identical job starts, the compared future payoffs coincide.
hints: Separate net hourly value when employed ($w - c$) from net hourly value when unemployed ($b - s$), and multiply only over expected unemployment duration.
Watch out for the classic trap: Use the period of actual payoff differences.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** Once the identical job starts, the compared future payoffs coincide.

The relevant loss occurs during the unemployment spell; later identical outcomes cancel.
questions.pitfall: Use the period of actual payoff differences.

questions.title: M052 · Deterrence at equilibrium
questions.promptMarkdown: Why can unemployment help discipline workers in this model?
options: Unemployment mechanically sets every wage to zero.
Workers enjoy unemployment more whenever unemployment rises.
Dismissal can imply a costly period without an equally valuable job.
The firm can observe effort perfectly when unemployment rises.
hints: Separate net hourly value when employed ($w - c$) from net hourly value when unemployed ($b - s$), and multiply only over expected unemployment duration.
Watch out for the classic trap: This describes the model’s mechanism, not a claim that unemployment is desirable.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** Dismissal can imply a costly period without an equally valuable job.

Costly job loss gives workers a reason to protect their jobs by exerting effort.
questions.pitfall: This describes the model’s mechanism, not a claim that unemployment is desirable.

questions.title: M053 · No-shirking areas
questions.promptMarkdown: At the minimum no-shirking wage, what relationship holds between the gain from shirking before detection and rent lost after dismissal?
options: The gain is total output and the loss is total tax revenue.
They are equal.
Both areas must always be zero.
The shirking gain must strictly exceed the loss.
hints: Separate net hourly value when employed ($w - c$) from net hourly value when unemployed ($b - s$), and multiply only over expected unemployment duration.
Watch out for the classic trap: The two areas represent alternatives over a stated time horizon.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** They are equal.

At the threshold, effort and shirking give equal total payoffs. A wage above it can make effort strictly preferable.
questions.pitfall: The two areas represent alternatives over a stated time horizon.

questions.title: M054 · Slower detection
questions.promptMarkdown: A shirking worker is caught later, with all other parameters fixed. What happens to the required no-shirking wage?
options: It must equal the unemployment rate.
It stays fixed by definition.
It rises.
It falls.
hints: Separate net hourly value when employed ($w - c$) from net hourly value when unemployed ($b - s$), and multiply only over expected unemployment duration.

questions.solutionMarkdown:

More time collecting pay without effort and less time suffering dismissal makes shirking more attractive. A higher wage is needed to deter it.

questions.title: M061 · Own price versus demand shift
questions.promptMarkdown: The price of apples falls, with income, tastes and other prices fixed. What happens in a standard demand diagram?

Watch out for the classic trap: P=MC does not imply zero total profit.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** Earlier units add profit while P>MC; additional units beyond that point reduce profit when MC>P.

A price taker receives P for an extra unit. Compare its marginal revenue with marginal cost.
questions.pitfall: P=MC does not imply zero total profit.

questions.title: M065 · Binding ceiling
questions.promptMarkdown: A price ceiling is set below the competitive equilibrium price. What follows in the standard model?

The ceiling is non-binding because it is below equilibrium.
Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied: a shortage.
Both curves shift until the ceiling disappears.

Watch out for the classic trap: A ceiling below equilibrium is binding.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer:** Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied: a shortage.

At the low controlled price, buyers want more and suppliers offer less than at equilibrium.
questions.pitfall: A ceiling below equilibrium is binding.

questions.title: M066 · Price above equilibrium

Both quantities must be zero.

Watch out for the classic trap: Adjustment along fixed curves is not automatically a shift.

**Correct Answer:** Excess supply puts downward pressure on price.

Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at that price.

questions.title: M067 · Producer surplus and profit
questions.promptMarkdown: A firm has producer surplus of 900 NOK and fixed cost of 250 NOK. Which statement is correct?

questions.title: S001 · Equal cash versus equal percentages
questions.promptMarkdown:
Top-decile average income is 800,000 NOK; bottom-decile average is 100,000. Compare a 20,000 NOK transfer to everyone with a 10% rise in all incomes. Explain the rich/poor ratio in each case.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Correct initial and post-transfer ratios.
Correct unchanged percentage-rise ratio.
Explain the difference in proportional gains.
Verify exact ratios: initial 8.0, post-transfer ≈ 6.83, equal-% rise 8.0.
hints: Start from the exact formula for the income ratio, growth rate, or average/marginal product of labour ($APL = Y/L$, $MPL = \Delta Y/\Delta L$).
Make sure your concise answer covers: Correct initial and post-transfer ratios; Correct unchanged percentage-rise ratio.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Initially the ratio is 8. After the transfer it is 820,000/120,000≈6.83. The same kroner payment is a larger percentage gain for the poorer group. After a common 10% rise the ratio is 880,000/110,000=8: multiplying both averages by the same factor leaves the ratio unchanged. These calculations concern this ratio; they do not alone describe every feature of the distribution.

questions.title: S002 · Total, average and marginal product
questions.promptMarkdown:
A farm with fixed land produces 500 units with 10 workers and 620 with 14. Explain what happened to total output and average product. Can you identify the marginal product of the 14th worker exactly?

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Correct total and average calculations.
Explain why output can rise while average product falls.
Distinguish interval average addition from exact marginal product.
hints: Start from the exact formula for the income ratio, growth rate, or average/marginal product of labour ($APL = Y/L$, $MPL = \Delta Y/\Delta L$).
Make sure your concise answer covers: Correct total and average calculations; Explain why output can rise while average product falls.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Total output increased by 120. Average product fell from 500/10=50 to 620/14≈44.29. Extra workers can add output while lowering output per worker when land is fixed. The average additional output across the four added workers is 120/4=30; the exact marginal product of the 14th worker is not identified from these two observations alone.

questions.title: S003 · Institutions and specialisation
questions.promptMarkdown:
Explain how private property, markets and firms can support specialisation. Avoid assuming that capitalism requires the absence of government.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Define the three institutions.
Link exchange/coordination to specialisation.
Explain a compatible role for government.
hints: Start from the exact formula for the income ratio, growth rate, or average/marginal product of labour ($APL = Y/L$, $MPL = \Delta Y/\Delta L$).
Make sure your concise answer covers: Define the three institutions; Link exchange/coordination to specialisation.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Private property provides rights over productive assets and incentives to maintain or use them. Markets allow voluntary exchange, so people can specialise in producing some goods while consuming many others. Firms coordinate inputs and people in production. Government can enforce contracts and property rights, supply public services and regulate markets within such a system. These institutions can support specialisation without implying that every outcome is efficient or equally distributed.

questions.title: S004 · Production versus welfare
questions.promptMarkdown:
A country’s real GDP per person rises while pollution and income inequality also rise. Explain why the GDP change does not settle whether wellbeing improved.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Define what real GDP per person measures.
Explain distribution and environmental limitations.
Give another relevant nonmarket limitation.
hints: Start from the exact formula for the income ratio, growth rate, or average/marginal product of labour ($APL = Y/L$, $MPL = \Delta Y/\Delta L$).
Make sure your concise answer covers: Define what real GDP per person measures; Explain distribution and environmental limitations.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Real GDP per person indicates average production per person at constant prices, not a complete welfare measure. It does not show who received the additional income, so unequal gains may matter. Environmental damage can reduce health and natural assets without being fully deducted. Unpaid work and leisure also contribute to wellbeing but are not captured comprehensively. The production gain is relevant evidence, but a welfare judgement needs distributional and nonmarket information as well.

A study session gives subjective benefit 1,300 NOK and effort cost 350. The best alternative is a shift paying 1,000 with effort cost 250. Calculate the opportunity cost and economic rent of studying, and explain the choice.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Compute both net payoffs.
Identify opportunity cost as 750.
Calculate rent of 200 and explain the decision.
hints: Write down the total cost equation $C = wL + pR$ (slope $-w/p$) or separate direct cost from the net value of the next-best reservation option.
Make sure your concise answer covers: Compute both net payoffs; Identify opportunity cost.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Studying has net value 1,300−350=950. The shift has net value 1,000−250=750, which is the opportunity cost of studying. Economic rent from studying is 950−750=200 NOK. Studying is preferred under the stated valuations because its net advantage over the best alternative is positive. The relevant forgone value is the shift’s net payoff, not its gross wage.

obsidianLink.heading: 2.1 Opportunity Cost, Reservation Options, and Economic Rent

pacing.rationale: Part 2 200-word short answer / numerical drill: 12m learning par, 6m exam par (~18m total for 3 Part 2 items).

questions.title: S006 · An isocost line in words and algebra
questions.promptMarkdown:
For labour L on x and energy R on y, total input cost is C=360L+120R. Derive the isocost slope and both intercepts when C=7,200. Explain a wage increase with energy price fixed.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Correct equation and slope.
Both correct intercepts and units.
Correct rotation explanation at fixed cost budget.
hints: Write down the total cost equation $C = wL + pR$ (slope $-w/p$) or separate direct cost from the net value of the next-best reservation option.
Make sure your concise answer covers: Correct equation and slope; Both correct intercepts and units.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Rearranging gives R=60−3L. The vertical intercept is 60 energy units and the horizontal intercept is 20 labour hours. The slope is −360/120=−3, meaning three energy units can be exchanged for one labour hour at constant cost. A higher wage raises w/p and makes the line steeper; for the same cost budget and energy price, the labour intercept moves inward while the energy intercept stays at 60.

obsidianLink.heading: 2.2 Technology, Dominance, and Isocost Lines

pacing.rationale: Part 2 200-word short answer / numerical drill: 12m learning par, 6m exam par (~18m total for 3 Part 2 items).

questions.title: S007 · Technology switch
questions.promptMarkdown:
Two processes produce the same batch. A uses 6 labour hours and 12 energy units; B uses 9 labour hours and 5 energy units. Wage is 200, energy price first 80 then 160. Compare costs and explain whether a switch occurs.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Correct initial cost ranking.
Correct new ranking and 520 saving.
Explain trade-off, relative prices and switching-cost assumption.
hints: Write down the total cost equation $C = wL + pR$ (slope $-w/p$) or separate direct cost from the net value of the next-best reservation option.
Make sure your concise answer covers: Correct initial cost ranking; Correct new ranking saving.
questions.solutionMarkdown: At energy price 80, A costs 6×200+12×80=2,160, while B costs 9×200+5×80=2,200, so A is cheaper by 40. At price 160, A costs 3,120 and B costs 2,600, so B is cheaper by 520. Neither technology physically dominates: A saves labour and B saves energy. The relative energy-price increase changes the cost ranking and creates an incentive to switch to B, before any additional switching costs.

obsidianLink.heading: 2.2 Technology, Dominance, and Isocost Lines

questions.title: S008 · Economic rent and sunk expenditure
questions.promptMarkdown:
A festival ticket bought earlier cost 500 NOK and cannot be resold or refunded. Attending gives enjoyment 900 and discomfort cost 200. Working instead gives wages 800 and effort cost 250. Explain the current decision and rent from attending.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Explain why the ticket cost is sunk.
Compute net benefits and opportunity cost.
Calculate rent 150 and give the decision.
hints: Write down the total cost equation $C = wL + pR$ (slope $-w/p$) or separate direct cost from the net value of the next-best reservation option.
Make sure your concise answer covers: Explain why the ticket cost is sunk; Compute net benefits and opportunity cost.
questions.solutionMarkdown: The historical ticket payment is sunk: it is unrecoverable under both current options. Attending has current net value 900−200=700. Working has net value 800−250=550, the best forgone alternative. Attending therefore has rent 700−550=150 NOK and is preferred under these assumptions. Counting the old payment only against attending would incorrectly make the decision depend on a cost that can no longer change.

obsidianLink.heading: 2.1 Opportunity Cost, Reservation Options, and Economic Rent

pacing.rationale: Part 2 200-word short answer / numerical drill: 12m learning par, 6m exam par (~18m total for 3 Part 2 items).

questions.title: S009 · Indifference curves and MRS
questions.promptMarkdown:
Explain an indifference curve for consumption and free time. Explain why MRS can change along one curve even though utility is constant.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Define equal utility along one curve.
Define MRS with axes and units.
Explain diminishing MRS without claiming utility changes.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Make sure your concise answer covers: Define equal utility along one curve; Define MRS with axes and units.
questions.solutionMarkdown: An indifference curve joins bundles giving the same utility. Moving along it changes the mix of consumption and free time while preserving overall satisfaction. MRS is the local consumption sacrifice per extra free hour that preserves utility, equal to the magnitude of the curve’s slope. With standard convex preferences, more free time and less consumption reduce willingness to sacrifice still more consumption, so MRS falls. Constant total utility does not imply a constant marginal trade-off.

obsidianLink.heading: 3.1 Preferences, Indifference Curves, and the Marginal Rate of Substitution ($MRS$)

pacing.rationale: Part 2 200-word short answer / numerical drill: 12m learning par, 6m exam par (~18m total for 3 Part 2 items).

questions.title: S010 · Budget and willingness
questions.promptMarkdown:
A worker keeps 240 NOK/hour, receives 160 NOK/day independently of work and has 16 free hours out of 24. Find maximum consumption and MRT. At this bundle MRS is 360 NOK/hour. Explain a beneficial local adjustment.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Correct work hours and consumption.
Correct MRT and its economic meaning.
Use MRS>MRT for the adjustment and avoid inventing an exact optimum.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Make sure your concise answer covers: Correct work hours and consumption; Correct MRT and its economic meaning.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Work is 24−16=8 hours, so maximum consumption is 240×8+160=2,080 NOK. MRT is the net hourly wage, 240 NOK/hour; the budget slope is −240. MRS of 360 exceeds MRT, so the worker values a small increase in free time more than the consumption it costs. Moving toward more free time and less work can increase utility, under standard smooth preferences. The information establishes a direction, not the exact new optimum.

obsidianLink.heading: 3.2 The Feasible Frontier and Optimal Choice ($MRS = MRT$)

questions.title: S011 · Transfer versus wage tax cut
questions.promptMarkdown:
Compare an unconditional daily transfer with a cut in a constant wage-income tax rate. Explain budget shape, MRT and effects on work, assuming free time is a normal good.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Transfer: parallel shift and unchanged MRT.
Tax cut: net wage/MRT rise and rotation.
Explain opposing effects and conditional labour-supply outcome.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Make sure your concise answer covers: Transfer: parallel shift and unchanged MRT; Tax cut: net wage/MRT rise and rotation.
questions.solutionMarkdown: A transfer raises non-labour income and shifts the budget line upward in parallel, leaving the net wage and MRT unchanged. Its income effect encourages more leisure and less work under the normal-good assumption. A wage tax cut raises the net hourly wage and makes the line steeper, pivoting around the zero-work bundle when other income is fixed. It creates an income effect toward more leisure and a substitution effect toward less leisure. Their relative sizes determine the final change in work. Preferences themselves need not change.

obsidianLink.heading: 3.3 Income and Substitution Effects of Wage and Tax Changes

questions.title: S012 · Reading a decomposition
questions.promptMarkdown:
A diagram labels old optimum E at t=15, hypothetical G at t=18.2 and new optimum F at t=16.4. G uses the old wage slope and lies on the same indifference curve as F. Calculate both effects and total change in work.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Correct +3.2 and −1.8 effects.
Correct +1.4 free time and −1.4 work.
Explain hypothetical G, unchanged old slope and equal final utility.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Make sure your concise answer covers: Correct +3.2 and −1.8 effects; Correct +1.4 free time and −1.4 work.
questions.solutionMarkdown: The diagram’s income effect E→G is 18.2−15=+3.2 free hours. Its substitution effect G→F is 16.4−18.2=−1.8 hours. Net free time rises by 1.4 hours, so work falls by 1.4 hours with a fixed day. G is hypothetical, separating purchasing power from relative prices. E and F are the actual before/after choices. G and F have equal utility; E belongs to a lower level. The construction is utility-compensated (Hicks-style), even if a course source uses a broader decomposition label.

questions.title: S013 · Employment rent with an identical replacement
questions.promptMarkdown:
Hourly wage is 210 NOK, effort disutility 30, benefit 75 and unemployment stigma 15, all hourly equivalents. Normal work is 32 hours/week; an identical job would be found after 25 weeks. Calculate rent per hour and the total loss from dismissal.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Compute employed and unemployed net values.
Calculate hourly rent 120.
Use 25×32 hours for total 96,000 and explain cancellation afterwards.
hints: Separate net hourly value when employed ($w - c$) from net hourly value when unemployed ($b - s$), and multiply only over expected unemployment duration.
Make sure your concise answer covers: Compute employed and unemployed net values; Calculate hourly rent.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Net job value is 210−30=180 NOK/hour. Net unemployment payoff is 75−15=60, so hourly employment rent is 120. The payoff difference lasts for 25×32=800 normal working hours. Total employment rent lost is 120×800=96,000 NOK. After the identical job begins, the compared payoffs coincide, so a longer common planning horizon does not add more loss.

obsidianLink.heading: 4.2 Employment Rent and the Cost of Job Loss

pacing.rationale: Part 2 200-word short answer / numerical drill: 12m learning par, 6m exam par (~18m total for 3 Part 2 items).

questions.title: S014 · Formula supplied: discipline threshold
questions.promptMarkdown:
A model gives weekly fallback r=6,000, effort cost c=1,500, horizon h=50 weeks and detection time s=10. Formula supplied: w_NS=r+c+[s/(h−s)]c. Calculate the wage and explain why later detection raises it.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Correct substitution and 7,875.
Explain the gain/loss equality.
Explain the two effects of later detection.
hints: Separate net hourly value when employed ($w - c$) from net hourly value when unemployed ($b - s$), and multiply only over expected unemployment duration.
Make sure your concise answer covers: Correct substitution; Explain the gain/loss equality.
questions.solutionMarkdown: The minimum wage is 6,000+1,500+(10/40)×1,500=7,875 NOK/week. At the threshold, the gain from avoiding effort before detection, cs, equals the job rent lost after firing, (w−c−r)(h−s). Delayed detection increases the time earning wages without effort and reduces the remaining time suffering dismissal within the fixed horizon. This makes shirking more attractive at the old wage, requiring a higher wage to restore the incentive.

obsidianLink.heading: 4.3 The Labour Discipline Model and No-Shirking Wage

questions.title: S015 · Incomplete contracts and unemployment
questions.promptMarkdown:
Explain why imperfect observation of effort can lead a firm to pay above the outside option. Explain why higher unemployment changes the wage needed for effort.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Explain observability/enforcement problem.
Connect above-fallback pay and job-loss cost.
Explain how unemployment changes incentives at a given wage.
hints: Separate net hourly value when employed ($w - c$) from net hourly value when unemployed ($b - s$), and multiply only over expected unemployment duration.
Make sure your concise answer covers: Explain observability/enforcement problem; Connect above-fallback pay and job-loss cost.
questions.solutionMarkdown: A contract cannot fully specify or enforce every aspect of effort. A worker needs something to lose from dismissal, so the job must provide a net advantage over the next-best alternative. This employment rent helps motivate effort. Higher unemployment generally makes a comparable replacement job harder to obtain, increasing the expected cost of dismissal at a given wage. A firm can then maintain effort at a lower required wage, other things equal. This is a mechanism within the model, not a claim that the employer knows each outside option perfectly.

obsidianLink.heading: 4.2 Employment Rent and the Cost of Job Loss

questions.title: S016 · Principal–agent problem
questions.promptMarkdown:
Explain why owners may struggle to ensure managers pursue their interests. Give two responses and one limitation.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Identify delegation, divergent interests and information.
Describe two relevant mechanisms.
Explain a substantive limitation.
hints: Separate net hourly value when employed ($w - c$) from net hourly value when unemployed ($b - s$), and multiply only over expected unemployment duration.
Make sure your concise answer covers: Identify delegation, divergent interests and information; Describe two relevant mechanisms.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Owners delegate decisions to managers, who may have better operational information and different objectives. Owners can monitor through boards, audits and reporting, and can link some remuneration to performance, for example shares or long-term results. Monitoring is costly and cannot observe every decision. Performance measures can also reward luck or encourage narrow targets and excessive risk. These mechanisms can improve alignment without eliminating asymmetric information or all conflicts of interest.
