questions.title: S017 · Why supply follows MC
questions.promptMarkdown:
Explain why a price-taking firm with increasing marginal cost chooses an interior operating output where P=MC. Does this imply that profit is zero?

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Explain marginal revenue for a price taker.
Compare P and MC on both sides.
Distinguish marginal condition from total profit.
hints: Check whether the shock changes buyers' WTP (shifts Demand), sellers' marginal cost (shifts Supply), or merely moves along an unchanged curve.
Make sure your concise answer covers: Explain marginal revenue for a price taker; Compare P and MC on both sides.
questions.solutionMarkdown: A price taker earns the market price on each additional unit. While price exceeds marginal cost, an extra unit adds more revenue than cost, so expanding increases profit. Beyond the point where MC exceeds price, further output reduces profit. Thus the interior operating optimum is P=MC under the stated conditions. Profit need not be zero because total profit depends on average total costs and fixed costs, not only the cost of the marginal unit.

obsidianLink.heading: 5.1 Demand (Willingness to Pay) and Supply (Marginal Cost)

pacing.rationale: Part 2 200-word short answer / numerical drill: 12m learning par, 6m exam par (~18m total for 3 Part 2 items).

questions.title: S018 · A demand increase and cheaper production
questions.promptMarkdown:
A normal good becomes more popular while a production innovation lowers marginal cost. Use supply and demand to explain what can and cannot be concluded about equilibrium price and quantity.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Identify both shifts.
Conclude quantity rises.
Explain price ambiguity from opposing effects.
hints: Check whether the shock changes buyers' WTP (shifts Demand), sellers' marginal cost (shifts Supply), or merely moves along an unchanged curve.
Make sure your concise answer covers: Identify both shifts; Conclude quantity rises.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Popularity shifts demand right; lower marginal cost shifts supply down/right. Both changes raise equilibrium quantity, so quantity increases under standard curves. Their effects on price oppose: the demand increase raises it and the supply increase lowers it. Without the sizes of the shifts, the final price direction is ambiguous. A price change caused by these shocks represents movement along a curve, while the underlying preference and technology changes shift curves.

obsidianLink.heading: 5.3 Comparative Statics: Curve Shifts, Steepness, and Tariffs

pacing.rationale: Part 2 200-word short answer / numerical drill: 12m learning par, 6m exam par (~18m total for 3 Part 2 items).

questions.title: S019 · Ceiling and shortage
questions.promptMarkdown:
Demand is Qd=120−2P and supply is Qs=2P. Calculate the competitive equilibrium. A ceiling of P=20 is imposed. Calculate the shortage and explain why the market does not clear.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Correct equilibrium P=30,Q=60.
Correct ceiling quantities and shortage=40.
Explain binding restriction and rationing.
hints: Check whether the shock changes buyers' WTP (shifts Demand), sellers' marginal cost (shifts Supply), or merely moves along an unchanged curve.
Make sure your concise answer covers: Correct equilibrium P=30,Q=60; Correct ceiling quantities and shortage=40.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Equilibrium solves 120−2P=2P, giving P=30 and Q=60. At the ceiling of 20, quantity demanded is 80 and supplied is 40, so the shortage is 40 units. The ceiling is below the clearing price and is binding. Buyers want more at that price than sellers offer. Actual trade is constrained by the short side in this simple model; rationing is needed, and a low posted price alone does not guarantee everyone can buy.

obsidianLink.heading: 5.2 Price-Taking Firms, Market Equilibrium, and Surplus

pacing.rationale: Part 2 200-word short answer / numerical drill: 12m learning par, 6m exam par (~18m total for 3 Part 2 items).

questions.title: S020 · Per-unit tariff incidence
questions.promptMarkdown:
Demand is P=120−Q and supply before a per-unit tariff is P=20+Q. A tariff of 20 shifts supply to P=40+Q. Find the old and new equilibria and explain who bears the price wedge.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Correct old and new equilibria.
Correct buyers’ price and net seller price.
Explain shared incidence and distinguish revenue from deadweight loss.
hints: Check whether the shock changes buyers' WTP (shifts Demand), sellers' marginal cost (shifts Supply), or merely moves along an unchanged curve.
Make sure your concise answer covers: Correct old and new equilibria; Correct buyers’ price and net seller price.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Initially 120−Q=20+Q, so Q=50 and buyers pay 70. After the tariff, 120−Q=40+Q gives Q=40 and buyers pay 80. Sellers receive 80−20=60 net of the tariff. Relative to the old price, buyers pay 10 more and sellers receive 10 less per unit. Quantity falls by 10. Tariff revenue is 20×40=800, a transfer distinct from the lost surplus on trades no longer made.

obsidianLink.heading: 5.3 Comparative Statics: Curve Shifts, Steepness, and Tariffs

questions.title: S021 · Three labour-market rates
questions.promptMarkdown:
Working-age population is 5,000, employed=3,200 and unemployed=300. Calculate the labour force, employment rate, unemployment rate and participation rate.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Correct labour force and inactive number.
Correct employment and participation rates.
Correct unemployment rate and denominator explanation.
hints: Distinguish factors that shift the upward-sloping WS curve (effort/benefits/coordination) from factors that shift the horizontal PS curve ($\lambda$, markup $\sigma$).
Make sure your concise answer covers: Correct labour force and inactive number; Correct employment and participation rates.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Labour force is 3,200+300=3,500; the other 1,500 are inactive. Employment rate is 3,200/5,000=64%. Unemployment rate is 300/3,500≈8.57%. Participation is 3,500/5,000=70%. The employment and unemployment rates do not sum to 100 because they have different denominators. Labour force includes those employed and those actively seeking and available for work, not every working-age person.

obsidianLink.heading: 6.1 Measuring Unemployment, Employment, and Real Wages

pacing.rationale: Part 2 200-word short answer / numerical drill: 12m learning par, 6m exam par (~18m total for 3 Part 2 items).

questions.title: S022 · Both rates rise
questions.promptMarkdown:
Initially P=1,000, E=600 and U=100. Then 100 inactive people enter the labour force: 60 find jobs and 40 seek work. P stays fixed. Show that employment and unemployment rates can both rise.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Correct initial rates.
Correct new E,U and both rates.
Explain entry from inactivity and different denominators.
hints: Distinguish factors that shift the upward-sloping WS curve (effort/benefits/coordination) from factors that shift the horizontal PS curve ($\lambda$, markup $\sigma$).
Make sure your concise answer covers: Correct initial rates; Correct new E,U and both rates.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Initially employment rate=600/1,000=60%, labour force=700 and unemployment rate=100/700≈14.29%. Afterwards E=660, U=140 and labour force=800. Employment rate rises to 66%, and unemployment rate rises to 140/800=17.5%. More people work, but unemployment also grows relative to its different denominator because previously inactive people start job seeking. The rates are not complements.

obsidianLink.heading: 6.2 The Macroeconomic WS–PS Model

questions.title: S023 · Read a WS–PS equilibrium
questions.promptMarkdown:
A diagram has N on x, real wage on y, labour force L=100 and equilibrium N*=88,w*=72. Explain unemployment and why neither hiring willingness nor acceptance of lower pay alone establishes a stable lower-wage outcome.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Correct unemployment calculation and units.
Interpret both curves and their intersection.
Explain acceptance versus effort incentives.
hints: Distinguish factors that shift the upward-sloping WS curve (effort/benefits/coordination) from factors that shift the horizontal PS curve ($\lambda$, markup $\sigma$).
Make sure your concise answer covers: Correct unemployment calculation and units; Interpret both curves and their intersection.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Unemployment is L−N=12, so the unemployment rate is 12/100=12% if both quantities use the same population units. The intersection equates the effort-motivating wage from WS with the real wage resulting from firms’ pricing on PS. An unemployed person might accept a lower wage, but that does not establish an incentive to exert effort once hired. Cutting pay can erode employment rent and make shirking attractive. The model therefore permits equilibrium unemployment.

obsidianLink.heading: 6.2 The Macroeconomic WS–PS Model

pacing.rationale: Part 2 200-word short answer / numerical drill: 12m learning par, 6m exam par (~18m total for 3 Part 2 items).

questions.title: S024 · Two different shocks
questions.promptMarkdown:
With a horizontal PS and upward WS, compare (i) higher unemployment benefits and (ii) stronger product-market competition. Hold other determinants fixed.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Benefits: correct curve and mechanism.
Benefits: correct employment and real-wage effects.
Competition: correct curve, mechanism and both effects.
hints: Distinguish factors that shift the upward-sloping WS curve (effort/benefits/coordination) from factors that shift the horizontal PS curve ($\lambda$, markup $\sigma$).
Make sure your concise answer covers: Benefits: correct curve and mechanism; Benefits: correct employment and real-wage effects.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Higher benefits improve the fallback and shift WS up. The intersection moves left along unchanged PS: employment falls and equilibrium real wage is unchanged. Stronger competition reduces the course-convention profit share/markup, raising PS. Along unchanged WS, the intersection moves up and right: real wage and employment rise. The mechanisms differ: the first changes wage-setting incentives, the second changes the real wage consistent with product-market pricing.

obsidianLink.heading: 6.3 Comparative Statics: Shifts in the WS and PS Curves

questions.title: S025 · Union bargaining and voice
questions.promptMarkdown:
Distinguish a union’s strike-bargaining effect from its voice effect in the simplified WS–PS model. Hold PS fixed.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Explain bargaining and upward WS.
Explain voice and downward WS.
State conditional equilibrium outcomes with PS fixed.
hints: Order the population from poorest (unemployed) to workers to owners on the Lorenz curve, or separate union strike-threat shifts from coordinated restraint.
Make sure your concise answer covers: Explain bargaining and upward WS; Explain voice and downward WS.
questions.solutionMarkdown: A credible strike threat can raise the wage demanded at each employment level, shifting WS up. With PS fixed, equilibrium employment falls while the economy-wide equilibrium real wage stays unchanged. A voice effect can improve work organisation or reduce effort disutility, lowering the wage needed for effort and shifting WS down. Employment rises along the same PS line without a lower equilibrium real wage. Productivity improvements, if separately introduced, could also move PS, but are not assumed here.

obsidianLink.heading: 7.2 Trade Unions and the Norwegian *Frontfagsmodellen*

pacing.rationale: Part 2 200-word short answer / numerical drill: 12m learning par, 6m exam par (~18m total for 3 Part 2 items).

questions.title: S026 · Frontfag and wage restraint
questions.promptMarkdown:
Explain why coordinated wage bargaining can improve employment in the course model even though workers seek good wages. Does a downward WS shift necessarily cut the final equilibrium real wage?

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Explain coordination and wage pressure.
Distinguish fixed-N comparison from equilibrium adjustment.
State higher employment and unchanged real wage conditional on PS.
hints: Order the population from poorest (unemployed) to workers to owners on the Lorenz curve, or separate union strike-threat shifts from coordinated restraint.
Make sure your concise answer covers: Explain coordination and wage pressure; Distinguish fixed-N comparison from equilibrium adjustment.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Coordinated bargaining can account for economy-wide employment, price pressure and export competitiveness rather than each union pursuing wage demands independently. Relative wage restraint shifts WS down. At the old employment level the wage pressure is lower, but employment adjusts upward until the new WS meets unchanged PS. The final real wage is therefore unchanged, while unemployment is lower. A lower wage-setting requirement at a fixed N is different from the final equilibrium wage after N changes.

questions.title: S027 · Build a Lorenz curve
questions.promptMarkdown:
There are 100 people: 12 have zero market income, 78 identical workers jointly receive 58% of income, and 10 identical owners receive 42%. Each owner earns more than each worker. State the ordered Lorenz coordinates and interpret them. Do not calculate Gini.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Correct first kink.
Correct cumulative worker kink and endpoint.
Explain ranking, cumulative shares and zero-income assumption.
hints: Order the population from poorest (unemployed) to workers to owners on the Lorenz curve, or separate union strike-threat shifts from coordinated restraint.
Make sure your concise answer covers: Correct first kink; Correct cumulative worker kink and endpoint.
questions.solutionMarkdown: The curve starts at (0,0). The 12 zero-income people give the first kink (12%,0%). Adding 78 workers gives cumulative population 90% and cumulative income 58%, so the second kink is (90%,58%). Adding the owners ends at (100%,100%). The population is ranked by income, and all plotted values are cumulative. The horizontal first segment reflects zero market income under the explicit assumption, not a universal claim about unemployment benefits.

obsidianLink.heading: 7.1 Lorenz Curves, the Gini Coefficient, and WS–PS Mapping

pacing.rationale: Part 2 200-word short answer / numerical drill: 12m learning par, 6m exam par (~18m total for 3 Part 2 items).

questions.title: S028 · Gini interpretation and a shift
questions.promptMarkdown:
A Lorenz curve moves toward the equality line at every interior population share. Explain what happens to inequality and Gini. Can a single Gini number uniquely identify a Lorenz curve?

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Explain equality line and smaller gap.
State lower inequality/Gini and zero at equality.
Explain why the scalar does not uniquely identify the distribution.
hints: Order the population from poorest (unemployed) to workers to owners on the Lorenz curve, or separate union strike-threat shifts from coordinated restraint.
Make sure your concise answer covers: Explain equality line and smaller gap; State lower inequality/Gini and zero at equality.
questions.solutionMarkdown: If the curve is everywhere closer to the equality line, the distribution is less unequal in the Lorenz sense and the area gap shrinks, so Gini falls. Perfect equality corresponds to zero Gini. A single Gini value does not uniquely identify the entire Lorenz curve: different distributions can have the same aggregate area gap. Interpretation does not require algebraically calculating a Gini coefficient here.

questions.title: S029 · GDP by value added
questions.promptMarkdown:
Farmers sell grain for 30 million NOK to bakers. Bakers buy electricity worth 5 million and sell bread for 90 million to final consumers. Grain and electricity are domestic with no intermediate inputs. Compute industry value added and total GDP.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Correct industry value added.
Correct GDP=90 and final-sales check.
Explain intermediate double counting.
hints: Avoid double-counting intermediate inputs in GDP, check both recession definitions (falling output vs. below potential), and test credit/behavioral limits to smoothing.
Make sure your concise answer covers: Correct industry value added; Correct GDP=90 and final-sales check.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Farmers add 30 million and electricity producers add 5 million. Bakers add 90−30−5=55 million. Total GDP is 30+5+55=90 million, matching final bread sales. Adding 30+5+90 would double count intermediate inputs already embodied in bread. Wages and profits distribute value added; they are not deducted as purchased intermediate goods/services in this calculation.

questions.title: S030 · Exports versus net exports
questions.promptMarkdown:
GDP is 6,000 billion NOK; C=2,500, I=1,400, G=1,000 and exports X=1,800. Find imports and net exports. Explain why imports are subtracted.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Correct imports 700.
Correct net exports 1,100 and distinction from exports.
Explain removal of foreign production from expenditure totals.
hints: Avoid double-counting intermediate inputs in GDP, check both recession definitions (falling output vs. below potential), and test credit/behavioral limits to smoothing.
Make sure your concise answer covers: Correct imports; Correct net exports and distinction from exports.
questions.solutionMarkdown: From GDP=C+I+G+X−M, imports are 2,500+1,400+1,000+1,800−6,000=700 billion. Net exports are X−M=1,100 billion; exports alone are 1,800. Imports are subtracted to remove foreign production already included in expenditures such as consumption or investment. They are not subtracted because foreign goods are intrinsically bad or because exports already contain the import adjustment.

questions.title: S031 · Real output and recession definitions
questions.promptMarkdown:
Nominal GDP rises by 8%, while the appropriate GDP price measure rises by 10%. Explain real GDP growth. Would positive nominal growth alone rule out a recession defined as falling real output?

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Correct exact or clearly approximate real growth.
Explain nominal growth versus quantity change.
Distinguish falling output from output relative to normal.
hints: Avoid double-counting intermediate inputs in GDP, check both recession definitions (falling output vs. below potential), and test credit/behavioral limits to smoothing.
Make sure your concise answer covers: Correct exact or clearly approximate real growth; Explain nominal growth versus quantity change.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Real GDP changes by 1.08/1.10−1≈−1.82%, so production volume falls despite higher nominal value. The approximation 8%−10%=−2% gives the same sign. Nominal GDP growth alone therefore cannot rule out falling real output. A different definition using output relative to its normal level would require information about that benchmark as well. The relevant price measure for economy-wide domestic production is the GDP deflator, not automatically the consumer price index.

questions.title: S032 · Smoothing and investment
questions.promptMarkdown:
Explain why temporary income changes may produce smaller consumption changes, and why investment can nevertheless move sharply. Include one limitation of consumption smoothing.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Explain temporary versus permanent income.
Identify a meaningful smoothing constraint.
Explain expectations and project timing in investment.
hints: Avoid double-counting intermediate inputs in GDP, check both recession definitions (falling output vs. below potential), and test credit/behavioral limits to smoothing.
Make sure your concise answer covers: Explain temporary versus permanent income; Identify a meaningful smoothing constraint.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Forward-looking households can save in good periods or borrow/use buffers during temporary income shortfalls, spreading consumption adjustments over time. A permanent income loss generally requires a larger lasting adjustment because lifetime resources fall more. Households without savings or credit may be unable to smooth. Firms’ investment depends on expected future sales and returns; expectations can change rapidly, and large projects can be postponed. Thus investment can be volatile even when consumption is comparatively stable.

questions.title: S033 · Price level and inflation
questions.promptMarkdown:
CPI is 100 in the base year, 120 last year and 117 this year. Calculate this year’s inflation and explain how prices can remain above the base year while inflation is negative.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Correct inflation −2.5%.
Correct 17% base-year comparison.
Explain level versus rate of change.
hints: Compare the real wage required for effort ($w^{WS}$) with the price-setting real wage ($w^{PS}$) to see whether a positive bargaining gap drives a wage–price spiral.
Make sure your concise answer covers: Correct inflation −2.5%; Correct% base-year comparison.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Inflation=(117−120)/120×100=−2.5%, so the economy has deflation for that interval. CPI=117 still means the measured basket is 17% more expensive than in the base year. Inflation compares consecutive price levels; the index relative to 100 compares current prices with the base. A level can fall without returning all the way to its earlier benchmark.

questions.title: S034 · Deflating consumption
questions.promptMarkdown:
Nominal consumption rises from 240 to 300 while CPI rises from 100 to 120. Calculate final real consumption in base-year prices and its growth. Explain the difference from nominal growth.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Correct final real consumption 250.
Correct real growth about 4.17%.
Contrast nominal 25% with quantity growth.
hints: Compare the real wage required for effort ($w^{WS}$) with the price-setting real wage ($w^{PS}$) to see whether a positive bargaining gap drives a wage–price spiral.
Make sure your concise answer covers: Correct final real consumption; Correct real growth%.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Final real consumption=300/120×100=250. Initial real consumption is 240 because CPI initially equals 100. Real growth=(250−240)/240×100≈4.17%, while nominal growth=(300−240)/240×100=25%. Most of the nominal increase reflects higher prices; only the deflated increase measures additional consumption volume using the stipulated appropriate price index.

questions.title: S035 · From bargaining gap to inflation
questions.promptMarkdown:
Employment is above N*, so WS lies above PS. Explain the wage–price process and why a higher nominal wage alone need not solve the conflict.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Link low unemployment to wage pressure.
Link wage costs to prices and W/P.
Explain repeated unresolved claims without inventing a numerical inflation rate.
hints: Compare the real wage required for effort ($w^{WS}$) with the price-setting real wage ($w^{PS}$) to see whether a positive bargaining gap drives a wage–price spiral.
Make sure your concise answer covers: Link low unemployment to wage pressure; Link wage costs to prices and W/P.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Low unemployment improves job alternatives and weakens the threat of job loss. Firms face pressure to raise nominal wages to attract and motivate workers. Given productivity and target pricing margins, higher wage costs lead firms to increase prices. This reduces the real gain from the nominal wage rise. If the incompatible claims persist at high employment, further wage and price increases can follow. The bargaining gap describes the inconsistency between wage-setting and price-setting real-wage claims. A different baseline inflation rate cannot be read from this diagram alone.

questions.title: S036 · Inflation, disinflation and purchasing power
questions.promptMarkdown:
Inflation falls from 7% to 3%, and nominal wages rise 2% in the latter year. Explain price-level direction and whether real wages rise. Give an exact or clearly approximate real-wage change.

*(Maximum 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Distinguish disinflation from deflation.
Correct direction of real wage.
Correct exact or clearly approximate calculation.
hints: Compare the real wage required for effort ($w^{WS}$) with the price-setting real wage ($w^{PS}$) to see whether a positive bargaining gap drives a wage–price spiral.
Make sure your concise answer covers: Distinguish disinflation from deflation; Correct direction of real wage.
questions.solutionMarkdown: Prices still rise by 3%; the fall in the positive inflation rate is disinflation, not deflation. With nominal wages rising only 2%, purchasing power falls: exact real-wage growth is 1.02/1.03−1≈−0.97%, approximately −1%. A positive nominal wage increase is insufficient to maintain real wages if relevant prices grow faster. The earlier 7% is not the denominator for this year’s real-wage calculation.

questions.title: C001 · A translator’s choice
questions.promptMarkdown:
A translator keeps 300 NOK/hour, has no other income and spends all earnings on daily consumption. The day has 24 hours. In the supplied diagram B=(12,3,600), E=(16,2,400) and D=(20,1,200). The green curve is tangent at E; the orange curve passes through B and D. Both goods are desirable.

- **a)** Explain the axes, the budget line and MRT. Calculate work hours at B and E. *(2 marks)*
- **b)** At B, the orange indifference curve is steeper than the budget line. Explain a utility-improving local change. *(3 marks)*
- **c)** Why are B and D equally preferred in the diagram, while E is preferred to both? *(2 marks)*
- **d)** At D, MRS is below MRT. Explain the adjustment and the tangency condition at E. Does tangency apply automatically at all endpoint choices? *(3 marks)*
rubricChecks: a) Define both axes and affordability boundary.
a) Correct MRT and work-hour calculations.
b) Interpret steepness as MRS>MRT.
b) Explain willingness versus market cost.
b) Give correct direction and utility implication.
c) Explain equal utility of B,D.
c) Explain higher affordable utility at E.
d) Correct adjustment at D.
d) Correct equal-slope condition at E.
d) Recognise endpoint qualification.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Structure your multi-part answer step by step: Define both axes and affordability boundary; Interpret steepness as MRS>MRT; Explain equal utility of B,D.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
- **a)** x is free time t; y is consumption c. The budget is c=300(24−t), with slope −300 and MRT=300 NOK/hour. B means 12 hours of work; E means 8. Points below the line are affordable; above it are not.
- **b)** MRS is greater than 300 at B. The translator values an extra small amount of leisure more than its market opportunity cost. Moving right along the budget line toward more leisure and less work can raise utility. B being affordable does not establish optimality.
- **c)** B and D lie on the same orange indifference curve and give the same utility despite different quantities. E is on the higher green curve. It is affordable and reaches a higher utility level; geometric distance from the origin is not the criterion.
- **d)** At D an extra free hour costs more than the person values it, so working a little more can improve utility. At E the marginal willingness and feasible trade-off match: MRS=MRT=300. This is the standard smooth interior optimum; an optimum at a time-endowment boundary need not satisfy equal slopes.

obsidianLink.heading: 3.2 The Feasible Frontier and Optimal Choice ($MRS = MRT$)

questions.title: C002 · Wage rise with opposing effects
questions.promptMarkdown:
A consultant’s net wage rises from 300 to 600 NOK/hour. The old chosen bundle is E=(16 free hours,2,400 NOK), the new choice F=(17,4,200). A hypothetical old-slope line is c=300(24−t)+1,740, tangent to the final indifference curve at G=(19.9,2,970).

- **a)** Explain why the actual budget line becomes steeper, and check consumption at E and F. *(2 marks)*
- **b)** Using the diagram’s E→G→F convention, calculate income, substitution and total changes in free time. *(3 marks)*
- **c)** Why does equal utility at F and G not mean they have equal MRS? *(2 marks)*
- **d)** Explain why this does not prove every wage rise reduces work. What is the role of the hypothetical 1,740 NOK? *(3 marks)*
rubricChecks: a) Correct opportunity-cost/pivot explanation.
a) Both consumption checks.
b) Correct +3.9.
b) Correct −2.9 and +1.
b) Distinguish comparison point from actual choices.
c) Separate utility level from local slope.
c) Correct MRS values from the two tangent slopes.
d) Explain opposing effects.
d) State conditional, not universal, dominance.
d) Interpret 1,740 as hypothetical income, not wage.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Structure your multi-part answer step by step: Correct opportunity-cost/pivot explanation; Correct +3.9; Separate utility level from local slope.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
- **a)** An extra free hour now costs 600 rather than 300 in forgone earnings. The line pivots around (24,0). Old E has 8×300=2,400 and new F has 7×600=4,200.
- **b)** Income effect:19.9−16=+3.9 hours. Substitution effect:17−19.9=−2.9. Total:+1 hour, equal to F−E. G is hypothetical and is not a third observed actual choice.
- **c)** They are different bundles on one indifference curve. Utility is constant along it, but its slope can vary. At F, tangency to the actual new line gives MRS=600; at G, tangency to the old-slope hypothetical line gives MRS=300.
- **d)** For normal leisure, greater purchasing power encourages more free time while the higher opportunity cost encourages less. In this example the income effect dominates, but another preference pattern could reverse the net change. The 1,740 is hypothetical non-labour income shifting the old-slope line in parallel; it is not added to the hourly wage. This is a utility-compensated graphical decomposition.

obsidianLink.heading: 3.3 Income and Substitution Effects of Wage and Tax Changes

questions.title: C003 · Cash grant versus lower wage tax
questions.promptMarkdown:
Gross hourly wage is 400 NOK. Initially the constant wage-income tax rate is 25%, non-labour income is zero and the chosen free time is 16 hours. Compare policy A: a 300 NOK unconditional daily grant; policy B: lowering the constant tax rate to 10%. Assume leisure is normal and standard smooth interior optima where relevant.

- **a)** Write the initial budget constraint and compute the initial bundle and MRT. *(2 marks)*
- **b)** For policy A, explain the line, opportunity cost and direction of the income effect. *(3 marks)*
- **c)** For policy B, compute MRT and explain both effects on leisure. *(2 marks)*
- **d)** Does either policy automatically shift the person’s preference map? Explain what MRS would equal at each new interior optimum, without claiming MRS is identical everywhere. *(3 marks)*
rubricChecks: a) Correct net wage and budget.
a) Correct bundle and MRT.
b) Correct new constraint/parallel shift.
b) Unchanged MRT and zero substitution effect.
b) Conditional direction for normal leisure.
c) Correct MRT=360.
c) Correct opposing effects and ambiguous net direction.
d) Distinguish preferences from budget changes.
d) Correct two equilibrium MRS values.
d) Explain local nature/interior assumption.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Structure your multi-part answer step by step: Correct net wage and budget; Correct new constraint/parallel shift; Correct MRT=360.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
- **a)** Net wage is 400×0.75=300. Budget is c=300(24−t). At t=16, work=8 and c=2,400. MRT is 300 NOK/hour.
- **b)** The constraint is c=300(24−t)+300. It shifts upward in parallel, so a free hour still costs 300. There is no substitution effect because relative prices are unchanged. With leisure normal, the grant encourages more leisure and fewer work hours.
- **c)** Net wage is 400×0.90=360. MRT rises to 360 and the budget line becomes steeper around (24,0). The income effect encourages more leisure; the substitution effect encourages less leisure because it is more expensive. The net outcome is not determined from the wage alone.
- **d)** The policies change the feasible set rather than tastes. A higher existing indifference curve becomes attainable. At A’s interior optimum, MRS=MRT=300; at B’s, MRS=MRT=360. MRS can differ at other bundles and can change along a single curve. An endpoint would need separate boundary reasoning.

questions.title: C004 · Dismissal and employment rent
questions.promptMarkdown:
Maja earns 240 NOK/hour, has effort cost 40, receives unemployment benefit equivalent to 95/hour and bears stigma cost equivalent to 15/hour. Normal hours are 30/week. A replacement identical job is expected after 18 weeks; she considers a common 100-week horizon. Ignore discounting.

- **a)** Calculate net values in the job and in unemployment, and hourly employment rent. *(2 marks)*
- **b)** Calculate total employment rent lost on dismissal. Explain why the 100-week horizon is not multiplied by hourly rent. *(3 marks)*
- **c)** Benefits rise by 20 NOK/hour equivalent. What changes in this comparison at a fixed wage? *(2 marks)*
- **d)** Connect the benefit increase to WS–PS. Hold productivity, pricing and labour force fixed. *(3 marks)*
rubricChecks: a) Correct net values.
a) Correct hourly rent and interpretation.
b) Correct relevant period and hours.
b) Correct total 64,800.
b) Explain why identical later outcomes cancel.
c) Correct new fallback and rent.
c) Interpret smaller job-loss cost, optionally correct total.
d) Mechanism through fallback/effort.
d) Correct WS and fixed PS.
d) Correct employment, unemployment and real-wage effects.
hints: Separate net hourly value when employed ($w - c$) from net hourly value when unemployed ($b - s$), and multiply only over expected unemployment duration.
Structure your multi-part answer step by step: Correct net values; Correct relevant period and hours; Correct new fallback and rent.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
- **a)** Job value=240−40=200. Unemployment payoff=95−15=80. Hourly rent=200−80=120 NOK. The wage is a cash payment; effort and stigma are money-equivalent utility costs.
- **b)** The payoff difference lasts 18 weeks, or 18×30=540 normal hours. Lost rent=120×540=64,800 NOK. After the identical replacement job starts, both paths yield the same payoffs, so weeks 19–100 cancel in the comparison.
- **c)** The fallback becomes 115−15=100. Hourly rent falls to 200−100=100. The job becomes less valuable relative to unemployment; if duration stays 18 weeks, total rent becomes 100×540=54,000.
- **d)** A better fallback weakens the threat of dismissal at each employment level. A higher wage is needed to maintain effort, so WS shifts up. PS is unchanged. Equilibrium employment falls and unemployment rises, while the equilibrium real wage remains at the PS height. This compares equilibria; it does not assume the wage stayed fixed after adjustment.

obsidianLink.heading: 4.2 Employment Rent and the Cost of Job Loss

questions.title: C005 · Two shaded areas and a supplied formula
questions.promptMarkdown:
A weekly model has fallback r=4,000 NOK, effort cost c=1,000, total horizon h=50 weeks and shirking detection time s=10 weeks. Assume deterministic detection, an identical weekly wage while hired, and fallback for the rest of the horizon after firing. Formula supplied: w_NS=r+c+[s/(h−s)]c.

- **a)** Describe the two payoff paths and write their total payoffs. *(2 marks)*
- **b)** Find the minimum no-shirking wage and verify equality of total payoffs at that wage. *(3 marks)*
- **c)** Detection is delayed to 20 weeks. Calculate the new threshold using the supplied formula. *(2 marks)*
- **d)** Explain the equal-area condition and one real-world information limitation. *(3 marks)*
rubricChecks: a) Correct effort path.
a) Correct shirking path and timing.
b) Correct wage 5,250.
b) Both payoff checks 212,500.
b) Interpret equality/strict preference.
c) Correct value about 5,666.67.
c) Explain why it rises.
d) Correct two areas.
d) Equality at threshold.
d) Specific information limitation without rejecting the mechanism.
hints: Separate net hourly value when employed ($w - c$) from net hourly value when unemployed ($b - s$), and multiply only over expected unemployment duration.
Structure your multi-part answer step by step: Correct effort path; Correct wage; Correct value.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
- **a)** Work properly:50(w−1,000). Shirk:10w+40×4,000. The first path keeps the job throughout; only the second is fired after week 10. Effort cost is avoided during shirking.
- **b)** w_NS=4,000+1,000+(10/40)×1,000=5,250. Work payoff=50×4,250=212,500. Shirking payoff=10×5,250+40×4,000=212,500. The worker is indifferent at the threshold; above it effort is strictly preferable under these assumptions.
- **c)** The new wage is 4,000+1,000+(20/30)×1,000≈5,666.67 NOK/week. Slower detection makes shirking attractive for longer and reduces the remaining punishment period, requiring a higher wage.
- **d)** Gain from shirking before detection is c×s. The lost job rent after firing is (w−c−r)(h−s). At the minimum wage these are equal. Firms may not know individual effort costs, private outside options or detection time precisely; the model supplies these inputs to isolate the incentive mechanism.

questions.title: C006 · Market equilibrium and a per-unit tariff
questions.promptMarkdown:
A competitive market is represented by inverse demand P=120−Q and supply P=20+Q. Quantity is in units and price in NOK/unit. A per-unit tariff of 20 shifts the buyer-price supply relation to P=40+Q. Assume all units traded are subject to the tariff, no externalities and no other changes.

- **a)** Find the initial equilibrium and explain why it clears the market. *(2 marks)*
- **b)** Find the new quantity, buyers’ price, sellers’ net price and tax incidence per unit. *(3 marks)*
- **c)** Calculate government tariff revenue. Why is it not identical to deadweight loss? *(2 marks)*
- **d)** Calculate initial CS and PS. Explain why quantity falls and buyers’ price rises by less than the tariff. *(3 marks)*
rubricChecks: a) Correct P=70,Q=50.
a) Interpret market clearing.
b) Correct Q=40 and buyer price=80.
b) Correct net seller price=60.
b) Correct incidence, 10 on each side.
c) Correct 800.
c) Explain transfer versus lost gains from trade.
d) Correct CS=1,250.
d) Correct PS=1,250.
d) Explain quantity adjustment and incomplete pass-through.
hints: Check whether the shock changes buyers' WTP (shifts Demand), sellers' marginal cost (shifts Supply), or merely moves along an unchanged curve.
Structure your multi-part answer step by step: Correct P=70,Q=50; Correct Q=40 and buyer price=80; Correct.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
- **a)** Set 120−Q=20+Q: Q=50 and P=70. At this quantity the buyers’ marginal willingness to pay equals sellers’ marginal supply cost; quantities demanded and supplied match.
- **b)** 120−Q=40+Q gives Q=40, buyer price=80. Sellers receive 80−20=60. Buyers pay 10 more than before; sellers receive 10 less. Their two changes sum to the 20 wedge.
- **c)** Revenue=20×40=800 NOK. It is transferred from market participants to government, whereas deadweight loss is the net surplus lost from trades no longer made. They are distinct accounting categories.
- **d)** CS=½×50×(120−70)=1,250. PS=½×50×(70−20)=1,250. The tariff raises supply costs and reduces traded quantity. With downward demand and upward supply, the equilibrium moves to a lower quantity along the shifted curve; buyers’ price rises only 10, with sellers bearing the other 10.

questions.promptMarkdown:
Demand is Qd=160−2P and supply Qs=2P. The competitive market has no externalities. A price ceiling of 30 is imposed. Later, consider a separate scenario with higher demand and a production innovation; do not combine it with the ceiling unless explicitly requested.

- **a)** Find competitive equilibrium and interpret a price above it. *(2 marks)*
- **b)** At the ceiling, compute demand, supply, shortage and maximum trade in the simple model. *(3 marks)*
- **c)** Why does a ceiling-induced increase in quantity demanded not mean the demand curve shifted? *(2 marks)*
- **d)** In the separate scenario, demand rises and production costs fall. Explain the equilibrium effects that can be signed without exact magnitudes. *(3 marks)*
rubricChecks: a) Correct P=40,Q=80.
a) Correct excess-supply explanation.
b) Correct Qd=100,Qs=60.
b) Correct shortage=40 and trade limit=60.
b) Explain binding cap/rationing.
c) Identify own-price movement.
c) Give a legitimate shift determinant.
d) Correct two shifts.
d) Correct higher quantity.
d) Correct ambiguous price with explanation.
hints: Check whether the shock changes buyers' WTP (shifts Demand), sellers' marginal cost (shifts Supply), or merely moves along an unchanged curve.
Structure your multi-part answer step by step: Correct P=40,Q=80; Correct Qd=100,Qs=60; Identify own-price movement.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
- **a)** 160−2P=2P gives P=40,Q=80. A higher price creates quantity supplied greater than demanded, exerting downward pressure if prices can adjust.
- **b)** At P=30, Qd=100 and Qs=60. Shortage=40. Without added production or imports, trade is limited to 60, the quantity offered by sellers. Some buyers are rationed. The cap is binding because it lies below equilibrium.
- **c)** The controlled own price changed while the other demand determinants remained fixed. The new quantity is a movement along the existing demand curve. A change in tastes, income or substitute prices would shift demand instead.
- **d)** Demand shifts right and supply down/right. Both effects raise quantity, so equilibrium quantity rises under the standard slopes. Price effects oppose: demand raises price and cheaper production lowers it. Without magnitudes, the price direction is ambiguous.

questions.title: C008 · Benefits and equilibrium unemployment
questions.promptMarkdown:
The supplied WS–PS diagram measures employment N as a percentage of working-age population and real wage on y. Labour force L=90, productivity λ=100 and price-setting real wage=60. Initial employment N*=80. After a benefit increase, the new WS intersects the same PS at N=75. Treat all stated population quantities as the same units.

- **a)** Calculate initial employment, participation and unemployment rates. Explain their denominators. *(2 marks)*
- **b)** Explain why WS slopes up and why higher benefits shift it rather than merely causing movement along it. *(3 marks)*
- **c)** Find the new unemployment rate and explain why real wage stays 60. *(2 marks)*
- **d)** Explain why lower wage offers from unemployed applicants do not automatically eliminate the original unemployment. *(3 marks)*
rubricChecks: a) Correct employment and participation rates.
a) Correct unemployment denominator and 11.11%.
b) Correct effort/job-loss mechanism.
b) Correct benefit shift at every N.
b) Distinguish shift from movement.
c) Correct 16.67%.
c) Correct fixed-PS real-wage explanation.
d) Acceptance versus effort.
d) Employment-rent mechanism.
d) Interpret equilibrium and model assumptions.
hints: Distinguish factors that shift the upward-sloping WS curve (effort/benefits/coordination) from factors that shift the horizontal PS curve ($\lambda$, markup $\sigma$).
Structure your multi-part answer step by step: Correct employment and participation rates; Correct effort/job-loss mechanism; Correct%.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
- **a)** Employment rate=80%; participation=90%. The unemployed are 90−80=10 percentage points of population. Their share of the labour force is 10/90≈11.11%. The remaining 10% of population are outside the labour force.
- **b)** At higher employment, comparable replacement jobs are easier to find, reducing dismissal costs at a fixed wage. Higher pay is then needed for effort. Benefits are a background determinant: raising them improves the fallback at every N, so the whole WS shifts up. A change in N alone would be movement along a fixed WS.
- **c)** Unemployment becomes 90−75=15 population points, or 15/90≈16.67% of labour force. PS remains at 60 because productivity and pricing are unchanged. The new intersection is leftward, at the same height.
- **d)** The model requires a wage high enough to motivate effort after hiring, not only one an applicant accepts. Cutting wages reduces the rent lost on dismissal and can make shirking attractive. At the intersection, WS incentives and PS pricing are compatible; unemployment persists as part of the job-loss deterrent in this stylised model.

questions.title: C009 · Union voice, bargaining and coordination
questions.promptMarkdown:
A model has horizontal PS at a real wage of 80 and upward-sloping WS. Labour force is 100, initially N=85. A voice reform reduces effort disutility and, holding other factors fixed, raises equilibrium employment to 90. A different policy strengthens uncoordinated strike bargaining and lowers equilibrium employment to 80.

- **a)** Explain the difference between the two union mechanisms. *(2 marks)*
- **b)** For each scenario, state the WS shift, real wage and unemployment rate. *(3 marks)*
- **c)** Why is a lower WS curve compatible with workers keeping the same equilibrium purchasing power? *(2 marks)*
- **d)** Explain how coordinated frontfag wage restraint is represented in this course model. Would this automatically raise PS? *(3 marks)*
rubricChecks: a) Explain voice mechanism.
a) Explain bargaining mechanism.
b) Correct voice shift and outcomes.
b) Correct bargaining shift and outcomes.
b) State baseline/conditional assumptions.
c) Explain fixed-N versus final equilibrium.
c) Explain rightward intersection at same PS height.
d) Explain coordination.
d) Correct WS/employment/real-wage result.
d) Distinguish PS determinants from wage-setting coordination.
hints: Order the population from poorest (unemployed) to workers to owners on the Lorenz curve, or separate union strike-threat shifts from coordinated restraint.
Structure your multi-part answer step by step: Explain voice mechanism; Correct voice shift and outcomes; Explain fixed-N versus final equilibrium.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
- **a)** Voice improves work organisation or makes effort less unpleasant, reducing the wage required for effort at each N. Bargaining power through a credible strike threat raises wage demands at each N. These can shift WS in opposite directions.
- **b)** Voice: WS down, wage stays 80, unemployment=(100−90)/100=10%. Bargaining: WS up, wage stays 80, unemployment=20%. Initially unemployment was 15%. These outcomes hold PS and labour force fixed.
- **c)** Lower WS means lower required pay at a fixed employment level. Employment then rises until the new curve meets PS at the original real-wage height of 80. The fixed-N comparison is different from the final equilibrium comparison.
- **d)** Coordination accounts for economy-wide wage-price pressure, employment and competitiveness relative to independent wage demands. It reduces wage pressure and shifts WS down, improving employment with unchanged equilibrium real wage when PS is fixed. It does not itself change productivity or the product-market profit share; separate changes in those determinants would be needed to move PS.

questions.title: C011 · A tourism economy and an income shock
questions.promptMarkdown:
An island has domestic fish producers selling 24 million NOK to restaurants and domestic electricity producers selling 6 million to restaurants. Both input industries have zero purchased intermediate inputs. Restaurants sell meals worth 80 million exclusively to foreign visitors. Separately, a household in this economy learns that its income will fall next year.

- **a)** Calculate value added in each industry and total GDP. *(2 marks)*
- **b)** What are exports from these transactions? If C=30, I=10 and G=5 million with this GDP and X, calculate imports. *(3 marks)*
- **c)** Explain how a forward-looking household’s response differs for temporary and permanent future income losses. *(2 marks)*
- **d)** Real output stops falling after a permanent destruction of productive capacity. Using D1=falling output and D2=output below current normal/potential output, explain why a permanent lower level need not mean permanent recession. *(3 marks)*
rubricChecks: a) Correct industry values.
a) Correct GDP=80 and double-counting explanation.
b) Correct exports and tourism classification.
b) Correct imports=45.
b) Correct net-exports distinction.
c) Temporary versus permanent lifetime-resource effect.
c) Early adjustment and/or credit constraint.
d) Correct D1 reasoning.
d) Correct updated-benchmark D2 reasoning.
d) Separate permanent level loss from continuing recession.
hints: Avoid double-counting intermediate inputs in GDP, check both recession definitions (falling output vs. below potential), and test credit/behavioral limits to smoothing.
Structure your multi-part answer step by step: Correct industry values; Correct exports and tourism classification; Temporary versus permanent lifetime-resource effect.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
- **a)** Fish value added=24, electricity=6, restaurants=80−24−6=50 million. GDP=24+6+50=80 million. Summing all gross sales would double count intermediates.
- **b)** Meals bought by foreign visitors are exports of services, so X=80 million. M=C+I+G+X−GDP=30+10+5+80−80=45 million. Net exports are 35, not 80.
- **c)** With borrowing/saving available, a household can start adjusting when credible news arrives and spread a temporary loss across time, producing a smaller immediate consumption response. A permanent loss reduces lifetime resources more and requires a larger sustained adjustment. Credit constraints may prevent desired smoothing.
- **d)** Under D1, once output stops falling the decline-based recession ends. Under D2, compare actual output with the new productive-capacity benchmark, not automatically with the obsolete pre-destruction trend. If capacity has permanently fallen and actual output equals its new normal, there is no remaining negative output gap. The level loss remains a welfare/resource loss; definitions concern activity relative to a specified benchmark.

questions.title: C012 · CPI, real spending and wage–price pressure
questions.promptMarkdown:
A consumption price index is 100 in 2020, 115 in 2024 and 120.75 in 2025. Nominal consumption in 2025 is 483 units measured on the corresponding spending scale. Nominal wages rise 6% during 2025. A separate WS–PS diagram has PS=60, equilibrium employment N*=80 and a high-employment point B at N=85 with WS=72.

- **a)** Calculate 2025 inflation and interpret CPI=120.75 relative to 2020. *(2 marks)*
- **b)** Find real 2025 consumption at 2020 prices and exact real-wage growth. Label any approximation. *(3 marks)*
- **c)** Read the bargaining gap at B in real-wage units, and explain the resulting pressure. *(2 marks)*
- **d)** Explain why returning to N* does not by itself prove inflation is zero. Distinguish disinflation from deflation. *(3 marks)*
rubricChecks: a) Correct 5%.
a) Correct 20.75% and distinction.
b) Correct consumption=400.
b) Correct exact growth about 0.95%.
b) Clearly distinguish approximation and direction.
c) Correct gap=12 with units.
c) Correct incompatible-claims mechanism.
d) Zero gap does not fix inflation at zero.
d) Explain constant W/P with possible positive nominal growth.
d) Correct definitions of disinflation/deflation.
hints: Compare the real wage required for effort ($w^{WS}$) with the price-setting real wage ($w^{PS}$) to see whether a positive bargaining gap drives a wage–price spiral.
Structure your multi-part answer step by step: Correct%; Correct consumption=400; Correct gap=12 with units.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
- **a)** Inflation=(120.75−115)/115×100=5%. The 2025 basket costs 20.75% more than in 2020, a cumulative base-year comparison distinct from annual inflation.
- **b)** Real consumption=483/120.75×100=400. Exact real-wage growth=(1.06/1.05−1)×100≈0.95%; subtracting rates gives an approximate 1%. Positive inflation does not rule out a real-wage increase when nominal wages rise faster.
- **c)** WS−PS=72−60=12 real-wage units. At employment above N*, workers’ wage-setting requirement exceeds the real wage consistent with firms’ pricing. Wage pressure raises costs and firms can raise prices to protect margins.
- **d)** At N*, WS and PS match and this source of excess wage-price pressure disappears. The numerical inflation rate still depends on expectations or other nominal wage/price dynamics; a constant real wage is compatible with equal positive nominal wage and price growth. Disinflation means slower inflation, possibly with prices still rising; deflation means a falling price level.

questions.title: Exam-Calibrated Q1 · Inequality & Production Functions
questions.promptMarkdown: In a country, the richest $10\%$ of the population has an average annual income of $1,200,000\text{ NOK}$, while the poorest $10\%$ has an average annual income of $150,000\text{ NOK}$. Suppose every inhabitant in both groups receives an unconditional cash transfer of $+30,000\text{ NOK}$. Which statement is **correct**?
options: The rich/poor ratio remains unchanged at $8.0$ because both groups received the exact same amount in kroner.
The rich/poor ratio decreases from $8.0$ to $6.83$.
The rich/poor ratio increases because the absolute income gap in kroner increases.
The rich/poor ratio only changes if both groups' incomes grow by the same percentage.
hints: Start from the exact formula for the income ratio, growth rate, or average/marginal product of labour ($APL = Y/L$, $MPL = \Delta Y/\Delta L$).
Watch out for the classic trap: Equal cash transfers in kroner give a larger percentage boost to the poor (lowering the 90/10 ratio), whereas equal percentage growth leaves the ratio unchanged.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Option: B)**
- **Initial rich/poor ratio**: $\frac{1,200,000}{150,000} = \mathbf{8.0}$.
- **After adding $+30,000\text{ NOK}$ to both**: $\frac{1,230,000}{180,000} = \mathbf{6.833} < 8.0$.
- **Why**: Adding an equal absolute amount in kroner represents a $+20\%$ increase for the poorest $10\%$ ($30\text{k}/150\text{k}$) vs. only $+2.5\%$ for the richest $10\%$ ($30\text{k}/1,200\text{k}$), lowering the ratio. (Equal *percentage* changes leave the ratio unchanged.)
questions.pitfall: Equal cash transfers in kroner give a larger percentage boost to the poor (lowering the 90/10 ratio), whereas equal percentage growth leaves the ratio unchanged.

questions.title: Exam-Calibrated Q2 · Isocost Lines & Technology Choice
questions.promptMarkdown: A firm uses labour ($L$, horizontal axis, wage $w = 400\text{ NOK/hour}$) and energy ($R$, vertical axis, price $p = 200\text{ NOK/unit}$). Which statement about the firm's isocost lines is **correct**?
options: The slope of the isocost lines is $-0.5$, and Technologies $A(4, 10)$ and $B(6, 6)$ lie on the same isocost line.
The slope of the isocost lines is $-2.0$, and Technologies $A(4, 10)$ and $B(6, 6)$ lie on the same isocost line with total cost $3,600\text{ NOK}$.
Technology $B(6, 6)$ dominates Technology $A(4, 10)$ because $6 + 6 < 4 + 10$.
If the wage rises to $w = 600\text{ NOK/hour}$, the isocost lines become flatter.
hints: Write down the total cost equation $C = wL + pR$ (slope $-w/p$) or separate direct cost from the net value of the next-best reservation option.
Watch out for the classic trap: Isocost slope is $-w/p$ (horizontal input price over vertical input price), not $-p/w$; two undominated technologies can share the same total cost.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Option: B)**
- **Slope**: $-\frac{w}{p} = -\frac{400}{200} = \mathbf{-2.0}$.
- **Cost check**: $C(A) = 400(4) + 200(10) = 1,600 + 2,000 = \mathbf{3,600\text{ NOK}}$; $C(B) = 400(6) + 200(6) = 2,400 + 1,200 = \mathbf{3,600\text{ NOK}}$ ($R = 18 - 2L$).Neither dominates the other because $A$ uses less labour while $B$ uses less energy.
questions.pitfall: Isocost slope is $-w/p$ (horizontal input price over vertical input price), not $-p/w$; two undominated technologies can share the same total cost.

questions.title: Exam-Calibrated Q3 · Optimal Choice: $MRS$ vs. $MRT$
questions.promptMarkdown: A worker with hourly wage $w = 300\text{ NOK/hour}$ is currently choosing $14\text{ hours}$ of free time ($10\text{ hours}$ of work) and $3,000\text{ NOK}$ of consumption. At this bundle, her Marginal Rate of Substitution ($MRS$) between free time and consumption is $450\text{ NOK}$. To maximize her utility, what should she do?
options: Keep working $10\text{ hours}$, because $3,000 / 10 = 300 = w$.
Work more hours (reduce free time), because $MRS > MRT$.
Work fewer hours (increase free time), because she values an extra hour of free time ($450\text{ NOK}$) at more than its market opportunity cost ($MRT = 300\text{ NOK}$).
Work more hours, because the substitution effect always dominates when $MRS = 450$.
hints: Compare the subjective willingness to trade ($MRS$, indifference curve steepness) against the market opportunity cost ($MRT = w$, budget slope).
Watch out for the classic trap: When $MRS > MRT$, the worker values an extra hour of free time above the hourly wage $w$, so utility rises by working fewer hours (more free time).
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Option: C)**
- At $(t=14, c=3000)$, $MRS = 450 > MRT = w = 300$. She is willing to give up $450\text{ NOK}$ of consumption to gain $1\text{ hour}$ of free time, whereas the market only requires her to give up $300\text{ NOK}$ in wage income. Moving right along the budget line (**more free time, less work**) increases her utility until $MRS$ falls to $300$.
questions.pitfall: When $MRS > MRT$, the worker values an extra hour of free time above the hourly wage $w$, so utility rises by working fewer hours (more free time).

questions.title: Exam-Calibrated Q4 · Competitive Markets: Shifts vs. Movements Along
questions.promptMarkdown: In a competitive market for Norwegian strawberries, which of the following events will cause a **rightward shift of the demand curve** for strawberries?
options: A fall in the market price of strawberries due to good summer weather.
A subsidy paid to strawberry farmers that lowers their marginal cost of picking berries.
A sharp increase in the price of raspberries (a substitute for strawberries) together with higher household incomes.
The introduction of new harvesting robots on strawberry farms.
hints: Check whether the shock changes buyers' WTP (shifts Demand), sellers' marginal cost (shifts Supply), or merely moves along an unchanged curve.
Watch out for the classic trap: A change in the good's own price causes a movement along the demand curve, whereas farmer subsidies and robots shift the supply curve.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Option: C)**
- A change in the price of strawberries (**A**) causes a **movement along** the demand curve. Farmer subsidies (**B**) and harvesting robots (**D**) lower marginal cost and shift the **supply curve** right. Higher price of a substitute (raspberries) and higher income (**C**) shift the **demand curve** right.
questions.pitfall: A change in the good's own price causes a movement along the demand curve, whereas farmer subsidies and robots shift the supply curve.

questions.title: Exam-Calibrated Q5 · Labour Market Statistics Trap
questions.promptMarkdown: In an economy with a working-age population of $2,000,000$, there are $1,300,000$ employed workers and $100,000$ unemployed workers. Suppose $100,000$ previously inactive students graduate and enter the labour force: $60,000$ immediately start jobs and $40,000$ are actively searching for work. What happens to the **employment rate** and the **unemployment rate**?
options: The employment rate increases from $65.0\%$ to $68.0\%$, and the unemployment rate **also increases** from $7.14\%$ to $9.33\%$.
Since the employment rate increases by $3.0$ percentage points, the unemployment rate must fall by $3.0$ percentage points.
Both the employment rate and the unemployment rate decrease because the labour force is larger.
The employment rate increases from $92.86\%$ to $90.67\%$.
hints: Distinguish factors that shift the upward-sloping WS curve (effort/benefits/coordination) from factors that shift the horizontal PS curve ($\lambda$, markup $\sigma$).
Watch out for the classic trap: Employment rate divides by working-age population while unemployment rate divides by the labour force—both rates can rise simultaneously when inactive graduates enter!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Option: A)**
- **Initial state**: $\text{Labour Force}_0 = 1,300\text{k} + 100\text{k} = 1,400\text{k}$.
  $$\text{Employment Rate}_0 = \frac{1,300\text{k}}{2,000\text{k}} = \mathbf{65.0\%}, \qquad \text{Unemployment Rate}_0 = \frac{100\text{k}}{1,400\text{k}} = \mathbf{7.14\%}$$
- **New state**: $\text{Employed}_1 = 1,360\text{k}$, $\text{Unemployed}_1 = 140\text{k}$, $\text{Labour Force}_1 = 1,500\text{k}$.
  $$\text{Employment Rate}_1 = \frac{1,360\text{k}}{2,000\text{k}} = \mathbf{68.0\%} \ (\uparrow), \qquad \text{Unemployment Rate}_1 = \frac{140\text{k}}{1,500\text{k}} = \mathbf{9.33\%} \ (\uparrow)$$
questions.pitfall: Employment rate divides by working-age population while unemployment rate divides by the labour force—both rates can rise simultaneously when inactive graduates enter!

questions.title: Exam-Calibrated Q6 · WS–PS Model & Equilibrium Real Wage
questions.promptMarkdown: In the macroeconomic WS–PS model, which of the following changes will **increase the equilibrium real wage ($w^*$)** in the economy?
options: A reduction in the disutility of effort due to better workplace ergonomics.
An increase in the unemployment benefit replacement rate from $62\%$ to $75\%$.
Coordinated wage restraint via the Norwegian *frontfag* model.
The entry of new competing firms in the product market (or an increase in labour productivity $\lambda$).
hints: Distinguish factors that shift the upward-sloping WS curve (effort/benefits/coordination) from factors that shift the horizontal PS curve ($\lambda$, markup $\sigma$).
Watch out for the classic trap: Shifts of the WS curve change equilibrium employment $N^*$ without changing $w^*$ because the PS curve is horizontal at $\lambda(1-\sigma)$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Option: D)**
- Options **A**, **B**, and **C** all shift the **upward-sloping WS curve** (changing equilibrium employment $N^*$ while leaving the equilibrium real wage unchanged along the horizontal PS curve). Only **D** shifts the **horizontal PS curve upward** ($w^{PS} = \lambda(1-\sigma)$), increasing **both** the equilibrium real wage $w^*$ and employment $N^*$.
questions.pitfall: Shifts of the WS curve change equilibrium employment $N^*$ without changing $w^*$ because the PS curve is horizontal at $\lambda(1-\sigma)$.

questions.title: Exam-Calibrated Q7 · Opportunity Cost & Economic Rent (`Spring 2025 Part 2 Q1` Style
questions.promptMarkdown:
You have won a free, non-refundable ticket to an outdoor concert this Saturday afternoon, which gives you a subjective enjoyment benefit of $900\text{ NOK}$, but standing in the rain has a discomfort cost of $150\text{ NOK}$. Your best alternative use of Saturday afternoon is working an extra shift at a café, which pays $800\text{ NOK}$ in wages and has an effort disutility of $250\text{ NOK}$.
1. What is the **opportunity cost** and the **economic cost** of attending the concert?
2. What is the **economic rent** of attending the concert, and should you go?
rubricChecks: Compute net value of concert (900 - 150 = 750 NOK) and café reservation option (800 - 250 = 550 NOK)
State opportunity cost (550 NOK) and economic cost (150 + 550 = 700 NOK)
Calculate positive economic rent (+200 NOK) and conclude to attend
hints: Write down the total cost equation $C = wL + pR$ (slope $-w/p$) or separate direct cost from the net value of the next-best reservation option.
Watch out for the classic trap: Opportunity cost is the net value (benefit minus effort cost) of the best foregone alternative, never the gross wage alone.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
1. **Net value of each option**:
   - **Concert (chosen option A)**: $\text{Benefit } (900\text{ NOK}) - \text{Direct discomfort cost } (150\text{ NOK}) = \mathbf{750\text{ NOK}}$.
   - **Working at the café (reservation option B)**: $\text{Wage } (800\text{ NOK}) - \text{Effort disutility } (250\text{ NOK}) = \mathbf{550\text{ NOK}}$.
   - The **opportunity cost** of attending the concert is the net value of the best foregone alternative (working at the café): **$550\text{ NOK}$**.
   - The **economic cost** of attending the concert is the sum of its direct cost and opportunity cost: $150\text{ NOK} + 550\text{ NOK} = \mathbf{700\text{ NOK}}$.
2. **Economic rent and decision**:
   $$\text{Economic Rent} = \text{Net Value}(\text{Concert}) - \text{Opportunity Cost} = 750 - 550 = \mathbf{200\text{ NOK}} \quad (= 900 - 700)$$
   Because the economic rent is strictly positive ($+200\text{ NOK} > 0$), **yes, you should attend the concert**.
questions.pitfall: Opportunity cost is the net value (benefit minus effort cost) of the best foregone alternative, never the gross wage alone.

questions.promptMarkdown:
Sofia works $37.5\text{ hours per week}$ at an hourly wage of $160\text{ NOK/hour}$. Her disutility of work effort is $25\text{ NOK/hour}$. 1. Calculate Sofia's **employment rent per hour** and her **total employment rent**.
2. Suppose instead that we measure payoffs weekly: Sofia's weekly reservation wage is $w_r = 6,000\text{ NOK}$, weekly effort cost is $c = 1,200\text{ NOK}$, her planning horizon is $h = 80\text{ weeks}$, and a shirking worker is caught and fired after $s = 20\text{ weeks}$. Calculate the firm's minimum **no-shirking weekly wage $w^{NS}$**.
rubricChecks: Compute net hourly employed value (135 NOK/h), unemployed value (50 NOK/h), and hourly rent (85 NOK/h)
Multiply by expected unemployment hours (37.5 * 32 = 1,200 h) to get 102,000 NOK total employment rent
Equate shirking gain (c*s) to lost rent to find no-shirking weekly wage w^NS = 7,600 NOK/week
hints: Separate net hourly value when employed ($w - c$) from net hourly value when unemployed ($b - s$), and multiply only over expected unemployment duration.
Watch out for the classic trap: Multiply hourly employment rent only by expected hours of unemployment ($37.5 \times 32$), not the entire 120-week planning horizon.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
1. **Sofia's Employment Rent**:
   - **Net hourly value when employed**: $w - c = 160 - 25 = \mathbf{135\text{ NOK/hour}}$.
   - **Net hourly value when unemployed**: $b - s = 65 - 15 = \mathbf{50\text{ NOK/hour}}$.
   - **Employment rent per hour**: $135 - 50 = \mathbf{85\text{ NOK/hour}}$.
   - **Expected hours of unemployment**: $37.5\text{ hours/week} \times 32\text{ weeks} = \mathbf{1,200\text{ hours}}$ *(weeks 33–120 are identical in both states and do not affect the cost of job loss)*.
   - **Total Employment Rent**: $85\text{ NOK/hour} \times 1,200\text{ hours} = \mathbf{102,000\text{ NOK}}$.
2. **Minimum No-Shirking Weekly Wage ($w^{NS}$)**:
   Equating the effort cost saved during the $s = 20$ weeks of shirking ($\text{Area A} = c \cdot s$) with the employment rent lost during the remaining $h - s = 60$ weeks ($\text{Area B} = (w - c - w_r)(h - s)$):
   $$w^{NS} = w_r + c + \left(\frac{s}{h - s}\right)c = 6,000 + 1,200 + \left(\frac{20}{80 - 20}\right)(1,200) = 7,200 + 400 = \mathbf{7,600\text{ NOK/week}}$$
questions.pitfall: Multiply hourly employment rent only by expected hours of unemployment ($37.5 \times 32$), not the entire 120-week planning horizon.

questions.title: Exam-Calibrated Q9 · Value-Added GDP & Two Recession Definitions (`Topic 8 Ex. 1–3` Style
questions.promptMarkdown:
In a small island economy with no government ($G=0$), fisherfolk catch fish worth $20\text{ million NOK}$ using $0$ intermediate inputs and sell all the fish to local restaurants. The restaurants buy $20\text{ million NOK}$ of fish and $5\text{ million NOK}$ of electricity (produced domestically with $0$ inputs) and sell meals worth $70\text{ million NOK}$ exclusively to foreign cruise tourists.
1. Calculate the economy's **GDP** using the value-added method and state the size of **Exports ($X$)**.
2. Suppose a volcanic eruption permanently destroys half of the island's fishing grounds, permanently lowering the economy's output level by $30\%$. Is the island in a permanent recession under **Definition 1** and **Definition 2** of a recession?
rubricChecks: Sum sector value added (20 + 5 + 45 = 70 million NOK GDP) and identify Exports X = 70 million NOK
Evaluate Definition 1 (recession only while output is actively falling during transition)
Evaluate Definition 2 (not a permanent recession because potential/normal capacity permanently fell)
hints: Avoid double-counting intermediate inputs in GDP, check both recession definitions (falling output vs. below potential), and test credit/behavioral limits to smoothing.
Watch out for the classic trap: Subtract intermediate fish and electricity inputs from restaurant sales to avoid double counting, and note a permanent capacity loss resets 'normal' output.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
1. **Value-Added GDP and Exports**:
   - **Fisherfolk value added**: $20 - 0 = 20\text{ mill. NOK}$.
   - **Electricity value added**: $5 - 0 = 5\text{ mill. NOK}$.
   - **Restaurants value added**: $70 - (20 + 5) = 45\text{ mill. NOK}$.
   - **Total GDP**: $\sum \text{Value Added} = 20 + 5 + 45 = \mathbf{70\text{ million NOK}}$ (which equals the market value of final meals sold to end-users, avoiding double counting of fish and electricity).
   - Because all meals are sold to foreign tourists, **Exports $X = \mathbf{70\text{ million NOK}}$**.
2. **Recession Definitions**:
   - **Definition 1 (Output is declining / negative growth)**: The economy is in a recession **only during the transition period while GDP is actively falling** by $30\%$; once output stabilizes at the lower level, the recession is over.
   - **Definition 2 (Output is below its normal/potential level)**: **No**, it is not a permanent recession because the volcanic eruption permanently reduced the island's productive capacity—the $30\%$ lower output is the economy's **"new normal"**.
questions.pitfall: Subtract intermediate fish and electricity inputs from restaurant sales to avoid double counting, and note a permanent capacity loss resets 'normal' output.

questions.title: Exam-Calibrated Q10 · Conflicting Claims & the Wage–Price Spiral (`V2026 Exam Part 2 Q3` Style
questions.promptMarkdown: Using the wage-setting and price-setting (WS–PS) model, explain how **persistent inflation** can arise from **conflicting claims on output** when aggregate demand is high and unemployment is low, and explain how an increase in unemployment dampens inflation. *(Max 200 words)*
rubricChecks: Define PS real wage w^PS = lambda(1 - sigma) and upward-sloping WS curve
Explain positive bargaining gap (w^WS > w^PS) when N > N* and resulting nominal wage-price spiral
Explain how higher unemployment raises cost of job loss and dampens nominal wage demands
hints: Compare the real wage required for effort ($w^{WS}$) with the price-setting real wage ($w^{PS}$) to see whether a positive bargaining gap drives a wage–price spiral.
Watch out for the classic trap: At low unemployment ($N > N^*$), $w^{WS} > w^{PS}$ creates conflicting claims exceeding $\lambda$, driving alternating $W \uparrow$ and $P \uparrow$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
In the WS–PS model, each worker produces $\lambda$ units of output, which is divided between the worker's real wage ($w$) and the firm's profit per worker ($\lambda - w$). The horizontal **PS curve** represents the real wage $w^{PS} = \lambda(1-\sigma)$ consistent with firms' profit-maximizing price markup $\sigma$, while the upward-sloping **WS curve** shows the real wage $w^{WS}$ needed to motivate workers at each employment level.

When aggregate demand is high and unemployment is low ($N > N^*$), the WS curve lies **above** the PS curve ($w^{WS} > w^{PS}$). There are **conflicting claims**: workers' real wage demands plus firms' target profit share exceed $100\%$ of output per worker $\lambda$ (a positive **bargaining gap**). Low unemployment reduces the cost of job loss, forcing firms to raise **nominal wages ($W \uparrow$)** to recruit and retain workers. Higher wage costs squeeze profit margins, so firms respond by raising **prices ($P \uparrow$)** to restore their markup $\sigma$. This erodes the real wage back to $w^{PS}$, triggering a continuous **wage–price spiral**.

Higher unemployment increases workers' fear of job loss (employment rent), weakening nominal wage demands and shrinking the bargaining gap, which slows cost and price growth (**disinflation**).
questions.pitfall: At low unemployment ($N > N^*$), $w^{WS} > w^{PS}$ creates conflicting claims exceeding $\lambda$, driving alternating $W \uparrow$ and $P \uparrow$.
